Section 01

Agency Operating Manual

1.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Operating Manual

1. Purpose of This Manual

This manual explains what Shawcliffe Digital is, how we think, what we sell, who we serve, what we avoid, and how we keep the business simple enough to run as a husband-and-wife agency.

This is not meant to be corporate bureaucracy.

This is meant to help us:

  • Sell clearly
  • Build repeatably
  • Deliver professionally
  • Avoid scope creep
  • Get paid
  • Support clients without chaos
  • Turn custom projects into reusable systems
  • Build archetype-specific templates over time
  • Grow monthly recurring revenue

The core rule:

Shawcliffe Digital does not sell random apps. We build simple business systems for local owner-operated businesses.

1.2 What Shawcliffe Digital Does

Plain-English Description

Shawcliffe Digital helps local owner-operated businesses turn customer interest into real leads, bookings, sales, reviews, and repeat business using simple digital systems.

We build:

  • Websites
  • Landing pages
  • Lead capture systems
  • Booking and inquiry systems
  • Quote request systems
  • Simple web/mobile apps
  • Owner dashboards
  • SMS/email/push notifications
  • Review request systems
  • QR code business cards and signage
  • Google Business Profile support
  • Local SEO basics
  • Simple automation systems
  • Ongoing support and maintenance plans

But internally, we do not think of these as separate random services.

We think of them as components inside a repeatable business system.

The Shawcliffe Digital Core Offer

We help local business owners stop losing customers because of:

  • Missed calls
  • Slow replies
  • Disorganized texts
  • Facebook message chaos
  • No clear website
  • Outdated prices
  • No booking process
  • No quote request process
  • No follow-up
  • No review system
  • Customers not knowing what is available
  • Customers not knowing whether the business is open
  • Owners doing everything manually

We replace that chaos with:

  • A professional online presence
  • A clear path for customers to inquire, book, order, or request a quote
  • A simple owner-facing dashboard
  • Automated notifications
  • Basic customer tracking
  • Follow-up systems
  • Review requests
  • Repeatable workflows

Simple Internal Positioning Statement

Use this whenever we need to explain the company quickly.

Shawcliffe Digital builds simple websites, apps, and customer systems for local owner-operated businesses so they can get more leads, save time, look professional, and stop losing customers through missed calls, messy messages, and manual admin.

Shorter Version

We build practical digital systems for local businesses that need more customers and less chaos.

Even Shorter Sales Version

We help small local businesses turn interest into booked work.

1.3 Who Shawcliffe Digital Serves

Shawcliffe Digital serves local owner-operated businesses.

These are businesses where the owner is usually still directly involved in the day-to-day work.

They may be:

  • Cutting hair
  • Cleaning houses
  • Baking cakes
  • Grooming dogs
  • Teaching lessons
  • Fixing vehicles
  • Selling produce
  • Giving quotes
  • Answering customer messages
  • Managing bookings
  • Posting updates manually
  • Trying to look professional while doing everything themselves

Our Ideal Client

An ideal Shawcliffe Digital client is:

TraitWhat It Means
Owner-operatedThe owner cares deeply because the business is personal.
LocalThe business serves a city, town, neighbourhood, parish, market, region, or service area.
PracticalThey want something that works, not a flashy tech toy.
BusyThey are losing time to admin, messages, quoting, scheduling, or updates.
Customer-facingThey need customers to contact them, book, buy, visit, or request service.
Reputation-basedReviews, referrals, and professionalism matter.
Willing to improveThey may not be tech-savvy, but they know something needs to change.
Able to pay somethingThey understand that professional help costs money.

Our 12 Main Business Archetypes

Shawcliffe Digital organizes clients into 12 main archetypes.

These archetypes are not just marketing categories. They are the foundation of our templates, sales scripts, discovery questions, proposal structure, pricing logic, component roadmap, and SOPs.

#ArchetypeExamples
1Personal Care Appointment BusinessesBarbers, hairdressers, nail techs, lash techs, massage therapists
2Home Service TradesWelders, plumbers, HVAC techs, electricians, handymen
3Home & Property MaintenanceCleaners, lawn care, snow removal, landscapers
4Food Producers & Specialty MakersBakers, cake makers, meal prep sellers, chocolatiers
5Mobile / Pop-Up SellersFruit stands, honey sellers, farmers’ market vendors, food trucks
6Pet & Animal ServicesDog groomers, pet sitters, dog walkers, trainers
7Vehicle & Equipment ServicesMobile mechanics, detailers, tire services, small engine repair
8Creative & Event ServicesPhotographers, DJs, videographers, florists, event planners
9Education, Coaching & InstructionTutors, music teachers, swimming instructors, martial arts coaches
10Health-Adjacent Local ProfessionalsPhysiotherapists, chiropractors, doulas, wellness clinics
11Local Retail / Boutique ShopsGift shops, thrift shops, boutiques, hobby shops
12Professional Local ServicesBookkeepers, tax preparers, consultants, notaries

1.4 What Shawcliffe Digital Is Not

This is important.

Shawcliffe Digital is not trying to be everything for everyone.

We Are Not

  • A giant marketing agency
  • A bloated software consultancy
  • A cheap “I will build anything” freelancer shop
  • A high-pressure ad agency
  • A Silicon Valley startup selling complicated SaaS to everyone
  • A design studio that only cares about aesthetics
  • A custom development company that reinvents every project from scratch
  • A “yes to everything” agency

We Should Avoid Projects That Are

Avoid ThisWhy
Vague “I need an app” ideas with no business caseHigh risk, unclear value, likely scope creep
Clients who want everything custom but have a tiny budgetBad fit and stressful

Clients who want complex marketplaces or social platformsToo big for our current model
Clients who want us to manage their whole businessNot our role
Clients who are hostile, disorganized, or disrespectful earlyThey will likely get worse

1.5 Shawcliffe Digital’s Positioning

Our Market Position

Shawcliffe Digital sits between:

  • DIY tools like Wix, Squarespace, Google Forms, Facebook pages, Calendly, Linktree, and spreadsheets
  • Large agencies that are too expensive, slow, or bloated for small owner-operated businesses
  • Custom software firms that build complex systems most local businesses do not need

Our position:

We build practical, professional, lightweight business systems for local owner-operators who have outgrown messy manual processes but do not need enterprise software.

Why Clients Would Hire Us Instead of DIY

Many clients can technically use DIY tools.

But the problem is usually not just the tool.

The problem is:

  • They do not know what to build
  • They do not know how the pieces connect
  • They do not have time
  • They do not want to fiddle with settings
  • Their website, forms, messages, and follow-up are disconnected
  • Their brand looks inconsistent
  • They forget to follow up
  • They do not know which system fits their business
  • They need someone to simplify the whole thing

Our answer:

You could piece this together yourself, but most busy owners do not have time to design the whole customer journey. We set up a simple system that fits how your business actually works.

Why Clients Would Hire Us Instead of a Big Agency

Big agencies may be better for:

  • Large ad budgets
  • Full brand campaigns
  • Corporate clients
  • Complex SEO retainers
  • Large content teams
  • Multi-location businesses

But many owner-operators need something simpler.

They need:

  • A better way to receive leads
  • A better way to book work
  • A better way to show services/prices
  • A better way to request reviews
  • A better way to update status or availability
  • A better way to follow up

Our answer:

You do not need a giant agency. You need a practical system that helps customers contact you, book you, pay you, review you, and come back.

1.6 Shawcliffe Digital’s Values

These values should guide sales, design, development, support, pricing, and client communication.

1. Practical Over Flashy

We build systems that solve real business problems.

A beautiful website that does not generate leads is not enough.

A fancy app that the owner never uses is a failure.

A simple form that brings in quote requests may be more valuable than an overdesigned app.

Internal rule:

Build the simplest useful version first.

2. Honest Sales

We do not scare, manipulate, exaggerate, or overpromise.

We explain the problem clearly, show the opportunity, and recommend a realistic next step.

Internal rule:

Sell value, not panic.

3. Local Business Respect

Owner-operators are not stupid because their systems are messy.

They are busy.

Many are doing the work, answering the phone, dealing with customers, quoting jobs, buying supplies, posting online, and handling family life.

Internal rule:

Respect the owner’s reality.

4. Repeatability

Every project should make future projects easier.

If we build something once, we ask:

  • Can this become a reusable component?
  • Can this become part of an archetype template?
  • Can this improve our sales script?
  • Can this become an SOP?
  • Can this become a demo?
  • Can this become a case study?

Internal rule:

Do not just deliver the project. Improve the system.

5. Simplicity for Clients

Most clients do not want to learn software.

They want to tap a button, update a field, see a lead, reply to a customer, or know what to do next.

Internal rule:

The owner dashboard must be simpler than the chaos it replaces.

6. Clear Boundaries

A small agency dies by unlimited informal requests.

We need to be friendly, but firm.

Internal rule:

Friendly does not mean unlimited.

7. Get Paid Properly

We should not begin serious build work without clear scope, written approval, and payment terms.

Internal rule:

No clear scope, no build. No payment, no launch.

1.7 Our Service Philosophy

We Build Business Systems, Not Random Digital Objects

A website by itself may not solve the business problem.

A booking form by itself may not solve the business problem.

A QR code by itself may not solve the business problem.

A dashboard by itself may not solve the business problem.

The system matters.

1.8 Our Archetype / Template Strategy

Why Archetypes Matter

We cannot treat every client as a blank-page custom project.

That creates:

  • Too much discovery work
  • Too much custom planning
  • Too much design variation
  • Too much development time
  • Too much testing complexity
  • Too much pricing confusion
  • Too much support chaos

Instead, Shawcliffe Digital uses 12 archetypes as repeatable template categories.

Each archetype has predictable patterns:

  • Similar customer problems
  • Similar owner problems
  • Similar missed-money opportunities
  • Similar component needs
  • Similar sales language
  • Similar onboarding questions
  • Similar project scopes
  • Similar upsells
  • Similar support needs

Internal Rule

First classify the client by archetype. Then choose components. Then customize only what matters.

Archetype Classification Questions

When evaluating a lead, ask:

  • Does the business mostly sell appointments?
  • Does the business mostly quote jobs?
  • Does the business sell products with changing availability?
  • Does the business operate from changing locations?
  • Does the business manage recurring clients?
  • Does the business need profiles for properties, pets, vehicles, or students?
  • Does the business need customers to upload photos/files?
  • Does the business need deposits or payments?
  • Does the business rely heavily on reviews?
  • Does the business need follow-up to turn leads into customers?

Quick Archetype Decision Guide

If the client says…Likely Archetype
“People message me to book.”Personal Care, Pet Services, Education, Health-Adjacent
“I need people to send photos before I quote.”Home Trades, Vehicle Services, Creative/Event
“I have repeat weekly/monthly clients.”Cleaning, Lawn Care, Pet Care, Coaching
“Customers ask what I have today.”Food Makers, Mobile/Pop-Up Sellers, Retail
“I move locations or sell at markets.”Mobile/Pop-Up Sellers, Food Trucks, Vendors
“I need intake forms or documents.”Health-Adjacent, Professional Services, Education
“I need to track pets.”Pet & Animal Services
“I need to track vehicles.”Vehicle & Equipment Services
“I need to track homes/properties.”Home & Property Maintenance
“I need to track students.”Education, Coaching & Instruction

1.9 Our Reusable Component Strategy

What a Component Is

A component is a reusable piece of a business system.

Examples:

  • Business Profile
  • Service / Product Menu
  • Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
  • Admin Dashboard
  • Notifications
  • Review Request System
  • Booking Request System
  • Photo / File Upload
  • Payments / Deposits
  • Status Tracker
  • Product Inventory / Limited Batch
  • Location / Pop-Up Tracker
  • Property Profiles
  • Pet Profiles
  • Vehicle Profiles
  • Student / Progress Profiles

A component should be reusable across multiple archetypes.

Why Components Matter

Components help us:

  • Build faster
  • Price more clearly
  • Avoid reinventing features
  • Create template packages
  • Train ourselves and future help
  • Test more consistently
  • Support clients more easily
  • Create demos
  • Sell based on business problems
  • Grow recurring revenue

Internal Component Rule

Every feature should either be a reusable component, a client-specific customization, or rejected as out of scope.

No vague middle ground.

1.11 What Kinds of Projects We Avoid

Hard No or Usually No

Avoid projects where:

Polite Decline Language

Use this when a project is not a fit.

Thanks for thinking of us. After looking at what you need, I do not think Shawcliffe Digital is the right fit for this particular project. We focus on practical websites, lead systems, booking systems, quote request systems, and simple owner dashboards for local owner-operated businesses. Your project sounds like it may need a larger custom development team or a more specialized provider. I would rather be honest than overpromise.

1.13 Balancing Custom Work with Reusable Systems

This is one of the most important operating principles.

Shawcliffe Digital must not become trapped in endless custom work.

But we also cannot sound like we are forcing every client into a rigid cookie-cutter template.

The balance:

The system is repeatable. The details are customized.

What Should Be Repeatable

  • Discovery process
  • Archetype classification
  • Proposal structure
  • Contract structure
  • Project workflow
  • Component library
  • QA checklists
  • Launch process
  • Support process
  • Pricing logic
  • Onboarding emails
  • Training documents
  • Starter layouts
  • Dashboard patterns
  • Form structures
  • Notification flows
  • Review request workflows

What Should Be Customized

  • Business name
  • Brand colors
  • Logo
  • Photos
  • Services/products
  • Prices
  • Location/service area
  • Tone of copy
  • Specific intake questions
  • Specific business rules
  • Specific dashboard labels
  • Specific customer-facing language
  • Specific add-ons

What Should Be Avoided Unless Paid For

  • Custom feature logic not useful to future clients
  • Complex integrations
  • Unusual workflows
  • Unlimited page design variations
  • Custom animations
  • Custom reporting dashboards
  • Complex user permissions
  • Multi-role systems
  • Special-case automations
  • Manual content loading beyond agreed scope

Internal Decision Rule for Custom Requests

When a client asks for a feature, ask:

  • Does this solve a real business problem?
  • Is this required for launch?
  • Is this useful for their archetype?
  • Can it become a reusable component?
  • Can it become a paid add-on?
  • Will it create support headaches?
  • Is it included in the current scope?
  • Should this wait until Phase 2?

Scope Response Template

Use this when a client asks for something outside the agreed scope.

That is a good idea, and it may be worth adding. It is not included in the current project scope, which is focused on getting your core system launched. We can either save it for a future upgrade, or I can price it as an add-on before we build it.

1.14 How We Keep Things Simple for Owner-Operators

Owner-operators are busy.

They do not want complicated software.

They want:

  • Fewer missed leads
  • Fewer repetitive messages
  • A better way to manage customers
  • A professional look
  • Simple updates
  • Clear notifications
  • Less admin
  • More booked work

Simplicity Rules

1. The Customer Path Must Be Obvious

Every customer-facing page should answer:

  • What do you do?
  • Who do you help?
  • Where do you serve?
  • How do I contact/book/order/request?
  • What happens after I submit?

2. The Owner Dashboard Must Be Simple

The owner should not need a manual for basic actions.

They should be able to:

  • Update hours
  • Update prices
  • Add/remove services
  • Mark open/closed/sold out
  • View leads
  • Respond to inquiries
  • Send or trigger review requests
  • Update availability
  • Check basic customer info

3. Fewer Buttons Are Better

Do not give the owner 40 settings if they need 5.

4. Use Their Language

Do not say:

  • “Manage dynamic inventory states”
  • “Configure lead pipeline object”
  • “Update metadata”

Say:

  • “Update today’s products”
  • “View new quote requests”
  • “Mark sold out”
  • “Send review request”

5. Build Around Their Workday

A cleaner may update recurring jobs at night.

A fruit seller may update inventory early morning and during the day.

A barber may check booking requests between clients.

A contractor may review quote requests in the evening.

The system should fit real life.

1.15 Shawcliffe Digital Project Filter

Before accepting a project, run it through this filter.

Project Fit Checklist

QuestionYes/No
Does the client fit one of our 12 archetypes?
Can we explain the business problem clearly?
Can we solve most of the problem with existing/reusable components?
Is the client realistic about budget and timeline?
Does the client understand what is included and not included?
Will this project help us improve a template, component, case study, or process?
Is there a monthly support or recurring revenue opportunity?
Can the owner realistically use the system?
Are we avoiding legal/compliance complexity we are not ready for?
Are we willing to work with this person for months or years?

Rule:

If we cannot confidently answer “yes” to most of these, pause before accepting.

1.17 Common Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Selling “Apps” Too Early

Many local owners do not wake up thinking, “I need an app.”

They think:

  • I need more customers
  • I missed another call
  • People keep asking the same questions
  • I forgot to reply
  • I need more reviews
  • My Facebook page is messy
  • Customers do not know if I am open
  • I need people to send better quote info

Better language:

“We build a simple system so customers can contact you, request service, and get updates without everything turning into texts and missed calls.”

Mistake 2: Saying Yes to Every Custom Request

Custom work feels exciting, but it can destroy profit.

Before saying yes, ask:

  • Is it in scope?
  • Is it reusable?
  • Is it paid?
  • Is it necessary for launch?
  • Will it create support burden?

Mistake 3: Building Before Scope Is Clear

Do not start serious development from a vague conversation.

Minimum needed:

  • Archetype
  • Business goal
  • Components included
  • Pages/screens included
  • Client responsibilities
  • Timeline
  • Price
  • Payment terms
  • Revision limits
  • Launch requirements

Mistake 4: Making the Dashboard Too Complicated

The dashboard should be boring and useful.

A business owner should be able to understand it while tired, distracted, and on their phone.

Mistake 5: Forgetting Monthly Revenue

A one-time build is good.

A one-time build plus support is better.

A reusable system with monthly support, hosting, notifications, review requests, CRM Lite, reporting, and improvements is stronger.

Every proposal should ask:

What would make sense for ongoing support?

Mistake 6: Acting Too Corporate

Local owner-operators do not need corporate jargon.

Use normal language.

Say:

  • “Here’s how customers will contact you.”
  • “Here’s where the quote requests go.”
  • “Here’s what you’ll update from your phone.”
  • “Here’s what is included.”
  • “Here’s what would be an add-on.”
  • “Here’s what happens after launch.”

1.18 Shawcliffe Digital Operating Principles

These are the internal rules that should guide daily decisions.

1. Start With the Business Problem

Not:

What app should we build?

Ask:

Where is this owner losing time, leads, money, reviews, or repeat business?

2. Classify by Archetype

Every lead should be assigned one primary archetype.

Some clients may overlap, but pick the main one.

Example:

  • A dog groomer with retail products is still primarily Pet & Animal Services.
  • A baker selling at markets is likely Food Producers & Specialty Makers, with Mobile / Pop-Up Seller elements.
  • A martial arts school is Education, Coaching & Instruction, even if it has memberships.

3. Choose Components Intentionally

Do not throw all 24 components into every project.

A starter website may only need:

  • Business Profile
  • Service / Product Menu
  • Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
  • Notifications

A more advanced system may add:

  • Admin Dashboard
  • CRM Lite
  • Review Request System
  • Booking Request System
  • Payments / Deposits

4. Sell the Outcome

Do not lead with:

We will build you a React app with a dashboard.

Lead with:

Customers will be able to request a quote, upload photos, and you will get the details in one place instead of chasing messages.

5. Protect the Build

Every project needs:

  • Clear scope
  • Client homework
  • Asset collection
  • Payment terms
  • Revision limits
  • Launch checklist
  • Support handoff

6. Improve the System After Every Project

After each launch, document:

  • What archetype was this?
  • Which components were used?
  • What did we reuse?
  • What did we build new?
  • What should become a template?
  • What caused confusion?
  • What should be added to the SOP?
  • What could become an upsell?

We will help you create a clear, professional, practical digital system that fits how your business actually works. We will keep it simple, avoid unnecessary complexity, and focus on helping customers take action — contact you, book you, request a quote, check availability, leave a review, or come back again.

  • Create one starter offer for a second archetype, such as barbers, cleaners, or contractors.

Build Soon

  • Archetype-specific discovery questions
  • Component library documentation
  • QA checklist
  • Launch checklist
  • Client onboarding email
  • Scope/change request policy
  • Monthly support plan descriptions

Nice Later

  • Full internal wiki
  • Video training library
  • Advanced reporting templates
  • AI receptionist workflows
  • Deep automation library
  • Formal hiring/training docs
  • Template marketplace-style catalog

1.23 Common Internal Decisions

Which Archetypes Should We Start With?

For early Shawcliffe Digital, prioritize archetypes that have clear, easy-to-explain pain.

Strong early options:

ArchetypeWhy It Is Strong
Mobile / Pop-Up SellersClear live status/inventory problem; great demo potential
Home Service TradesStrong quote request and photo upload need
Home & Property MaintenanceRecurring clients and scheduling pain
Personal Care Appointment BusinessesBooking, reviews, rebooking, customer retention
Pet & Animal ServicesBooking plus pet profiles is easy to understand
Food Producers & Specialty MakersMenus, preorders, batches, availability

Which Components Should We Build First?

Early components with the widest use:

  • Business Profile
  • Service / Product Menu
  • Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
  • Notifications
  • Admin Dashboard
  • Booking Request System
  • Photo / File Upload
  • Review Request System
  • Customer Database / CRM Lite
  • Status Tracker
  • Product Inventory / Limited Batch
  • Location / Pop-Up Tracker

These cover many starter systems without getting too advanced.

1.24 Definition of Done for Section 1

This section is complete when Shawcliffe Digital has:

  • A clear explanation of what the agency does
  • A clear definition of who the agency serves
  • A clear “business systems, not apps” philosophy
  • A practical positioning statement
  • A working archetype strategy
  • A working reusable component strategy
  • A project acceptance filter
  • A project avoidance list
  • A definition of project success
  • A custom-vs-repeatable decision framework
  • A simple explanation of how to keep systems owner-friendly
  • Copy/paste language for sales and boundaries
  • Immediate action items for implementation

1.25 Key Takeaways

  • Shawcliffe Digital should not position itself as “an app builder.”
  • The stronger position is: simple business systems for local owner-operators.
  • The 12 archetypes prevent every project from becoming custom chaos.
  • The 24 reusable components make sales, pricing, building, QA, support, and upgrades easier.
  • The agency should customize business details, not reinvent the entire system every time.
  • Small agency survival depends on clear scope, payment terms, reusable systems, and support boundaries.
  • Every client project should improve the internal machine: templates, components, SOPs, demos, or case studies.

1.26 Questions to Answer Before Moving to Section 2

Before building the full archetype strategy, Shawcliffe Digital should answer:

  • Which 2–3 archetypes do we want to target first?
  • Which archetype do we already have the strongest demo for?
  • Which archetype has the easiest sales story in Calgary/local markets?
  • Which archetype is most likely to pay for monthly support?
  • Which archetype is most likely to produce referrals?
  • Which component can we build once and reuse immediately?
  • Are we more comfortable starting with websites, dashboards, lead systems, or live-status systems?
  • What is our minimum project price below which we should politely decline?
  • What monthly support plan do we want every client to consider?
  • What kind of client would cause the most stress for us right now?

Section 02

Archetype Strategy

2.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Strategy Document

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains Shawcliffe Digital’s 12 owner-operated business archetypes.

The goal is to stop treating every lead like a totally custom project.

Instead, every new lead should be quickly sorted into an archetype so we can decide:

  • What problems they probably have
  • What system they likely need
  • Which reusable components apply
  • What starter offer fits
  • What upsells make sense
  • What monthly support could be sold
  • What red flags to watch for

The internal rule:

First identify the archetype. Then choose the system. Then choose the components. Then customize the details.

2.2 How Shawcliffe Digital Should Use Archetypes

Every client should be assigned:

  • Primary archetype
    The main way the business makes money.
  • Secondary archetype if needed
    Only if the business truly overlaps.
  • Core business problem
    Leads, bookings, quotes, inventory, status updates, reviews, follow-up, recurring clients, etc.
  • Component package
    The reusable system/app components needed to solve the problem.

Example

A baker who sells custom cakes and also attends farmers’ markets:

CategoryDecision
Primary archetypeFood Producers & Specialty Makers
Secondary archetypeMobile / Pop-Up Sellers
Core problemCustom cake inquiries plus changing market availability
Starter systemCake Inquiry & Preorder System
Likely add-onMarket Availability / Limited Batch Updates
Useful componentsBusiness Profile, Service/Product Menu, Lead Capture, Photo Upload, Payments/Deposits, Product Inventory, Notifications, Admin Dashboard

Most Shawcliffe projects will fall into one or more of these patterns.

Understanding these patterns makes selling and building much easier.

The owner may be solo or have a small team. The business is often personal, relationship-based, and local.

Sales Angle

Simple Pitch

We help barbers, stylists, and personal care businesses make it easier for customers to see services, request appointments, rebook, and leave reviews without everything getting lost in texts and DMs.

Pain-Based Pitch

If people are messaging you from Instagram, Facebook, texts, and phone calls, it is easy to miss bookings or repeat the same answers all day. We can give customers one simple place to request an appointment and see what you offer.

Money-Saving / Time-Saving Angle

Every missed inquiry, forgotten rebooking, or review you never ask for is money left on the table. A simple booking and review system helps you keep more of the clients you already earned.

Red Flags / Bad-Fit Situations

  • Owner wants a complex full calendar system but does not want to pay for complexity
  • Owner refuses to clarify services/prices
  • Owner wants unlimited social media posting included
  • Owner expects guaranteed new clients instantly
  • Owner will not respond to booking requests promptly
  • Owner has no cancellation/no-show policy but expects the system to fix no-shows
  • Owner only wants “a pretty website” and does not care about booking, reviews, or follow-up

Do you need photos/files before giving an answer?Trades, events, vehicles, professional
Do you sell products that change daily or seasonally?Food, mobile sellers, retail
Do you serve repeat clients on a schedule?Cleaning, lawn care, pet care, education
Do you need to track properties, pets, vehicles, or students?Profile-based archetypes
Do customers often ask if you are open or what is available?Mobile/pop-up, retail, food
Do you need intake forms or documents?Wellness, professional, education
Do reviews matter a lot in your field?Almost all
Where do inquiries currently come from?Reveals chaos points

2.21 Red Flag Patterns Across All Archetypes

Watch for these early.

Client Red Flags

  • “I just need an app” but cannot explain the business problem
  • “This should be easy” before understanding scope
  • “Can you just…” repeated many times
  • No budget but wants custom work
  • Refuses deposit/payment structure
  • Refuses to provide content
  • Wants unlimited revisions
  • Wants guaranteed leads
  • Expects instant SEO results
  • Is rude or dismissive during sales
  • Says past providers were all terrible but gives vague reasons
  • Wants us to manage daily operations manually
  • Wants complex automation before basic process is clear

Project Red Flags

  • No clear offer
  • No clear customer path
  • Too many integrations
  • Too many custom roles/users
  • Heavy privacy/compliance risk
  • No clear launch definition
  • No reusable component value
  • No recurring revenue potential
  • Client content not ready
  • Client expects us to invent their business strategy from scratch

2.22 Must-Have Now vs Nice-to-Have Later

Must-Have Now

Shawcliffe Digital should immediately create:

  • One-page summary of all 12 archetypes
  • Archetype classification checklist
  • Starter offer for each early target archetype
  • Discovery questions for top 3 archetypes
  • Component shortlist for top 3 archetypes
  • Sales pitch for top 3 archetypes
  • Red flag checklist
  • Project fit checklist
  • Demo system for at least one archetype
  • Basic pricing bands by archetype/system type

Nice-to-Have Later

Build later after real client patterns emerge:

  • Full archetype-specific proposal library
  • Full demo for every archetype
  • Industry-specific landing pages for all 12 archetypes
  • Case studies by archetype
  • Advanced automation playbooks
  • Detailed support burden scoring by archetype
  • Template marketplace/catalog
  • Archetype-specific training videos

2.23 Common Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Treating Every Business as Unique

Every business has unique details.

But most owner-operated businesses have repeatable patterns.

Do not start from scratch every time.

Mistake 2: Selling the Component Instead of the Outcome

Do not say:

You need CRM Lite and automated notifications.

Say:

You need a simple way to see who contacted you, what they asked for, and who still needs a follow-up.

Mistake 3: Offering Too Much Too Early

A barber may not need:

  • Advanced analytics
  • AI workflows
  • Full mobile app
  • Complex memberships
  • Push notifications

They may need:

  • Services
  • Booking request
  • Review request
  • Rebooking reminder

Start there.

Mistake 4: Ignoring Support Burden

Some components create more ongoing support:

  • Notifications
  • Payments
  • Admin dashboards
  • Inventory/status updates
  • Profile systems
  • Automations
  • Analytics

Price support accordingly.

Mistake 5: Missing the Monthly Revenue Angle

Every archetype has a natural monthly support reason.

Examples:

  • Barbers: booking/review support
  • Contractors: quote lead tracking
  • Cleaners: recurring clients
  • Bakers: menu/product updates
  • Fruit stands: seasonal live status
  • Dog groomers: pet profiles and reminders
  • Tutors: student progress/resources

2.24 Definition of Done for Section 2

This section is complete when Shawcliffe Digital has:

  • Defined all 12 archetypes clearly
  • Identified common customer problems for each archetype
  • Identified common owner problems for each archetype
  • Identified missed-money opportunities for each archetype
  • Mapped likely Shawcliffe components to each archetype
  • Created a likely starter offer for each archetype
  • Identified upsell opportunities for each archetype
  • Identified recurring revenue opportunities for each archetype
  • Written a basic sales angle for each archetype
  • Listed red flags and bad-fit situations for each archetype
  • Identified best early target archetypes
  • Created an internal framework for classifying leads

2.25 Key Takeaways

  • Shawcliffe Digital should classify every lead by archetype before proposing anything.
  • The first question is not “what app do they want?” but “what kind of business system do they need?”
  • The strongest early archetypes are likely:
    • Mobile / Pop-Up Sellers
    • Home Service Trades
    • Personal Care Appointment Businesses
    • Home & Property Maintenance
    • Food Producers & Specialty Makers
    • Pet & Animal Services
  • Most archetypes need the same foundation components:
    • Business Profile
    • Service / Product Menu
    • Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
    • Notifications
    • Admin Dashboard
    • CRM Lite
    • Review Request System
  • The niche profile components create strong template opportunities:
    • Property Profiles
    • Pet Profiles
    • Vehicle Profiles
    • Student / Progress Profiles
  • The sales message should always be tied to time, money, missed opportunities, professionalism, and reduced chaos.
  • Avoid projects where the client wants custom complexity but has no budget, no clarity, or no willingness to use the system.

2.27 Immediate Action Items for Shawcliffe Digital

Do First

  • Pick the first 3 archetypes to actively sell.
  • Create one demo system for the strongest archetype.
  • Write one-page sales sheets for the top 3 archetypes.
  • Create discovery forms for the top 3 archetypes.
  • Create starter offer names and rough price ranges.
  • Create a lead tracking sheet with an “Archetype” column.
  • Create a “Likely Components Needed” column in the lead tracker.
  • Create a red flag checklist for leads.
  • Decide which archetypes to avoid for now.
  • Build/document the foundation components that support the most archetypes.

Recommended First 3 Archetypes

For Shawcliffe Digital right now:

  • Mobile / Pop-Up Sellers
    Because the roadside seller live status system is distinctive, visual, and easy to explain.
  • Home Service Trades
    Because quote request systems solve an obvious pain and apply to many businesses.
  • Personal Care Appointment Businesses
    Because booking, rebooking, reviews, and customer retention are easy to explain.

Recommended First 8 Components to Prioritize

  • Business Profile
  • Service / Product Menu
  • Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
  • Notifications
  • Admin Dashboard
  • Booking Request System
  • Photo / File Upload
  • Review Request System

These cover a huge portion of early offers.

2.28 Questions to Answer Before Moving to Section 3

Before building the reusable component library, Shawcliffe Digital should answer:

  • Which 3 archetypes are we going to actively pursue first?
  • Which archetype should get the first polished demo?
  • Which starter offer is easiest for us to explain in one sentence?
  • Which offer is easiest for us to build quickly?
  • Which archetype is most likely to pay monthly?
  • Which archetype has the least compliance/privacy risk?
  • Which archetype do we personally understand best?
  • Which archetype has the clearest local pain in Calgary and surrounding areas?
  • Which components are already partly built?
  • Which components need proper internal documentation first?

Section 03

Reusable Component Library

3.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Component Catalog

1. Purpose of This Section

This section defines Shawcliffe Digital’s 24 reusable system/app components.

These components are the building blocks of Shawcliffe Digital’s client systems.

The goal is to stop thinking:

“What custom thing should we build for this client?”

And start thinking:

“Which reusable components solve this archetype’s problem?”

Every proposal, project plan, SOP, QA checklist, pricing estimate, and support plan should reference these components.

3.2 How to Use This Component Library

For each client, Shawcliffe Digital should identify:

  • Business archetype
  • Main business problem
  • Core customer action
  • Required components
  • Optional components
  • Phase 2 upgrade components
  • Monthly support needs

Example

Client

Roadside fruit stand.

Archetype

Mobile / Pop-Up Seller.

Main Problem

Customers do not know what is available, whether the stand is open, or whether it is sold out.

Components Needed

ComponentWhy
Business ProfileBasic business identity
Service / Product MenuFruit/products and prices
Admin DashboardOwner updates products/status
NotificationsCustomers or owner receive updates
Status TrackerOpen/closed/sold out
Product Inventory / Limited BatchToday’s available fruit
Location / Pop-Up TrackerWhere the stand is today
Customer Database / CRM LiteCustomer update list

3.3 Component Package Levels

Not every component belongs in every package.

Use this simple internal structure.

Starter Package

Simple public-facing presence and basic lead capture.

Usually includes:

  • Business Profile
  • Service / Product Menu
  • Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
  • Basic Notifications
  • Basic Review Request System if simple

Growth Package

A stronger system that helps manage leads, bookings, updates, reviews, or customer records.

May include:

  • Admin Dashboard
  • Customer Database / CRM Lite
  • Booking Request System
  • Photo / File Upload
  • Payments / Deposits
  • Status Tracker
  • Product Inventory / Limited Batch
  • Recurring Schedule
  • Basic profile components

Premium Package

More advanced business workflows, automation, reporting, integrations, or custom logic.

May include:

  • Advanced Analytics / Campaign Tracking
  • Advanced Automation / AI Workflows
  • Larger dashboards
  • Multi-step customer workflows
  • Profile systems with history
  • Complex notifications
  • Campaign/reporting systems
  • Higher-touch support

3.5 Component 1: Business Profile

What It Does

The Business Profile stores and displays the basic identity of the business.

This is the foundation for every client system.

It answers:

  • Who is this business?
  • What do they do?
  • Where are they?
  • How do customers contact them?
  • When are they open?
  • What area do they serve?
  • What should the business look and sound like?

Most Relevant Archetypes

RelevanceArchetypes
EssentialAll 12 archetypes

Every client needs this.

Client Problem It Solves

Many owner-operators have business information scattered across:

  • Facebook
  • Instagram
  • Google Business Profile
  • Old websites
  • Business cards
  • Text messages
  • Memory

This causes confusion when hours, services, phone numbers, prices, or locations are inconsistent.

Inputs Required From Client

  • Business name
  • Owner name
  • Phone number
  • Email address
  • Address, location, or service area
  • Hours
  • Social media links
  • Google Business Profile link if available
  • Logo
  • Brand colors if available
  • Short business description
  • Long business description
  • Main services/products
  • Preferred customer action
  • Photos if available

Internal Build Notes

  • This should be standardized across every template.
  • Use consistent fields internally.
  • Make sure business info can be reused across website, forms, dashboards, emails, notifications, QR codes, and review requests.
  • If the client has changing hours, consider connecting this to Admin Dashboard.
  • If the client is mobile or seasonal, include service area and status fields.

Testing Requirements

  • Confirm phone number works.
  • Confirm email link works.
  • Confirm map/address is correct.
  • Confirm hours display properly on mobile.
  • Confirm social links work.
  • Confirm business name is spelled correctly.
  • Confirm logo displays properly.
  • Confirm service area is clear.
  • Confirm Google Business Profile link is correct if included.

Pricing Implications

Usually included in every project.

Can increase cost if:

  • Client has no brand identity
  • Client needs copywriting
  • Client needs logo cleanup
  • Client has multiple locations
  • Client has seasonal hours
  • Client has multiple service areas
  • Client needs Google Business Profile cleanup

Package Fit

PackageFit
StarterEssential
GrowthEssential
PremiumEssential

Recurring Revenue Potential

Low by itself.

Medium if tied to:

  • Monthly updates
  • Seasonal hours
  • Google Business Profile support
  • Location/status changes
  • Local SEO support

Definition of Done

Business Profile is done when:

  • All core business info is complete
  • Contact methods are verified
  • Location/service area is clear
  • Hours are correct
  • Brand identity is applied
  • Customer action is obvious
  • Client has approved all public-facing info

3.6 Component 2: Service / Product Menu

What It Does

The Service / Product Menu lists what the business sells.

It may include:

  • Services
  • Products
  • Packages
  • Prices
  • Starting prices
  • Descriptions
  • Categories
  • Add-ons
  • Availability
  • Lead times
  • Service duration
  • Product quantities
  • Booking or inquiry links

Most Relevant Archetypes

RelevanceArchetypes
EssentialAll 12 archetypes
Especially importantPersonal Care, Food Makers, Mobile Sellers, Retail, Trades, Pet Services, Education

Client Problem It Solves

Customers often hesitate or message repeatedly when they cannot understand:

  • What is offered
  • What it costs
  • What is included
  • What the difference is between options
  • Whether something is available
  • How to take the next step

Inputs Required From Client

  • List of services/products
  • Categories
  • Descriptions
  • Prices or starting prices
  • Duration if appointment-based
  • Lead time if custom/order-based
  • Photos if relevant
  • Add-ons
  • Packages
  • Availability limitations
  • Policies or disclaimers
  • Which items should be featured

Internal Build Notes

  • Keep names simple and customer-friendly.
  • Avoid overwhelming the customer with too many choices.
  • For trades, use service categories rather than exact prices if pricing varies.
  • For food and retail, allow availability/status if needed.
  • For personal care, include duration and booking action.
  • For education, include package/session structure.
  • For professional services, include “starting at” or “request consultation” language where pricing varies.

Testing Requirements

  • Confirm each service/product displays correctly.
  • Confirm prices match client approval.
  • Confirm buttons/forms route correctly.
  • Confirm mobile layout is readable.
  • Confirm inactive/sold-out/unavailable items behave correctly if applicable.
  • Confirm categories are not confusing.
  • Confirm spelling and formatting.

Pricing Implications

Included in most starter projects.

Price increases when:

  • Large menu
  • Many categories
  • Frequent updates
  • Live inventory needed
  • Product photos need editing
  • Complex packages
  • Custom pricing logic
  • Client needs copywriting

Package Fit

PackageFit
StarterEssential
GrowthEssential
PremiumEssential with more advanced logic

Recurring Revenue Potential

Medium.

Supports recurring revenue through:

  • Menu updates
  • Seasonal changes
  • Price updates
  • Product launches
  • Promotions
  • Limited batch updates
  • Package changes

Definition of Done

Service / Product Menu is done when:

  • All approved services/products are listed
  • Descriptions are clear
  • Prices or quote language are approved
  • Customer action is clear
  • Menu works on mobile
  • Client can update it if dashboard access is included

3.7 Component 3: Lead Capture / Inquiry Form

What It Does

The Lead Capture / Inquiry Form collects customer information and sends it to the business.

This is one of Shawcliffe Digital’s most important components.

It turns casual interest into a structured lead.

Most Relevant Archetypes

RelevanceArchetypes
EssentialAlmost all
Especially importantTrades, Property Maintenance, Food Makers, Events, Professional Services, Vehicle Services

Client Problem It Solves

Instead of messy texts like:

“How much?”

The owner receives structured information like:

  • Name
  • Contact info
  • Service requested
  • Location
  • Timeline
  • Details
  • Photos/files if needed
  • Preferred contact method

Inputs Required From Client

  • What information they need from customers
  • Required fields
  • Optional fields
  • Service categories
  • Contact preferences
  • Confirmation message
  • Notification recipients
  • Privacy/disclaimer language if needed
  • Follow-up instructions

Internal Build Notes

  • Keep forms short enough that customers complete them.
  • Use conditional fields only when useful.
  • Ask the minimum needed to qualify the lead.
  • For trades, include location, job type, urgency, and photos.
  • For food, include date, quantity, flavour/product, pickup/delivery.
  • For events, include event date, venue, guest count, budget/package.
  • For professional services, include issue type and document needs.
  • Always send confirmation to customer if possible.
  • Always notify owner.

Testing Requirements

  • Submit test lead.
  • Confirm owner receives notification.
  • Confirm customer confirmation works.
  • Confirm required fields behave properly.
  • Confirm spam protection works if included.
  • Confirm form works on mobile.
  • Confirm data saves correctly if CRM Lite is included.
  • Confirm error messages are understandable.

Pricing Implications

Starter if simple.

Growth if:

  • Multi-step form
  • Conditional logic
  • File upload
  • CRM connection
  • Custom routing
  • Notifications
  • Automations
  • Multiple service-specific forms

Package Fit

PackageFit
StarterBasic inquiry/contact form
GrowthStructured quote/booking/preorder form
PremiumMulti-step form with routing, automations, analytics

Recurring Revenue Potential

Medium to high.

Supports recurring revenue through:

  • CRM Lite
  • Lead follow-up
  • Analytics
  • Spam/security monitoring
  • Form updates
  • New service forms
  • Campaign tracking

Definition of Done

Lead Capture / Inquiry Form is done when:

  • Form collects the right info
  • Owner receives lead notification
  • Customer receives confirmation if included
  • Lead data is stored if applicable
  • Mobile experience works
  • Client approves fields and wording
  • Test submissions pass

3.8 Component 4: Admin Dashboard

What It Does

The Admin Dashboard is the owner-facing control panel.

It lets the business owner update their system without needing Shawcliffe for every small change.

Possible dashboard actions:

  • Update hours
  • Update status
  • Update products
  • Update prices
  • View leads
  • View customers
  • Update services
  • Mark sold out
  • Change location
  • Send review request
  • View bookings
  • Manage profiles

Most Relevant Archetypes

RelevanceArchetypes
EssentialMobile Sellers, Food Makers, Retail
Very usefulPersonal Care, Trades, Property Maintenance, Pet Services, Education, Vehicles
OptionalVery simple website-only clients

Client Problem It Solves

Owners need control without technical complexity.

They should not need to text Shawcliffe every time they want to update:

  • “Closed today”
  • “Sold out”
  • “New price”
  • “New service”
  • “Taking Christmas orders”
  • “New location”

Inputs Required From Client

  • What they need to update
  • Who needs dashboard access
  • What fields should be editable
  • What should not be editable
  • Login email
  • Roles if more than one user
  • Preferred dashboard labels
  • Update frequency

Internal Build Notes

  • Keep dashboard extremely simple.
  • Use plain labels.
  • Avoid technical terms.
  • Build around common actions, not database structure.
  • Use safe defaults.
  • Restrict dangerous settings.
  • For early systems, one owner login is usually enough.
  • Do not overbuild permissions early unless paid.
  • Add help text near important controls.

Testing Requirements

  • Owner login works.
  • Password reset works.
  • Editable fields save properly.
  • Updates appear on customer-facing side.
  • Mobile dashboard works.
  • Owner cannot break layout with bad input.
  • Status changes update immediately if needed.
  • Permission boundaries work if applicable.
  • Dashboard is understandable without explanation.

Pricing Implications

Admin Dashboard moves a project from simple website to business system.

Price should increase when:

  • Many editable fields
  • Multiple users
  • Role permissions
  • Complex workflows
  • Inventory/status management
  • CRM management
  • Profile management
  • Analytics views
  • Automation controls

Package Fit

PackageFit
StarterUsually not included, unless very basic
GrowthCommon
PremiumAdvanced dashboard

Recurring Revenue Potential

Medium to high.

Dashboards create ongoing support needs:

  • Login help
  • Updates
  • Training
  • Bug fixes
  • New fields
  • Workflow changes
  • Feature upgrades

Definition of Done

Admin Dashboard is done when:

  • Owner can log in
  • Owner can update agreed fields
  • Changes display correctly
  • Dashboard works on mobile
  • Dangerous settings are protected
  • Client has basic training
  • Client approves dashboard workflow

Without CRM Lite, leads disappear into:

CRM Lite helps prevent:

Usually Growth or Premium.

3.10 Component 6: Notifications

What It Does

Notifications alert owners and/or customers when something important happens.

Possible notification types:

  • New lead
  • New booking request
  • Quote request received
  • Customer confirmation
  • Status update
  • Sold-out update
  • Appointment reminder
  • Review request
  • Payment/deposit reminder
  • Follow-up reminder

Channels may include:

  • Email
  • SMS
  • Push notification
  • Internal dashboard alert

Most Relevant Archetypes

RelevanceArchetypes
EssentialAlmost all
Especially importantMobile Sellers, Personal Care, Trades, Pet Services, Education, Food, Vehicles

Client Problem It Solves

Owners miss opportunities when they do not know a lead came in.

Customers lose trust when they submit something and hear nothing.

Notifications help create speed and confidence.

Inputs Required From Client

  • Who receives notifications
  • Email addresses
  • Phone numbers
  • Notification types
  • Customer confirmation wording
  • Urgency expectations
  • Quiet hours if applicable
  • SMS consent requirements if messaging customers
  • Branding/tone

Internal Build Notes

  • Start with email notifications where possible.
  • SMS is powerful but must be priced and handled carefully because it may have usage costs.
  • Avoid over-notifying.
  • Use clear subject lines.
  • Include useful lead details in the notification.
  • Make notifications actionable.
  • If customer SMS/email is included, make consent and opt-out clear where needed.
  • Do not promise instant response unless client can deliver it.

Testing Requirements

  • Test owner email.
  • Test owner SMS if included.
  • Test customer confirmation email/SMS.
  • Confirm notifications do not go to spam.
  • Confirm message content is correct.
  • Confirm links work.
  • Confirm notification triggers fire only when intended.
  • Confirm unsubscribes/opt-outs if applicable.
  • Confirm timezone/time displays correctly.

Pricing Implications

Basic email notifications can be included in Starter.

SMS, push, automation, reminders, or multi-recipient routing should increase price.

Also account for:

  • SMS platform costs
  • Email service costs
  • Support burden
  • Failed delivery troubleshooting
  • Consent/compliance setup

Package Fit

PackageFit
StarterBasic email notifications
GrowthSMS/email workflows
PremiumAdvanced routing, reminders, automation

Recurring Revenue Potential

High.

Notifications are one of the clearest reasons for monthly fees because they may involve:

  • Usage costs
  • Monitoring
  • Support
  • Updates
  • Deliverability
  • Reminder workflows
  • Customer communication

Definition of Done

Notifications are done when:

  • Correct people receive correct messages
  • Customer confirmations work if included
  • Test messages are approved
  • Delivery is verified
  • Usage costs are understood
  • Client understands limits and responsibilities

The Review Request System helps clients ask happy customers for reviews, usually Google reviews.

RelevanceArchetypes
UsefulAll 12 archetypes

Many happy customers would leave reviews if asked at the right time.

Most owners forget to ask.

Reviews help with:

  • Conversion

  • Professional appearance

Inputs Required From Client

  • Google review link
  • Preferred review request wording
  • When to ask for review
  • Who should receive requests
  • Whether SMS/email is used
  • Customer list if sending to past customers
  • Testimonial approval process if using testimonials
  • Any industry-specific rules or sensitivities

Internal Build Notes

  • Keep review requests simple and friendly.
  • Do not pressure customers.
  • Do not offer improper incentives for positive reviews.
  • Do not ask only for positive reviews in a misleading way.
  • For health-adjacent/professional services, be careful with rules and client privacy.
  • QR review cards can be a strong physical add-on.
  • Tie review request to “completed service” where possible.

Testing Requirements

  • Review link opens correct Google profile.
  • SMS/email wording is correct.
  • Manual trigger works if included.
  • Automation trigger works if included.
  • Customer record logs request if CRM connected.
  • QR code works.
  • Mobile experience works.
  • Client approves wording.

Pricing Implications

Basic review link/QR can be Starter.

Automated review workflow belongs in Growth or Premium.

Price increases with:

  • CRM connection
  • SMS
  • Automation
  • Customer segmentation
  • Testimonial display
  • Reporting

Package Fit

PackageFit

High.

3.12 Component 8: Booking Request System

What It Does

The Booking Request System lets customers request an appointment, lesson, service time, consultation, or event booking.

3.13 Component 9: Photo / File Upload

  • Notes save.
  • Multiple pets per owner works if included.
  • Photos upload if included.
  • Service history works if included.
  • Mobile view works.
  • Owner can find pet quickly.

Pricing Implications

Growth/Premium component.

Price increases with:

  • Multiple pets
  • Service history
  • Document uploads
  • Recurring schedules
  • Customer portal
  • Reminders
  • Staff permissions

Package Fit

PackageFit
StarterNot included
GrowthBasic pet profiles
PremiumPet history, reminders, portal

Recurring Revenue Potential

High.

Pet Profiles make the system valuable long-term because records build over time.

Definition of Done

Pet Profiles are done when:

  • Pet details are captured
  • Owner can view/update profiles
  • Profiles connect to bookings if included
  • Notes/history work
  • Client approves fields
  • Privacy/safety expectations are clear

3.24 Component 20: Vehicle Profiles

What It Does

Vehicle Profiles store details about a customer’s vehicle, trailer, machine, or equipment.

Examples:

  • Make
  • Model
  • Year
  • VIN if needed
  • Plate if needed
  • Mileage/hours
  • Photos
  • Issue history
  • Service history
  • Maintenance reminders
  • Customer owner info

Most Relevant Archetypes

RelevanceArchetypes
EssentialVehicle & Equipment Services
UsefulTrades with equipment service
OptionalFleet-support professional services

Client Problem It Solves

Vehicle service providers waste time when customers do not provide basic vehicle details.

Profiles also support repeat maintenance and seasonal reminders.

Inputs Required From Client

  • Required vehicle fields
  • Whether VIN/plate is needed
  • Service history needs
  • Photo needs
  • Reminder needs
  • Customer info
  • Privacy expectations
  • Fleet support needs if applicable

Internal Build Notes

  • Avoid collecting VIN unless client truly needs it.
  • Connect to Lead Capture / Inquiry Form.
  • Connect to Photo Upload.
  • Connect to Recurring Schedule or reminders for maintenance.
  • Use vehicle profile to support repeat business.
  • Keep early version simple.

Testing Requirements

  • Vehicle record creation works.
  • Customer inquiry creates/links vehicle if included.
  • Photos attach if included.
  • Service notes save.
  • Search works if included.
  • Reminders work if included.
  • Mobile owner view works.

Growth/Premium.

Price increases with:

  • Fleet accounts

  • File/photo storage

Package Fit

PackageFit

High.

Supports monthly value through:

  • Maintenance reminders

Vehicle Profiles are done when:

3.25 Component 21: Student / Progress Profiles

What It Does

Student / Progress Profiles track learners, clients, or participants over time.

Examples:

  • Student name
  • Parent/contact info
  • Subject/program
  • Goals
  • Lesson notes
  • Attendance
  • Progress milestones
  • Homework
  • Skill levels
  • Parent communication notes

Most Relevant Archetypes

RelevanceArchetypes
EssentialEducation, Coaching & Instruction
UsefulFitness trainers, wellness coaches
OptionalPet training if animal progress is tracked

Client Problem It Solves

Instructors need to show progress, remember lesson notes, and communicate value.

Without progress tracking, long-term teaching feels less organized.

Inputs Required From Client

  • Student fields
  • Progress categories
  • Lesson note format
  • Attendance needs
  • Parent communication needs
  • Homework/resource needs
  • Package/session tracking
  • Privacy expectations
  • Who can view progress

Internal Build Notes

  • Keep progress tracking simple.
  • Avoid full learning management system early.
  • Connect to Booking Request and Recurring Schedule.
  • Connect to Resource Library for homework.
  • For parent-facing views, be extra careful with access.
  • Internal notes and customer-visible notes may need separation.

Testing Requirements

  • Student profile creation works.
  • Notes save.
  • Progress fields update.
  • Attendance/session tracking works if included.
  • Parent communication works if included.
  • Resource links work.
  • Access permissions work if applicable.
  • Mobile view works.

Pricing Implications

Growth/Premium.

Price increases with:

  • Parent portal
  • Progress reports

  • Homework/resource delivery
  • Attendance tracking

Package Fit

PackageFit
StarterNot included

Recurring Revenue Potential

High.

Definition of Done

Student / Progress Profiles are done when:

3.26 Component 22: Resource Library

What It Does

The Resource Library stores helpful information for customers.

Examples:

  • FAQs
  • Prep instructions
  • Care instructions
  • Policies
  • Downloadable forms
  • How-to guides
  • Lesson resources
  • Maintenance tips
  • Before/after instructions
  • Service explanations

Most Relevant Archetypes

RelevanceArchetypes
Very usefulEducation, Wellness, Professional Services, Pet Services
UsefulFood Makers, Trades, Vehicles, Personal Care, Retail
OptionalMobile Sellers

Client Problem It Solves

Owners repeat the same explanations over and over.

A Resource Library gives customers a place to get answers.

Inputs Required From Client

  • FAQ answers
  • Policies
  • Instructions
  • Download files
  • Photos/videos if relevant
  • Categories
  • Which resources are public/private
  • Update frequency
  • Tone/wording approval

Internal Build Notes

  • Start simple.
  • Do not create regulated advice without client review.
  • Use short sections.
  • Link resources from forms and confirmations.
  • For education, use lesson/homework resources.
  • For pet services, use prep/care instructions.
  • For professional services, use document checklists and process guides.

Testing Requirements

  • Resource links work.
  • Downloads open.
  • Mobile readability works.
  • Categories are clear.
  • Search works if included.
  • Private resources protected if applicable.
  • Client approves all content.

Pricing Implications

Basic FAQ/resource page can be Starter.

Larger organized library is Growth.

Private/resource portal is Premium.

Package Fit

PackageFit
StarterBasic FAQ/resources
GrowthOrganized resource library
PremiumPrivate/customer-specific resources

Recurring Revenue Potential

Medium.

Monthly updates can include:

  • New FAQs
  • Seasonal instructions
  • Policies
  • Guides
  • Customer education
  • Download updates

Definition of Done

  • Resources are organized
  • Customer questions are answered
  • Links/downloads work
  • Mobile readability is strong

3.27 Component 23: Advanced Analytics / Campaign Tracking

What It Does

Advanced Analytics / Campaign Tracking helps track where leads, visits, QR scans, campaigns, or conversions come from.

Examples:

  • Website traffic
  • Form submissions
  • Lead source
  • QR code scans
  • Google Business Profile clicks
  • Ad campaign conversions
  • Landing page performance
  • Review request results
  • Monthly reports

Most Relevant Archetypes

RelevanceArchetypes
UsefulAll growth-focused clients
Especially usefulTrades, Retail, Events, Professional Services, Mobile Sellers, Food Makers

Client Problem It Solves

Owners often do not know which marketing efforts are working.

Analytics help answer:

  • Where are leads coming from?
  • Which QR code is being scanned?
  • Which service page gets interest?
  • Are campaigns producing inquiries?
  • What should we improve?

Inputs Required From Client

  • Website/app goals
  • Campaign sources
  • QR code locations
  • Ad platforms if any
  • Reporting needs
  • Conversion definitions
  • Access to analytics/search tools
  • Monthly review preference

Internal Build Notes

  • Do not overcomplicate early.
  • Track only what affects decisions.
  • Use simple monthly reporting.
  • QR tracking is useful for physical signage/cards.
  • Define conversions clearly.
  • For ads, tracking must be set up before campaign starts.
  • Avoid drowning the client in metrics.

Testing Requirements

  • Analytics installed.
  • Events/conversions fire.
  • Forms are tracked.
  • QR codes route correctly.
  • UTM links work if used.
  • Reports show useful data.
  • Client can understand report.
  • Test traffic appears.

Pricing Implications

Premium or monthly add-on.

Price increases with:

  • Multiple campaigns
  • Multiple landing pages
  • Ad platform tracking
  • QR campaign tracking
  • Dashboards
  • Monthly reporting
  • Conversion analysis

Package Fit

PackageFit
StarterBasic analytics only
GrowthBasic conversion/source tracking
PremiumAdvanced campaign dashboard/reporting

Recurring Revenue Potential

High.

Analytics create monthly value through:

  • Reporting
  • Recommendations
  • Campaign improvement
  • Upsell identification
  • Lead source tracking

Definition of Done

Advanced Analytics / Campaign Tracking is done when:

  • Tracking is installed
  • Key actions are measured
  • Campaign links work
  • QR codes are trackable if included
  • Client understands what is being tracked
  • Monthly reporting process is defined

3.28 Component 24: Advanced Automation / AI Workflows

What It Does

Advanced Automation / AI Workflows automate higher-level business tasks.

Examples:

  • AI receptionist
  • Lead routing
  • Smart follow-up
  • Message drafting
  • Lead scoring
  • Appointment reminders
  • Missed call text-back
  • Review request automation
  • Internal task creation
  • Customer segmentation
  • FAQ chatbot

Most Relevant Archetypes

RelevanceArchetypes
Useful laterAll archetypes with enough volume
Especially usefulTrades, Personal Care, Pet Services, Professional Services, Wellness, Vehicles

Client Problem It Solves

Owners become overwhelmed when lead volume, messages, and follow-up tasks grow.

Automation can reduce manual work — but only after the basic process is clear.

Inputs Required From Client

  • Current workflow
  • Common customer questions
  • Follow-up rules
  • Message tone
  • Escalation rules
  • What automation can/cannot say
  • Business policies
  • Customer consent needs
  • Tool access
  • Failure handling expectations

Internal Build Notes

This should usually not be the first thing sold.

Before automation, the client needs:

  • Clear services
  • Clear inquiry process
  • Clear response expectations
  • Clear policies
  • Working lead capture
  • Working notifications
  • CRM or customer tracking

Automation on top of chaos creates automated chaos.

Testing Requirements

  • Test common scenarios.
  • Test edge cases.
  • Test escalation to human.
  • Test wrong/unclear inputs.
  • Test message tone.
  • Test opt-out/consent if messaging.
  • Test internal task creation.
  • Test failure alerts.
  • Confirm client reviews all automated wording.

Pricing Implications

Premium.

This should never be priced like a simple form.

Price must account for:

  • Setup
  • Testing
  • Prompt/workflow design
  • Monitoring
  • Usage fees
  • Updates
  • Risk
  • Support burden

Package Fit

PackageFit
StarterNo
GrowthRare, simple automations only
PremiumYes

Recurring Revenue Potential

Very high.

Automation requires ongoing:

  • Monitoring
  • Updates
  • Usage fees
  • Error handling
  • Workflow improvement
  • Client training
  • Compliance awareness

Definition of Done

Advanced Automation / AI Workflows are done when:

  • Workflow is clearly mapped
  • Client approves automation boundaries
  • Common scenarios pass testing
  • Escalation works
  • Failure handling exists
  • Client understands limitations
  • Monthly monitoring/support is defined

3.29 Component Groups by Build Priority

Must-Have Now

These should be built/documented first because they serve the widest number of archetypes.

  • Business Profile
  • Service / Product Menu
  • Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
  • Notifications
  • Admin Dashboard
  • Review Request System
  • Booking Request System

Build Soon

These unlock stronger archetype templates and monthly revenue.

  • Customer Database / CRM Lite
  • Payments / Deposits
  • Status Tracker
  • Product Inventory / Limited Batch
  • Location / Pop-Up Tracker
  • Recurring Schedule
  • Document Checklist / File Portal
  • Resource Library

Nice-to-Have Later

These are powerful but should not distract from early sales and delivery.

  • Packages / Memberships
  • Loyalty / Rewards / Referrals
  • Property Profiles
  • Pet Profiles
  • Vehicle Profiles
  • Student / Progress Profiles
  • Advanced Analytics / Campaign Tracking
  • Advanced Automation / AI Workflows

Note: Profile components are “later” only because they are more specialized. If Shawcliffe chooses Pet Services, Vehicle Services, Property Maintenance, or Education as an early niche, move the matching profile component earlier.

3.30 Component Pricing Rules

Simple Pricing Logic

Each component affects price based on:

FactorLow ComplexityHigh Complexity
DataFew fieldsMany custom fields
UpdatesStaticClient-editable dashboard
WorkflowOne stepMulti-step process
NotificationsOne emailSMS/email/routing/reminders
StorageNo storageFiles/photos/documents
IntegrationsNonePayments, calendars, CRM, analytics
UsersOne ownerMultiple staff/roles
RiskPublic infoSensitive data/payment/automation
SupportRare changesFrequent updates/troubleshooting

Internal Pricing Rule

A component is not priced only by how hard it is to build. It is priced by build complexity, business value, support burden, and risk.

3.31 Component Support Burden

Some components create more support than others.

Low Support Burden

  • Business Profile
  • Static Service / Product Menu
  • Basic Resource Library
  • Basic Review Link

Medium Support Burden

  • Lead Capture Forms
  • Booking Requests
  • Photo Upload
  • Status Tracker
  • Product Inventory
  • Location Tracker
  • Payments/Deposits

High Support Burden

  • Admin Dashboard
  • CRM Lite
  • Notifications
  • Recurring Schedule
  • Profile Systems
  • Advanced Analytics
  • Advanced Automation / AI Workflows

3.32 Component Reuse Rule

After every project, ask:

  • Did we build a new component?
  • Did we improve an existing component?
  • Did we create a new variation for an archetype?
  • Did we create reusable fields?
  • Did we create reusable copy?
  • Did we create a reusable QA checklist?
  • Did this create a recurring support need?
  • Should this become part of a starter offer?
  • Should this be documented before the next client?
  • Did this component create more support burden than expected?

3.34 Must-Have Now vs Nice-to-Have Later

Must-Have Now

Before taking on more clients, Shawcliffe should have clean internal notes for:

  • Business Profile
  • Service / Product Menu
  • Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
  • Notifications
  • Admin Dashboard
  • Review Request System
  • Booking Request System
  • Photo / File Upload

These are the base of most sellable systems.

Nice-to-Have Later

Do not delay selling because these are not perfect:

  • Advanced dashboards
  • Full CRM
  • Complex profile systems
  • Advanced analytics
  • AI receptionist
  • Full automation
  • Loyalty systems
  • Payment subscriptions
  • Customer portals

Build these when a real client or demo justifies them.

3.35 Common Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Calling Everything Custom

If a form, dashboard, status update, booking request, or profile system can be reused, treat it as a component.

Mistake 2: Selling Too Many Components at Once

A client does not need all 24 components.

Sell the smallest system that solves the main problem, then create an upgrade path.

Mistake 3: Forgetting Client Inputs

Most delays happen because the client has not provided:

  • Services
  • Prices
  • Photos
  • Policies
  • Descriptions
  • Access
  • Review link
  • Payment account
  • Business info

Every component needs a client input checklist.

Mistake 4: Underpricing Notifications and Dashboards

These seem simple but create support.

SMS, dashboard access, reminders, and automations should not be casually thrown in for free.

Mistake 5: Building Advanced Automation Before the Basic System Works

Do not automate a broken process.

First fix:

  • Lead capture
  • Services
  • Notifications
  • Follow-up
  • Customer tracking

Then automate.

3.36 Definition of Done for Section 3

This section is complete when Shawcliffe Digital has:

  • Defined all 24 reusable components
  • Identified which archetypes need each component
  • Clarified what problem each component solves
  • Listed client inputs required for each component
  • Created internal build notes
  • Created testing requirements
  • Identified pricing implications
  • Assigned package fit: Starter, Growth, Premium
  • Identified recurring revenue potential
  • Created definition of done for each component
  • Grouped components by build priority
  • Created a reusable component documentation template

3.37 Key Takeaways

  • Shawcliffe Digital should sell systems made from reusable components.
  • The most important early components are:
    • Business Profile
    • Service / Product Menu
    • Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
    • Notifications
    • Admin Dashboard
    • Review Request System
    • Booking Request System
    • Photo / File Upload
  • Components should be priced based on business value, complexity, support burden, and risk.
  • Admin dashboards, notifications, CRM, profiles, automation, and analytics create recurring revenue but also require support.
  • Every client project should improve the component library.
  • Do not build advanced automation before the basic customer journey works.

4.7 Best Components to Build First

If Shawcliffe Digital wants to cast the widest net quickly, build in this order.

Phase 1: Universal Foundation

These components are needed for almost every client.

1. Business Profile

Why first:

  • Every client needs it.
  • It feeds websites, dashboards, forms, emails, notifications, QR codes, and proposals.

2. Service / Product Menu

Why second:

  • Every client needs to explain what they sell.
  • This becomes the foundation for booking, quote requests, orders, and packages.

3. Lead Capture / Inquiry Form

Why third:

  • This is the basic conversion engine.
  • It turns visitors into leads.

4. Notifications

Why fourth:

  • A lead system is weak if the owner does not know a lead arrived.
  • Notifications create immediate perceived value.

Phase 2: Owner Control and Reputation

These make the system feel more valuable than a normal website.

5. Admin Dashboard

Why fifth:

  • Lets owners update things themselves.
  • Creates the difference between “website” and “business system.”

6. Review Request System

Why sixth:

  • Useful for almost every local business.
  • Easy to explain.
  • Strong monthly value.

7. Customer Database / CRM Lite

4.20 Common Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Building the Most Interesting Component First

Advanced AI workflows, dashboards, and profile systems are interesting.

But they do not cast the widest net first.

Build the components that sell the most projects first.

Mistake 2: Building Niche Profiles Too Early

Pet Profiles, Vehicle Profiles, Property Profiles, and Student Profiles are valuable.

But each mainly serves one archetype.

Build them after deciding to target that archetype seriously.

Mistake 3: Treating Admin Dashboard as Free

Dashboards are powerful but support-heavy.

They should be priced properly and included intentionally.

Mistake 4: Selling Advanced Analytics Too Early

Most tiny owner-operators do not need dashboards full of charts at first.

They need:

  • More leads
  • Better inquiries
  • Less chaos
  • Reviews
  • Follow-up

Analytics matters later.

Mistake 5: Forgetting Physical-World Use

Many Shawcliffe systems should connect to the physical world through:

  • QR code business cards
  • Signs
  • Stickers
  • Review cards
  • Booth signage
  • Vehicle decals
  • Counter cards

Especially for:

  • Mobile sellers
  • Retail shops
  • Personal care
  • Food producers
  • Pet services
  • Trades

4.21 Internal Decision Rules

Use these rules when choosing components.

Rule 1: Every Client Gets a Foundation

Almost every project needs:

  • Business Profile
  • Service / Product Menu
  • Lead Capture or Booking/Inquiry action
  • Notifications

Rule 2: Pick One Primary Workflow

Do not give the client five systems at once.

Choose the main workflow:

  • Booking
  • Quote request
  • Preorder
  • Live status
  • Recurring service
  • Intake/document collection
  • Review/follow-up

Rule 3: Add the Niche Component Only If It Matters

Do not add Pet Profiles, Vehicle Profiles, Property Profiles, or Student Profiles unless they clearly improve the client’s daily work.

Rule 4: Dashboard Means Support

If the client can edit it, they can break it, misunderstand it, or need help with it.

Price accordingly.

Rule 5: Notifications Mean Ongoing Responsibility

SMS/email/push workflows should be attached to a monthly support plan where possible.

Rule 6: Automation Comes After Clarity

Do not automate a messy process.

First define the customer journey.

Then automate parts of it.

4.23 Key Takeaways

  • Shawcliffe should build the widest-use components first, not the most interesting components first.
  • The foundation components are:
    • Business Profile
    • Service / Product Menu
    • Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
    • Notifications
  • The early differentiators are:
    • Admin Dashboard
    • Review Request System
    • CRM Lite
    • Booking Request System
    • Photo / File Upload
  • The first strong templates should be:
    • Local Business Starter System
    • Contractor Quote Request System
    • Barber Booking & Review System
    • Roadside Seller Live Status System
  • The most reusable system clusters are:
    • Appointment systems
    • Quote request systems
    • Recurring client systems
    • Live status/inventory systems
    • Intake/document systems
  • Niche profile components are valuable, but should be built when Shawcliffe commits to that niche.
  • Advanced analytics and AI workflows should come later, after the basic business system works.
