  • Who handles support requests?
  • Who handles invoices and payment follow-up?
  • How will we avoid both people assuming the other person handled something?
← Reusable Component LibraryNext: Core Internal Roles →
Section 05

Core Internal Roles

5.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Roles & Responsibility Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

Shawcliffe Digital is currently a lean husband-and-wife agency.

That means we do not need a bloated org chart.

But we do need clear ownership.

When a small agency fails operationally, it usually is not because nobody cared. It is because everyone assumed someone else was handling:

  • The follow-up
  • The invoice
  • The scope boundary
  • The client assets
  • The QA
  • The launch checklist
  • The support request
  • The password
  • The proposal
  • The revision deadline
  • The documentation update

This section defines the practical “hats” inside Shawcliffe Digital.

The goal is simple:

Every important task must have one clear owner, even if the same person wears several hats.

5.2 Core Operating Principle

Roles Are Hats, Not Corporate Titles

At the beginning, Shawcliffe Digital does not need 12 employees.

It needs 12 clearly defined roles that can be divided between two people.

One person may handle:

  • Sales
  • Client relationships
  • Strategy
  • Project management
  • Billing follow-up

Another person may handle:

  • Development
  • Technical setup
  • QA
  • Template architecture
  • Build documentation

Some roles will overlap.

That is okay.

What is not okay:

“I thought you were doing that.”

5.3 Shawcliffe Digital’s Core Roles

Shawcliffe Digital should define these roles internally:

#RoleMain Purpose
1Sales / Client RelationshipsFind leads, start conversations, build trust, close projects
2StrategyDecide what the client actually needs
3Project ManagementKeep the project moving from lead to launch
4DesignMake the system clear, professional, and usable
5DevelopmentBuild the website/app/system/components
6QA / TestingMake sure everything works before launch
7Client SupportHandle post-launch questions, fixes, and updates
8Billing / AdminMake sure proposals, invoices, payments, and records are handled
9Research & DevelopmentExplore new archetypes, tools, ideas, and system improvements
10Template / Product DevelopmentTurn repeated work into reusable Shawcliffe templates
11Documentation MaintenanceKeep SOPs, component docs, templates, and checklists current
12Client SuccessMake sure the client is actually getting value after launch

5.5 Role 1: Sales / Client Relationships

Purpose

Sales is responsible for finding, starting, and developing client conversations that lead to paid work.

This role is not just “selling.”

It includes:

  • Listening
  • Building trust
  • Identifying business problems
  • Explaining Shawcliffe clearly
  • Handling objections
  • Following up
  • Knowing when to walk away

Primary Responsibilities

ResponsibilityDescription
Lead generationFind potential clients through local networks, referrals, outreach, Facebook groups, Google Maps, markets, community, etc.
First contactStart warm, practical conversations.
Relationship buildingHelp owners feel understood, not pressured.
Initial qualificationDecide whether the lead is worth a discovery call.
Archetype identificationSort the business into one of the 12 archetypes.
Pain identificationFind missed leads, time waste, admin chaos, review gaps, booking issues, etc.
Offer explanationExplain Shawcliffe as business systems, not just apps.
Proposal handoffCollect enough info to prepare proposal.
Follow-upPolitely follow up after conversations/proposals.
ClosingGuide client to agreement, payment, and onboarding.

Must-Have Sales Checklist

Before a proposal goes out, sales should know:

  • Business name
  • Owner/contact person
  • Archetype
  • Main problem
  • Current customer flow
  • Current pain
  • Components likely needed
  • Budget comfort
  • Urgency
  • Decision maker
  • Timeline
  • Red flags
  • Monthly support opportunity

Client-Facing Language

We are not here to sell you random tech. We are trying to understand where customers are getting stuck, where you are losing time, and what simple system would help your business run smoother.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Talking about apps before understanding the problem
  • Offering a price too early
  • Promising features before checking feasibility
  • Taking every lead seriously even when red flags are obvious
  • Letting clients define the whole scope casually
  • Forgetting to follow up
  • Selling custom work at template prices

Definition of Done

Sales has done its job when:

  • The lead is qualified or declined
  • The archetype is identified
  • The main pain is clear
  • The likely system is understood
  • Budget/timeline are roughly known
  • Red flags are noted
  • Next step is clear
  • Discovery/proposal/onboarding is handed off properly

5.6 Role 2: Strategy

Purpose

Strategy decides what Shawcliffe should actually build and why.

This role protects the agency from building random features that do not solve a business problem.

Primary Responsibilities

ResponsibilityDescription
Diagnose business problemIdentify where the client loses time, money, customers, reviews, or repeat business.
Choose archetypeMatch client to one of 12 archetypes.
Select componentsChoose which of the 24 components are required.
Define system typeWebsite, lead system, booking system, quote system, live status system, etc.
Prioritize launch scopeDecide what belongs in Phase 1 vs later.
Protect simplicityKeep the system usable for the owner.
Identify recurring valueDecide what monthly support makes sense.
Identify template opportunityDecide whether the project improves a reusable Shawcliffe template.

Strategy Questions

Before building, ask:

  • What is the business trying to get more of?
  • What is the owner tired of doing manually?
  • Where are customers confused?
  • Where are leads being lost?
  • What repeated questions can the system answer?
  • What workflow needs to be organized?
  • Which archetype does this resemble most?
  • Which reusable components solve the problem?
  • What can wait until Phase 2?
  • What monthly support would genuinely help?

Strategic Decision Rule

If a feature does not help the client get customers, save time, reduce missed opportunities, improve follow-up, build trust, or simplify operations, it probably does not belong in Phase 1.

Definition of Done

Strategy is complete when:

  • The project has a clear business goal
  • The archetype is chosen
  • The component list is defined
  • The system type is clear
  • The scope is realistic
  • Phase 1 and future upgrades are separated
  • Both Shawcliffe partners agree the project is worth doing

5.7 Role 3: Project Management

Purpose

Project management keeps the project from drifting.

This role is responsible for turning a signed project into a launched project.

Primary Responsibilities

ResponsibilityDescription
Create project planOutline stages, tasks, owner, and timeline.
Collect assetsLogo, photos, content, services, prices, access.
Track client homeworkMake sure client provides what is needed.
Maintain scopeCompare requests against agreed components.
Schedule reviewsSet internal and client review points.
Track blockersIdentify what is slowing the project.
Communicate updatesKeep client informed.
Manage revisionsKeep revisions organized and limited.
Prepare launchMake sure launch checklist is complete.
Post-launch handoffMove client into support/maintenance process.

Simple Project Management Board

Every project should have these columns:

ColumnMeaning
Lead / Not Sold YetStill in sales stage
Proposal SentWaiting on decision
Contract / Payment PendingSold, but not ready to build
OnboardingCollecting assets/content/access
PlanningConfirming scope/components
BuildDevelopment/design in progress
Internal QAShawcliffe testing
Client ReviewClient checking work
RevisionsApproved revision round
Pre-LaunchFinal checks
LaunchedLive
Support / Care PlanOngoing support

Project Manager Checklist

For every active project, the project manager should know:

  • What is the project?
  • What archetype is it?
  • Which components are included?
  • What is not included?
  • What has client approved?
  • What are we waiting on?
  • What is the next action?
  • Who owns that action?
  • Is payment current?
  • Is launch blocked?
  • Is scope creeping?

Client-Facing Language

To keep the project moving smoothly, we will keep everything organized around the agreed scope, the content we need from you, review points, and launch checklist. If new ideas come up, we can either save them for later or quote them as add-ons.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Building before onboarding is complete
  • Letting client feedback arrive through scattered texts
  • Not writing down decisions
  • Allowing unlimited revision rounds
  • Not tracking blockers
  • Not confirming what is out of scope
  • Not knowing whether payment has been made

Definition of Done

Project management is working when:

  • Every project has a clear status
  • Every project has one next action
  • Client homework is tracked
  • Scope is visible
  • Payment status is visible
  • Launch checklist is visible
  • Nothing important lives only in memory

5.8 Role 4: Design

Purpose

Design makes the system clear, professional, usable, and trustworthy.

For Shawcliffe, design is not just decoration.

Design should help customers understand what to do next.

Primary Responsibilities

ResponsibilityDescription
Page layoutOrganize content clearly.
Customer journeyMake the next action obvious.
Visual trustMake the business look professional.
Mobile usabilityDesign for phone-first users.
Brand consistencyUse logo, colours, tone, photos consistently.
Form clarityMake forms easy to complete.
Dashboard usabilityMake owner controls simple.
Accessibility basicsUse readable text, contrast, simple navigation.

Design Priorities for Owner-Operators

Every design should answer:

  • What does this business do?
  • Who is it for?
  • Where is it located or what area does it serve?
  • What does it cost or how do I find out?
  • What should I do next?
  • Can I trust this business?
  • What happens after I submit/book/request?

Design by Archetype

ArchetypeDesign Priority
Personal CareServices, prices, booking, reviews, photos
TradesTrust, service areas, quote request, photos
Property MaintenancePackages, recurring service, property details
Food MakersMenu, photos, lead time, preorder
Mobile SellersOpen status, location, today’s products
Pet ServicesServices, booking, pet intake, trust
Vehicle ServicesService request, vehicle details, before/after
EventsPortfolio, packages, event inquiry
EducationPrograms, schedule, student/parent clarity
WellnessTrust, intake, policies, booking
RetailHours, location, products, promos
Professional ServicesTrust, process, intake, documents

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Designing for desktop first
  • Making things too fancy
  • Hiding the call-to-action
  • Overloading pages with text
  • Using vague buttons like “Submit” instead of “Request a Quote”
  • Making dashboards look technical
  • Using stock imagery that feels fake
  • Forgetting older or less tech-savvy users

Definition of Done

Design is done when:

  • Customer path is obvious
  • Mobile layout works
  • Brand is consistent
  • Forms are understandable
  • Dashboard is simple
  • Client has approved look and structure
  • Design supports the business goal

5.9 Role 5: Development

Purpose

Development builds the actual system.

This includes websites, apps, dashboards, databases, forms, notifications, integrations, hosting, and reusable components.

Primary Responsibilities

ResponsibilityDescription
Technical architectureDecide how the system should be structured.
Component buildBuild reusable Shawcliffe components.
Client system buildAssemble components into client-specific system.
Database setupStore leads, products, profiles, etc.
IntegrationsEmail, SMS, payments, analytics, calendars, etc.
Admin dashboardBuild owner-facing controls.
DeploymentLaunch system to hosting/domain.
Security basicsProtect access, forms, data, and credentials.
Technical documentationNote how the system works internally.

Development Principles

1. Build Reusable First

If a feature is likely to apply to multiple archetypes, build it as a reusable component.

2. Keep the First Version Simple

Do not build a full SaaS platform when a simple dashboard and form will solve the client’s problem.

3. Avoid Custom Traps

If the logic is unique, expensive, and not reusable, it should be priced accordingly or moved to Phase 2.

4. Build for Support

A system is not done when it works once.

It must be understandable, maintainable, and supportable.

Developer Checklist

Before launch, development should confirm:

  • Pages/screens built
  • Forms connected
  • Database fields correct
  • Notifications working
  • Dashboard working
  • Admin permissions correct
  • Mobile layout functional
  • Hosting configured
  • Domain/SSL ready
  • Backups considered
  • Analytics connected if included
  • Test data removed
  • Client-specific content loaded
  • Known limitations documented

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Building too much custom logic
  • Not documenting how the system works
  • Making dashboard fields too technical
  • Not accounting for support burden
  • Not testing on mobile
  • Not protecting admin access
  • Forgetting edge cases
  • Building features not included in the scope

Definition of Done

Development is done when:

  • All included components are built
  • System works end-to-end
  • Technical setup is stable
  • Client content is loaded
  • Admin controls work
  • Known limitations are documented
  • QA can begin

5.10 Role 6: QA / Testing

Purpose

QA makes sure the system actually works before the client or public relies on it.

This is not optional.

Tiny agencies often skip QA because they are busy.

That creates embarrassment, support chaos, and trust loss.

Primary Responsibilities

ResponsibilityDescription
Test customer journeyCan a customer complete the intended action?
Test owner journeyCan the owner use the dashboard/workflow?
Test formsSubmissions, required fields, errors.
Test notificationsEmail/SMS/push/internal alerts.
Test mobilePhone layout and usability.
Test linksNavigation, social links, payment links, review links.
Test contentSpelling, prices, services, business info.
Test edge casesEmpty fields, bad input, sold out, closed, upload errors.
Test launch setupDomain, SSL, analytics, tracking, backups.

QA Ownership Model

QA should have two passes.

QA PassOwnerFocus
Customer/business QACurtisDoes this make sense to a real customer and owner?
Technical QACassandraDoes the system function properly and securely?

Both passes matter.

One catches business confusion.

The other catches technical problems.

QA Checklist by System Type

System TypeMust Test
Starter WebsiteMobile, links, forms, business info, SEO basics
Lead CaptureForm submission, notifications, CRM entry
Booking SystemDate/time, service selection, confirmation
Quote RequestJob details, photo upload, owner notification
Roadside SellerStatus, inventory, location, dashboard updates
Review SystemReview link, QR code, request wording
CRM LiteLead creation, status updates, notes
PaymentsPayment link, amount, confirmation
DashboardLogin, updates, permissions, mobile usability

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Only testing on desktop
  • Testing as the builder, not as a confused customer
  • Forgetting customer confirmation messages
  • Forgetting owner notifications
  • Not testing real phone numbers/emails
  • Not testing bad input
  • Not checking spelling/prices
  • Letting client discover obvious bugs

Definition of Done

QA is done when:

  • Critical customer path works
  • Critical owner path works
  • Mobile testing passes
  • Forms and notifications pass
  • Links work
  • Content is approved
  • Known issues are either fixed or documented
  • Launch checklist can begin

5.11 Role 7: Client Support

Purpose

Client support handles questions, fixes, updates, and post-launch requests.

Support must be friendly but bounded.

A small agency cannot survive unlimited “quick changes.”

Primary Responsibilities

ResponsibilityDescription
Receive support requestsOne clear support channel.
Triage requestsBug, update, training issue, new feature, emergency.
Respond clearlyAcknowledge and set expectation.
Fix bugsHandle included technical issues.
Manage small updatesWithin support plan limits.
Quote larger changesTurn scope creep into paid work.
Track historyKeep log of requests.
Suggest upgradesRecommend useful components when appropriate.

Support Categories

CategoryMeaningExample
BugSomething included is brokenForm not sending
Small updateMinor content changeUpdate holiday hours
Training issueClient forgot how to use systemHow to mark sold out
Change requestNew feature or larger changeAdd deposits
EmergencySite/system down or critical issueWebsite offline
Out of scopeNot covered by planBuild new page/campaign

Client-Facing Support Language

Send support requests through one message or email thread so we can track them properly. Small updates and fixes are handled according to your support plan. Larger changes or new features will be quoted before we build them.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Accepting support through too many channels
  • Replying instantly to everything
  • Doing unpaid change requests
  • Not logging support requests
  • Letting clients bypass sales/project management and go straight to development
  • Not distinguishing bugs from new requests
  • Not having support tiers

Definition of Done

Client support is working when:

  • Clients know how to request help
  • Requests are logged
  • Bugs and updates are separated
  • Support plan limits are clear
  • Larger changes become paid work
  • Development is protected from constant interruption

5.12 Role 8: Billing / Admin

Purpose

Billing/admin makes sure the business is actually operating like a business.

This includes proposals, contracts, invoices, payments, subscriptions, records, renewals, and internal organization.

Primary Responsibilities

ResponsibilityDescription
Proposal trackingKnow what has been sent and accepted.
Contract/SOW trackingMake sure scope is agreed in writing.
Invoice creationSend invoices clearly and promptly.
Payment trackingKnow what has been paid and what is outstanding.
Subscription trackingTrack monthly plans and renewal dates.
Expense trackingTrack tools, hosting, SMS, domains, subscriptions.
Client recordsStore business info, access, documents, approvals.
Renewal/cancellation trackingKnow when plans renew or end.
Tax/bookkeeping handoffKeep records organized for accounting.

Billing Rules

Rule 1: No Serious Build Without Payment Terms

Before build starts:

  • Scope must be approved
  • Price must be approved
  • Payment terms must be approved
  • Initial payment must be received if required

Rule 2: No Launch With Unresolved Payment

Do not launch major work if payment terms are not satisfied.

Rule 3: Monthly Support Must Be Tracked

Every monthly plan should have:

  • Start date
  • Amount
  • What is included
  • Billing date
  • Payment method/status
  • Cancellation terms

Admin Checklist

For each client, store:

  • Proposal
  • Signed agreement/SOW
  • Invoice/payment record
  • Client contact info
  • Archetype
  • Components included
  • Components excluded
  • Support plan
  • Login/access notes
  • Launch date
  • Renewal date
  • Support history
  • Approval records

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Starting work without payment
  • Not sending invoices promptly
  • Forgetting monthly renewals
  • Not tracking support inclusions
  • Mixing personal and business expenses
  • Not storing client approvals
  • Not knowing which clients are active on support plans

Definition of Done

Billing/admin is working when:

  • Every client has a record
  • Every project has a proposal/SOW
  • Every payment is tracked
  • Every monthly plan is tracked
  • Every subscription/tool cost is known
  • Nothing financial depends on memory

5.13 Role 9: Research & Development

Purpose

R&D helps Shawcliffe improve its services, tools, components, demos, templates, and offers.

This is not random tinkering.

R&D must support future sales and delivery.

Primary Responsibilities

ResponsibilityDescription
Research archetypesLearn how different local businesses operate.
Research pain pointsIdentify missed-money and time-waste problems.
Research toolsEvaluate tools for forms, SMS, hosting, payments, CRM, analytics.
Prototype demosBuild internal examples to show clients.
Test new componentsExplore reusable features.
Improve workflowsMake existing systems easier to build/support.
Study competitorsUnderstand what alternatives clients may compare us to.
Track lessons learnedTurn project experience into better templates.

Good R&D Questions

  • Which local businesses have repeated customer communication problems?
  • Which archetypes have the clearest pain?
  • Which components are requested repeatedly?
  • Which components can become monthly revenue?
  • Which features cause too much support?
  • Which demos help sales conversations?
  • Which tools reduce build time?
  • Which tools create dependency or cost risk?

R&D Rule

R&D should create something sellable, reusable, or operationally useful.

Not just interesting.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Building shiny demos nobody wants
  • Researching forever instead of selling
  • Chasing complex AI before basic systems are proven
  • Adding tools without considering support
  • Building components without matching them to archetypes
  • Confusing “possible” with “profitable”

Definition of Done

R&D is useful when it produces one of these:

  • New reusable component
  • Improved existing component
  • Demo system
  • Sales insight
  • Better SOP
  • Better tool choice
  • Better pricing logic
  • Better archetype understanding
  • New recurring revenue opportunity

5.14 Role 10: Template / Product Development

Purpose

Template/product development turns repeated client work into reusable Shawcliffe systems.

This is central to the agency strategy.

Without this role, Shawcliffe becomes a custom job shop.

Primary Responsibilities

ResponsibilityDescription
Build archetype templatesCreate reusable systems for each business type.
Maintain component libraryImprove reusable components.
Create demosBuild showable examples for sales.
Standardize fieldsUse reusable form/dashboard/database structures.
Standardize flowsBooking, quote request, review request, status update, etc.
Package offersTurn templates into sellable starter/growth/premium offers.
Document variationsNote differences by archetype.
Improve build speedMake each similar project easier than the last.

Template Development Examples

TemplateReusable BaseCustom Details
Contractor Quote Request SystemQuote form, photo upload, notifications, CRMTrade type, services, service area
Roadside Seller Live Status SystemStatus, inventory, location, dashboardProducts, prices, locations
Barber Booking & Review SystemService menu, booking request, review flowServices, prices, policies
Dog Groomer Pet Profile SystemBooking + pet intake fieldsBreed/service rules, policies
Tutor Progress SystemStudent profile + lesson notesSubjects, milestones, resources

Template Development Rule

Every finished project should make the next similar project faster, clearer, or easier to sell.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Treating every build as one-off
  • Not documenting reusable pieces
  • Hardcoding too many client-specific details
  • Building templates before understanding real client needs
  • Ignoring support burden
  • Not creating demos from internal templates

Definition of Done

Template/product development is working when:

  • Common archetypes have reusable starter systems
  • Components can be assembled quickly
  • Proposals reference known component bundles
  • SOPs exist for repeated builds
  • Demos support sales
  • New projects improve the library

5.15 Role 11: Documentation Maintenance

Purpose

Documentation maintenance keeps Shawcliffe organized without creating corporate bloat.

Documentation should help us:

  • Sell
  • Build
  • Test
  • Launch
  • Support
  • Train
  • Reuse

If a document does not help one of those things, it may not be needed yet.

Primary Responsibilities

ResponsibilityDescription
Maintain SOPsKeep build/support processes current.
Maintain component docsUpdate component notes after builds.
Maintain templatesKeep proposals, emails, checklists usable.
Record decisionsStore important scope/pricing/process decisions.
Update QA checklistsAdd new failure points after each project.
Update onboarding docsImprove client homework requests.
Document lessons learnedCapture what went wrong/right.
Organize file structureKeep internal folders clean.

Documents That Matter Most Early

DocumentWhy It Matters
Lead TrackerPrevents lost sales opportunities
Discovery ChecklistHelps sales identify real problems
Proposal TemplateHelps sell clearly
SOW / Scope ChecklistPrevents scope creep
Client Onboarding ChecklistPrevents delays
Component LibraryEnables repeatable systems
QA ChecklistPrevents embarrassing launch issues
Launch ChecklistPrevents missing critical steps
Support LogPrevents support chaos
Pricing SheetPrevents random quoting

Documentation Rule

Document the thing the second time you repeat it.

First time: learn.
Second time: document.
Third time: improve and standardize.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Writing huge documents nobody uses
  • Not documenting because “we’ll remember”
  • Keeping docs scattered
  • Not updating docs after mistakes
  • Creating SOPs that do not match reality
  • Writing for imaginary employees instead of current needs

Definition of Done

Documentation maintenance is working when:

  • The latest process is easy to find
  • Templates are usable
  • Component docs are current
  • QA checklists improve after mistakes
  • New projects are easier because old lessons were captured

5.16 Role 12: Client Success

Purpose

Client success makes sure the client is not just launched, but actually using the system and getting value.

A client who does not use the system will eventually cancel support.

Primary Responsibilities

ResponsibilityDescription
Post-launch check-inMake sure client knows how to use system.
Usage reviewAsk whether leads/bookings/updates are working.
Identify confusionFind where client is stuck.
Suggest improvementsRecommend useful next components.
Track winsGather testimonials and case studies.
Encourage reviews/referralsAsk happy clients to refer.
RetentionGive clients a reason to stay monthly.

Client Success Questions

Ask after launch:

  • Are you receiving inquiries properly?
  • Are customers using the form/booking/status page?
  • Are you getting fewer repeated questions?
  • Is anything confusing?
  • Are you using the dashboard?
  • Have you asked for reviews?
  • Are there leads you forgot to follow up with?
  • Is there a next improvement that would save time?
  • Would this make a good case study?
  • Do you know another owner who needs something similar?

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Launching and disappearing
  • Not checking whether client uses dashboard
  • Not asking for feedback
  • Not collecting testimonials
  • Not suggesting logical upgrades
  • Not tracking outcomes
  • Not turning success into referrals

Definition of Done

Client success is working when:

  • Clients use what was built
  • Problems are caught early
  • Monthly support feels valuable
  • Shawcliffe identifies upsells naturally
  • Testimonials/case studies are collected
  • Referrals are requested professionally

  • Support log

That is enough to run professionally without drowning in paperwork.

Outsource only after the process is clear.

Do not outsource chaos.

The first outside help should probably not be another strategist.

The first help should likely be one of:

The right first hire depends on where Shawcliffe feels the most bottleneck.

5.22 Meeting Rhythm for a Two-Person Agency

Shawcliffe does not need endless meetings.

But it does need a predictable rhythm.

Weekly 30-Minute Agency Check-In

Agenda

  • Active leads
  • Proposals waiting
  • Active projects
  • Client blockers
  • Build blockers
  • Support requests
  • Payments/invoices
  • Component/template improvements
  • Top priority for the week

10-Minute Project Check-In

Use when a project is active.

Questions

  • What is the current stage?
  • What are we waiting on?
  • What is the next task?
  • Who owns it?
  • Is scope still controlled?
  • Is client communication needed?
  • Is payment current?
  • Is launch date realistic?

Monthly Business Review

Once per month, review:

  • Leads contacted
  • Conversations started
  • Discovery calls
  • Proposals sent
  • Proposals accepted
  • Revenue collected
  • Monthly recurring revenue
  • Active support clients
  • Most requested components
  • Components causing support
  • Best archetype opportunities
  • Documentation updates needed

5.23 Internal Communication Rules

Because this is a husband-and-wife agency, clear communication matters even more.

Business stress can easily leak into personal life.

Rules

1. Use a Shared Project Board

Do not rely only on verbal memory.

2. Write Down Decisions

Especially:

  • Price
  • Scope
  • Components included
  • Client promises
  • Launch timing
  • Support commitments

3. Protect Development Time

Client requests should go through triage before becoming development interruptions.

4. No Surprise Scope

Do not promise features without checking build complexity.

5. No Surprise Deadlines

Do not promise a launch date without checking technical workload.

6. Separate “Idea” From “Commitment”

A client saying “could we add…” is not the same as Shawcliffe agreeing to add it.

Sales to Project Handoff

Before moving from sales to project, confirm:

  • Client name
  • Contact info

Strategy to Development Handoff

Before development starts, confirm:

  • Required dashboard fields
  • Required notifications
  • CRM/database needs
  • Integrations
  • Client assets received
  • Client copy/content approved or drafted
  • Launch expectations
  • Out-of-scope items

Development to QA Handoff

Before QA starts, confirm:

  • Build complete
  • Test data ready
  • Admin login ready
  • Forms connected
  • Notifications connected
  • Dashboard connected
  • Known limitations documented
  • Items needing special testing flagged

QA to Launch Handoff

Before launch, confirm:

  • Critical bugs fixed
  • Client approved content/design
  • Domain/hosting ready
  • SSL ready
  • Analytics ready if included
  • Forms tested
  • Notifications tested
  • Dashboard tested
  • QR codes tested if included
  • Backup/support plan ready
  • Launch announcement discussed

Launch to Support Handoff

After launch, confirm:

  • Client has training
  • Client knows support channel
  • Support plan is active or declined
  • Login info delivered securely
  • Known limitations documented
  • First check-in scheduled
  • Support log created
  • Upsell opportunities noted

  • Avoid unpaid extras

5.26 Role Boundaries

Sales Should Not

  • Promise custom features without technical review
  • Promise timelines without checking workload
  • Discount heavily without discussion
  • Include advanced components casually
  • Say yes to unlimited revisions
  • Avoid hard scope conversations

Development Should Not

  • Accept direct scope changes from client without project owner
  • Build unpaid extras because they are interesting
  • Skip documentation for reusable components
  • Launch without QA
  • Hide technical risks
  • Overbuild beyond business need

Project Management Should Not

  • Let client homework remain vague
  • Allow feedback from five different places
  • Move to build without content/assets
  • Ignore payment status
  • Fail to communicate blockers

Support Should Not

  • Treat every request as urgent
  • Do free new features
  • Accept requests through scattered channels forever
  • Ignore repeated training issues
  • Let monthly plans become unlimited work

5.27 Must-Have Now vs Nice-to-Have Later

Must-Have Now

Shawcliffe should immediately define:

  • Who owns sales
  • Who owns project management
  • Who owns development
  • Who owns QA
  • Who owns billing
  • Who owns support triage
  • Who approves scope
  • Who approves launch
  • Where tasks are tracked
  • Where client records live

Must-Have Role Documents

Create these now:

  • Responsibility Matrix
  • Sales-to-Project Handoff Checklist
  • Development Handoff Checklist
  • QA-to-Launch Checklist
  • Support Triage Checklist
  • Weekly Agency Check-In Agenda
  • Project Board Template
  • Client Record Template

Nice-to-Have Later

These can wait:

  • Formal hiring plan
  • Employee handbook
  • Detailed department SOPs
  • Performance review system
  • Complex ticketing process
  • Dedicated account management process
  • Advanced internal wiki
  • Formal training curriculum

5.28 Common Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Acting Like “Small” Means “No Process”

Small agencies need less process, not zero process.

A tiny agency still needs:

  • Scope
  • Payment tracking
  • QA
  • Support boundaries
  • Project tracking

Mistake 2: Both People Owning Everything

Shared opinion is fine.

Shared ownership is dangerous.

Every task needs one owner.

Mistake 3: Letting Clients Interrupt Development Directly

Client asks Curtis.
Curtis triages.
Cassandra builds what is approved.

That protects development time.

Mistake 4: Treating Documentation as Separate From Delivery

Documentation should be created from real work.

After each project, update:

  • Component notes
  • QA checklist
  • Sales script
  • Discovery questions
  • Support notes

Mistake 5: No Billing Owner

Someone must be responsible for money.

Not emotionally.
Not vaguely.
Clearly.

Mistake 6: No Launch Approval Owner

Both business and technical approval matter.

Do not launch because one person assumes the other tested it.

5.29 Definition of Done for Section 5

This section is complete when Shawcliffe Digital has:

  • Defined core internal roles
  • Assigned practical ownership between husband and wife
  • Identified which roles can be combined early
  • Clarified what cannot be ignored even while tiny
  • Identified what can be outsourced later
  • Identified possible future growth roles
  • Created a responsibility matrix
  • Created handoff checklists
  • Created meeting rhythm
  • Created role boundaries
  • Created must-have role documents
  • Defined how to prevent “I thought you were doing that”

5.30 Key Takeaways

  • Shawcliffe Digital does not need corporate departments, but it does need clear ownership.
  • Roles should be treated as hats, not job titles.
  • Curtis should likely own sales, client relationships, project management, support triage, billing follow-up, and plain-English documentation.
  • Cassandra should likely own development, technical architecture, technical QA, deployment, component implementation, and technical R&D.
  • Strategy, pricing, scope approval, launch approval, and template roadmap should be shared.
  • Every task needs one owner.
  • The most dangerous small-agency phrase is: “I thought you handled that.”
  • Support requests should be triaged before they reach development.
  • Documentation should grow from real repeated work, not imaginary corporate needs.
  • The first future hire should probably reduce admin/project/support burden, not add complexity.

Section 06

Client Journey Process

6.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Client Workflow

1. Purpose of This Section

This section defines Shawcliffe Digital’s full client journey from first contact to long-term support.

The goal is to make every project feel calm, professional, and repeatable.

This process helps us:

  • Avoid missed leads
  • Qualify clients properly
  • Identify the business archetype
  • Choose the right reusable components
  • Scope the project clearly
  • Get paid before deep work
  • Collect client assets efficiently
  • Build without chaos
  • Test before launch
  • Train the client
  • Move the client into monthly support
  • Suggest upgrades naturally
  • Turn successful projects into referrals and case studies

The internal rule:

Every client should move through the same basic journey, even if the project is small.

Small project does not mean no process.

6.2 Client Journey Overview

The Full Shawcliffe Client Journey

StageStepMain Purpose
1Lead Comes InCapture the opportunity
2Initial ConversationUnderstand the surface-level need
3QualificationDecide if the lead is worth pursuing
4Discovery CallUnderstand the real business problem
5Archetype IdentificationClassify the business
6Component SelectionChoose the reusable system pieces
7ProposalPresent the recommended system
8Contract / PaymentConfirm scope and get paid
9OnboardingCollect assets, content, access, and details
10Project PlanningTurn the sale into a build plan
11Design / BuildAssemble and customize the system
12Internal ReviewShawcliffe checks before client review
13Client ReviewClient gives structured feedback
14RevisionsComplete agreed changes
15LaunchMake the system live
16TrainingTeach the owner how to use it
17Monthly SupportMaintain and improve the system
18Upsells / RetentionAdd value over time
19Referral / Case StudyTurn success into future sales

6.3 The Client Journey as a Simple Flow

Basic Flow

Lead
→ Initial conversation
→ Qualify
→ Discovery
→ Archetype
→ Components
→ Proposal
→ Contract/payment
→ Onboarding
→ Build
→ QA
→ Client review
→ Revisions
→ Launch
→ Training
→ Support
→ Upgrade/referral

Important Rule

Do not skip from:

“Someone is interested”

straight to:

“Let’s build something.”

That creates chaos.

Minimum path before building:

  • Qualified lead
  • Archetype identified
  • Components selected
  • Scope written
  • Payment terms approved
  • Client assets requested
  • Project plan created

6.4 Step 1: Lead Comes In

Goal

Capture the lead so it does not disappear.

A lead may come from:

  • Referral
  • Facebook group
  • Community connection
  • Google search
  • Website inquiry
  • Cold outreach reply
  • Business card/QR code
  • Market conversation
  • Existing client referral
  • Family/friend introduction
  • Walk-up conversation with a local owner

Owner

TaskOwner
Capture leadCurtis
Add to trackerCurtis
Technical note if neededCassandra, only if technical fit is unclear

Checklist

Record the lead immediately.

FieldExample
Business nameExample Website Lead
Contact person[Contact Name]

Likely archetypeProfessional/local organization, not exact owner-operated archetype

Client-Facing Language

Use this when someone first expresses interest:

Thanks for reaching out. We help local businesses and small organizations build simple websites, apps, and customer systems that make it easier for people to contact you, book, request information, or stay updated. I can ask a few quick questions first to see what would actually make sense.

Internal Notes

Every lead should go into a tracker.

Do not rely on:

  • Memory
  • Text thread only
  • Facebook message only
  • “I’ll remember”
  • Verbal conversation only

A lead is not real internally until it is recorded.

Red Flags

  • “I need an app” but no clear problem
  • “How much for a website?” with no details
  • “We do not have much budget” before scope is known
  • “Can you just quickly build…”
  • Committee/client group unclear
  • No decision maker identified
  • Wants immediate price without conversation

Output of This Step

A lead record exists with:

  • Business name
  • Contact person
  • Source
  • Initial need
  • Next action
  • Follow-up date

6.5 Step 2: Initial Conversation

Goal

Understand the surface-level need and decide whether to continue.

This is not full discovery yet.

The purpose is to answer:

  • What kind of business is this?
  • What do they think they need?
  • Is there a real business problem?
  • Are they likely a fit?
  • Should we book a discovery call?

Owner

TaskOwner
Initial conversationCurtis
Technical feasibility inputCassandra if needed
Lead notesCurtis

Initial Questions

Ask a few simple questions.

Quick Questions

  • What kind of business do you run?
  • What are you hoping to improve?
  • How do customers currently contact you?
  • Where are things getting messy right now?
  • Are you mainly trying to get more leads, save time, organize bookings, collect quote requests, update customers, or look more professional?
  • Do you already have a website or system?
  • Is this something you want soon, or are you just exploring?

Client-Facing Language

Before talking about price or features, I like to understand what problem we are solving. A simple website, a booking system, and a quote request system are all different, so I want to make sure I am not recommending the wrong thing.

Internal Notes

At this point, do not over-explain all 24 components.

Listen first.

You are looking for clues:

What They SayWhat It Might Mean
“People keep messaging me the same questions.”Resource Library, Service Menu, Lead Capture
“I miss calls while working.”Lead Capture, Notifications, CRM Lite
“People ask if I’m open.”Status Tracker
“People ask what I have today.”Product Inventory / Limited Batch
“I need better quote requests.”Lead Capture, Photo Upload
“I forget to follow up.”CRM Lite
“I need more reviews.”Review Request System
“Everything is in texts.”CRM Lite, Dashboard, Lead Capture

Red Flags

  • Client refuses to explain business problem
  • Client only wants the cheapest option
  • Client seems hostile or dismissive
  • Client expects guaranteed leads immediately
  • Client wants a large custom system but says budget is tiny
  • Client cannot identify who will decide
  • Client wants a price before any scope discussion

Output of This Step

Decision:

  • Book discovery call
  • Send simple info
  • Decline politely
  • Follow up later
  • Ask Cassandra for technical feasibility first

6.6 Step 3: Qualification

Goal

Decide whether the lead is worth serious time.

Qualification protects Shawcliffe from bad-fit clients and unpaid consulting.

Owner

TaskOwner
QualificationCurtis
Technical feasibility checkCassandra
Final accept/decline decisionShared if complex

Qualification Criteria

QuestionGood SignBad Sign
Do they fit an archetype?Yes, clear categoryTotally custom/vague
Do they have a real problem?Missed leads, time waste, poor booking, etc.“I just want something cool”
Can our components help?Yes, reusable system fitNeeds complex custom software
Do they have budget?Understands professional work costsWants everything cheap/free
Are they respectful?Communicates normallyPushy, rude, dismissive
Are they responsive?Answers basic questionsAvoids details
Is timeline realistic?Flexible or clearWants rush without paying
Is there recurring potential?Support, updates, reviews, CRM, notificationsOne-off only, no maintenance interest
Can this become reusable?Yes, improves templateOne-off oddity

Qualification Score

Use a simple score.

ScoreMeaning
8–10Strong lead
5–7Possible, needs caution
3–4Weak fit
0–2Decline or do not pursue

Score These 10 Items

  • Fits one of 12 archetypes
  • Clear business problem
  • Budget likely exists
  • Owner is respectful
  • Timeline is realistic
  • Reusable component fit
  • Monthly support potential
  • Decision maker accessible
  • Client can provide content/assets
  • Project is low-risk enough for us

Client-Facing Language

If qualified:

This sounds like the kind of problem we help with. The next step would be a short discovery call where we map how customers currently contact you and what simple system would make the most sense.

If not qualified:

Based on what you described, I do not think we are the best fit for this project. We focus on practical websites, lead systems, booking systems, quote request systems, and owner dashboards for local businesses. I would rather be honest than overpromise.

Internal Notes

Do not spend hours planning a solution for an unqualified lead.

A qualified lead should have:

  • A business problem
  • A business owner or decision maker
  • A rough budget possibility
  • A system fit
  • A next step

Red Flags

  • “Can you send a full plan first?”
  • “I have no budget right now, but this could be big later.”
  • “I just need you to build my app idea.”
  • “This should only take a few hours.”
  • “I need it this weekend.”
  • “I already had three developers and they were all idiots.”
  • “Can you guarantee I’ll get customers?”

Output of This Step

Lead is marked as:

  • Qualified
  • Needs more info
  • Not a fit
  • Follow-up later

6.7 Step 4: Discovery Call

Goal

Understand the real business workflow and identify the best system.

Discovery should reveal:

  • How customers find the business
  • How customers contact the business
  • Where leads get missed
  • Where time is wasted
  • Where money is lost
  • What customer questions repeat
  • What needs to be automated or organized
  • Which archetype applies
  • Which reusable components are needed

Owner

TaskOwner
Run discovery callCurtis
Technical questionsCassandra if present or follow-up
NotesCurtis
Component feasibilityCassandra reviews after

Discovery Call Structure

PartTimePurpose
Intro2 minutesSet tone
Business overview5 minutesUnderstand business
Customer journey10 minutesHow customers currently move from interest to sale
Pain points10 minutesFind time/money/customer problems
Current tools5 minutesWebsite, social, forms, calendar, Google, etc.
Ideal outcome5 minutesWhat would make project worth it
Budget/timeline5 minutesCheck fit
Next steps3 minutesExplain proposal process

Core Discovery Questions

Business Basics

  • What do you sell or provide?
  • Who is your ideal customer?
  • What area do you serve?
  • Are you solo, or do you have staff?
  • What services/products make you the most money?

Customer Flow

  • How do customers usually find you?
  • What do they do next?
  • Do they call, text, DM, email, visit, or book online?
  • What happens after they contact you?
  • Where do things get messy?

Time Waste

  • What questions do customers ask over and over?
  • What do you find yourself typing repeatedly?
  • What admin task do you hate most?
  • What do you forget to follow up on?
  • What takes time but does not directly make money?

Missed Money

  • Where do leads get lost?
  • What kind of customer inquiries are usually bad or incomplete?
  • What do people ask for that you do not have a system for?
  • Do you ask customers for reviews?
  • Do you have a way to encourage repeat business?

Current System

  • Do you have a website?
  • Do you use Facebook/Instagram?
  • Do you use Google Business Profile?
  • Do you use forms, booking software, spreadsheets, or CRM?
  • What works okay right now?

Ideal Outcome

  • If this project worked perfectly, what would be easier?
  • What would make this worth the money?
  • What do you want customers to be able to do?
  • What do you want to stop doing manually?
  • What would be a clear win in the first 30–60 days?

Client-Facing Language

The point of this call is not to bury you in tech. I want to understand how customers currently move through your business and where things are costing you time, money, or missed opportunities. Then we can recommend a simple system that fits how you actually work.

Internal Notes

Discovery is where Shawcliffe should listen for component clues.

Component Clue Table

Client ProblemLikely Component
“People ask what I offer.”Service / Product Menu
“People message everywhere.”Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
“I miss messages.”Notifications
“I forget who contacted me.”CRM Lite
“I need photos before quoting.”Photo / File Upload
“People want to book.”Booking Request System
“Customers do not know if I’m open.”Status Tracker
“I sell out.”Product Inventory / Limited Batch
“I move locations.”Location / Pop-Up Tracker
“I need deposits.”Payments / Deposits
“I have repeat customers.”Recurring Schedule
“I track homes/pets/vehicles/students.”Profile Component
“People ask the same policies.”Resource Library
“I need documents before starting.”Document Checklist / File Portal
“I want to know what marketing works.”Analytics
“I need help replying/routing leads.”Automation / AI later

Red Flags

  • Client wants us to diagnose their whole business for free
  • Client is evasive about budget
  • Client cannot explain what they sell
  • Client wants features but no business goal
  • Client wants us to guarantee revenue
  • Client wants advanced custom software before basic process
  • Client interrupts or dismisses reasonable questions
  • Client has unrealistic deadline
  • Client says “I’ll send everything” but has no assets ready

Output of This Step

Discovery notes with:

  • Business overview
  • Archetype
  • Current customer journey
  • Pain points
  • Missed-money opportunities
  • Recommended system type
  • Likely components
  • Budget/timeline notes
  • Red flags
  • Proposal recommendation

Classify the business into one primary Shawcliffe archetype.

Client-Facing Language

Internally, we group businesses into a few common patterns so we are not reinventing the wheel every time. Your business fits closest to our [archetype] system, which means we can start from a proven structure and customize the details for you.

Red Flags

  • Business does not fit any clear archetype
  • Business model is not clear
  • Client wants multiple business models solved at once
  • Client changes direction during discovery
  • Client wants one system for unrelated businesses
  • Too many audiences, offers, or workflows

Output of This Step

Client record includes:

  • Primary archetype
  • Secondary archetype if needed
  • Reason for classification
  • Matching starter offer
  • Likely components

Do not include everything.

Client-Facing Language

We break projects into components so the scope stays clear. For your first version, I would focus on the pieces that solve the biggest problem first. Then we can add more once the core system is working.

Internal Notes

A proposal should clearly show:

  • Components included
  • Components not included
  • Optional add-ons
  • Future upgrade path

This prevents:

  • “I thought that was included”
  • Scope creep
  • Underpricing
  • Overbuilding

Red Flags

  • Client wants all 24 components
  • Client wants advanced automation first
  • Client does not want to choose priorities
  • Client wants dashboard/admin control but no support plan
  • Client wants SMS but does not want monthly fees
  • Client wants payments without clear policies
  • Client wants sensitive document collection without proper safeguards

A component list sorted into:

Client-Facing Proposal Language

Based on our conversation, the main issue is not simply that you need “a website.” The bigger opportunity is to make it easier for customers to [book/request a quote/check availability/preorder/contact you] without everything getting scattered across texts, calls, and DMs.

We recommend starting with a simple [system name] that includes the core pieces needed to solve that problem now, with a clear path to add more later.

Internal Notes

Keep proposal language plain.

Avoid:

  • Technical jargon
  • Too many package options
  • Endless feature lists
  • Weak boundaries
  • Unclear support terms

Use the archetype and components as the structure.

Red Flags

  • Client asks for major unpaid revisions to proposal
  • Client tries to negotiate scope up and price down

  • Client says “we’ll figure out the details later”
  • Client wants immediate build before agreement/payment
  • Client asks for ownership/access terms that are unclear

  • Forms built
  • Notifications connected
  • Dashboard built if included
  • CRM/data configured if included
  • Add-ons connected if included
  • Internal review completed

Review Stage

  • Client review sent
  • Feedback received in structured format
  • Revisions categorized
  • Included revisions completed
  • Add-ons quoted if needed
  • Final QA completed
  • Client approval received

Launch Stage

  • Payment status checked
  • Domain/hosting/SSL complete
  • Forms tested
  • Notifications tested
  • Dashboard tested
  • Mobile tested
  • QR codes tested if included
  • Analytics connected if included

  • Support handoff completed

  • Case study considered

6.24 Client Journey by Archetype

Personal Care Appointment Businesses

Main journey emphasis:

  • Discovery should focus on booking, rebooking, no-shows, reviews, prices, services, and DMs.
  • Proposal should likely recommend Booking Request + Review Request + CRM Lite.
  • Training should focus on managing appointment requests and review follow-up.

Home Service Trades

Main journey emphasis:

  • Discovery should focus on quote quality, photos, location, job type, urgency, missed calls, and follow-up.
  • Proposal should likely recommend Quote Request + Photo Upload + Notifications + CRM Lite.
  • Training should focus on reviewing quote requests and following up.

Home & Property Maintenance

Main journey emphasis:

  • Discovery should focus on recurring work, property notes, access instructions, service areas, and seasonal reminders.
  • Proposal should likely recommend Recurring Client System.
  • Training should focus on property details, recurring schedules, and customer notes.

Food Producers & Specialty Makers

Main journey emphasis:

  • Discovery should focus on menus, custom orders, lead times, deposits, limited batches, and pickup/delivery.
  • Proposal should likely recommend Menu + Preorder + Limited Batch System.
  • Training should focus on updating products, availability, and order requests.

Mobile / Pop-Up Sellers

Main journey emphasis:

  • Discovery should focus on status, location, daily inventory, sold-out updates, QR signs, and customer alerts.
  • Proposal should likely recommend Live Status System.
  • Training should focus on dashboard updates from phone.

Pet & Animal Services

Main journey emphasis:

  • Discovery should focus on booking, pet details, behaviour notes, allergies, recurring service, and reminders.
  • Proposal should likely recommend Booking + Pet Profile System.
  • Training should focus on pet profiles and booking requests.

Vehicle & Equipment Services

Main journey emphasis:

  • Discovery should focus on vehicle details, photos, issue description, location, urgency, and repeat maintenance.
  • Proposal should likely recommend Vehicle Service Request System.
  • Training should focus on reviewing vehicle requests and tracking service history.

Creative & Event Services

Main journey emphasis:

  • Discovery should focus on date, venue, package, budget, inspiration, deposits, and follow-up.
  • Proposal should likely recommend Event Inquiry System.
  • Training should focus on reviewing inquiries and tracking event leads.

Education, Coaching & Instruction

Main journey emphasis:

  • Discovery should focus on inquiries, scheduling, packages, student progress, parent communication, and resources.
  • Proposal should likely recommend Student Booking & Progress System.
  • Training should focus on student notes and resources.

Health-Adjacent Local Professionals

Main journey emphasis:

  • Discovery should focus on service clarity, intake, policies, booking, resources, and privacy boundaries.
  • Proposal should likely recommend Intake & Booking System.
  • Training should focus on intake forms and resource updates.

Local Retail / Boutique Shops

Main journey emphasis:

  • Discovery should focus on local visibility, hours, products, promos, events, customer list, reviews, and QR codes.
  • Proposal should likely recommend Promo & Review System.
  • Training should focus on updating promos/products and requesting reviews.

Professional Local Services

Main journey emphasis:

  • Discovery should focus on qualification, intake, documents, consultation requests, process clarity, and follow-up.
  • Proposal should likely recommend Inquiry & Intake System.
  • Training should focus on reviewing intake submissions and document checklists.

Must-Have Now

Shawcliffe needs a simple version of this process immediately.

Create:

Nice-to-Have Later

Do not delay sales waiting for:

  • Fully automated CRM

  • Advanced ticketing system
  • Full video training library
  • Full case study library
  • Automated reporting dashboard

Use simple tools first.

6.26 Common Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Skipping Qualification

Not every interested person is a good client.

Bad-fit clients cost more than they pay.

Mistake 2: Building From a Conversation Instead of a Scope

A conversation is not a scope.

A text message is not a scope.

A vague “website/app” request is not a scope.

Mistake 3: Not Separating Included vs Not Included

Every proposal should say both.

Included components.
Not included components.

That protects everyone.

Mistake 4: Starting Before Client Homework Is Ready

If the client has not provided services, prices, photos, policies, or access, the project will stall.

Mistake 5: Letting Review Become Redesign

Client review is for corrections and agreed revisions, not unlimited reinvention.

Mistake 6: Launching Without Testing

Forms, notifications, dashboard, mobile, links, QR codes, and payment links must be tested.

Mistake 7: Launching Without Support Boundaries

After launch, the client must know:

  • How to ask for help
  • What is included
  • What is not included
  • What costs extra
  • What response time to expect

6.27 Definition of Done for Section 6

This section is complete when Shawcliffe Digital has:

  • A full lead-to-support client journey
  • Clear stage-by-stage responsibilities
  • Checklists for each step
  • Client-facing language for each step
  • Internal notes for avoiding chaos
  • Red flags at each stage
  • Defined outputs for each step
  • A master client journey checklist
  • Archetype-specific journey notes
  • Must-have process documents identified
  • Clear rules for sales, onboarding, build, review, launch, support, and retention

6.28 Key Takeaways

  • Shawcliffe should not jump from interest to build.
  • Every lead should be captured, qualified, classified by archetype, and mapped to components.
  • Discovery should uncover the real business problem, not just the requested feature.
  • Every proposal should include components included, components not included, price, timeline, client responsibilities, and monthly support.
  • Serious build should not begin without approved scope and payment terms.
  • Client onboarding is where many projects slow down, so it needs a checklist.
  • Client review must be structured to avoid unlimited revisions.
  • Launch requires testing, approval, payment status, training, and support handoff.
  • Monthly support should be bounded, tracked, and tied to real ongoing value.
  • Upsells should come from real client needs, not random pressure.
  • Successful projects should become case studies, referrals, and better templates.

Section 07

Sales Process Documentation

7.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Sales Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section defines Shawcliffe Digital’s practical sales process.

The goal is not to become pushy, fake, slick, or corporate.

The goal is to help local owner-operated businesses clearly understand:

  • What problem they have
  • Why the problem costs them time or money
  • What simple system would help
  • Why Shawcliffe Digital is a good fit
  • What the next step is

Shawcliffe Digital should sell like a local, practical, trustworthy husband-and-wife agency.

The core sales rule:

We do not pressure people into buying tech. We help business owners see where they are losing customers, time, reviews, or follow-up — then we offer a simple system to fix it.

7.2 Shawcliffe Digital Sales Philosophy

We Sell Business Outcomes, Not Features

Do not lead with:

  • “We build apps.”
  • “We use dashboards.”
  • “We can integrate SMS.”
  • “We can build custom forms.”
  • “We can create a CRM.”

Lead with:

  • “You are missing quote requests.”
  • “Customers do not know how to book.”
  • “You are answering the same questions repeatedly.”
  • “Your leads are scattered across texts and DMs.”
  • “Happy customers are not being asked for reviews.”
  • “Customers do not know if you are open or sold out.”
  • “You need one simple place where customers can take the next step.”

What We Really Sell

What Clients Think They WantWhat They Actually Need
WebsiteA professional customer path
AppA simpler business workflow
Contact formBetter lead capture
Booking pageLess scheduling chaos
DashboardOwner control
SMSFaster customer updates
CRMNo forgotten leads
SEOMore local visibility
QR codePhysical-to-digital customer action
AutomationLess manual follow-up
Review linkReputation growth

Sales Tone

Shawcliffe’s tone should be:

  • Friendly
  • Local
  • Plain-spoken
  • Curious
  • Practical
  • Respectful
  • Honest
  • Calm
  • Confident
  • Not desperate
  • Not manipulative
  • Not corporate

Sales Promise

We help local owner-operated businesses turn customer interest into organized leads, bookings, quote requests, reviews, and repeat business using simple websites, apps, dashboards, forms, notifications, and follow-up systems.

7.5 Cold Outreach

Cold outreach means contacting a business owner who has not asked for help.

This must be respectful and specific.

Do not send generic spam.

Good Cold Outreach Targets

Look for businesses that:

  • Have no website
  • Have a very outdated website
  • Only use Facebook/Instagram
  • Have poor or inconsistent Google Business Profile info
  • Have no clear booking/request process
  • Have no review link/process
  • Have changing inventory/status but no live update system
  • Ask customers to “DM to order”
  • Are clearly owner-operated
  • Match one of Shawcliffe’s 12 archetypes

Cold Outreach Rules

Do

  • Be specific
  • Be brief
  • Mention a real observation
  • Offer a simple improvement
  • Make the next step easy
  • Sound human
  • Respect silence

Do Not

  • Insult their current website
  • Pretend you know their business better than they do
  • Use fake urgency
  • Send huge paragraphs
  • Promise guaranteed leads
  • Spam repeatedly
  • Use manipulative fear tactics

General Cold Outreach Message

Hi [Name], I’m Curtis from Shawcliffe Digital. We help local owner-operated businesses set up simple websites, quote forms, booking systems, review request systems, and owner dashboards.

I noticed [specific observation — example: your business seems to rely mostly on Facebook / customers have to message for quotes / your menu or availability changes often].

A simple system could make it easier for customers to [request a quote / book / see what’s available / contact you] without everything getting buried in messages.

No pressure — I just thought it might be useful. Would it be okay if I sent you a quick example?

Better Cold Outreach Formula

Use this structure:

  • Who I am
  • Why I’m contacting you
  • Specific observation
  • Simple business problem
  • Simple possible solution
  • Low-pressure next step

Cold Outreach Follow-Up

Hi [Name], just following up once. I know you’re busy. The idea I had was a simple [quote request / booking / live status / preorder] system so customers can [specific customer action] more easily. No worries if it is not a priority right now.

7.6 Warm Outreach

Warm outreach means contacting someone where some relationship already exists.

This may include:

  • Family referral
  • Friend referral
  • Community connection
  • Existing acquaintance
  • Someone met at a market
  • Someone who asked casually
  • Someone who knows Shawcliffe through another person

Warm outreach should feel personal and natural.

Warm Outreach Message

Hi [Name], it was good talking with you about [business/project]. Shawcliffe Digital helps small local businesses set up simple websites and customer systems — things like quote forms, booking requests, review requests, customer follow-up, and owner dashboards.

From what you mentioned, it sounds like the biggest opportunity might be making it easier for customers to [specific action]. I’d be happy to ask a few questions and see what kind of simple system would actually make sense.

Referral Introduction Response

When someone introduces Shawcliffe to a lead:

Hi [Name], nice to meet you. [Referrer] mentioned you might be looking for help with [website/system/project]. We help local businesses and small organizations create practical websites and simple customer systems so people can contact, book, request info, or stay updated more easily.

Before recommending anything, I’d want to understand what you need the site/system to actually do for you.

After an In-Person Conversation

Hi [Name], this is Curtis from Shawcliffe Digital. Good chatting with you earlier. I was thinking about what you said regarding [missed calls / quote requests / booking messages / product updates]. That is exactly the kind of practical problem we help with.

The simple version would be a system where customers can [action], and you receive the details in one organized place.

7.8 Discovery Call Questions

Discovery is where Shawcliffe finds the real sales opportunity.

Do not rush to pitch.

Universal Discovery Questions

Business Basics

  • What kind of business do you run?
  • How long have you been doing it?
  • Are you solo, or do you have staff?
  • What area do you serve?
  • What services/products make you the most money?
  • What kind of customer do you want more of?

Current Customer Flow

  • How do customers usually find you?
  • What do they do next?
  • Do they call, text, email, DM, book online, or walk in?
  • Where do customer messages usually come from?
  • What happens after someone contacts you?

Pain and Chaos

  • What gets messy?
  • What do you repeat over and over?
  • What do customers often ask before they buy/book?
  • What do you forget to follow up on?
  • Where do leads get missed?
  • Where do customers get confused?

Time and Money

  • What admin task wastes the most time?
  • What type of inquiry is usually incomplete?
  • What kind of customer is not worth your time?
  • What do you wish customers would tell you upfront?
  • Where do you think money is being left on the table?

Current Tools

  • Do you have a website?
  • Do you use Google Business Profile?
  • Do you use Facebook/Instagram?
  • Do you use booking software?
  • Do you use forms?
  • Do you track leads anywhere?
  • Do you ask customers for reviews?

Ideal Outcome

  • What would make this project worth it?
  • What would you like customers to be able to do?
  • What would you like to stop doing manually?
  • What would make your business look more professional?
  • What would help you follow up better?
  • What would you want working first?

Budget and Timeline

  • Is this urgent, or are you planning ahead?
  • Do you have a rough budget in mind?
  • Are you looking for a starter version or a more complete system?
  • Are you open to monthly support after launch?
  • Who else needs to approve this?

7.13 How to Explain Shawcliffe’s Services Simply

The 10-Second Explanation

We build simple websites, apps, and customer systems for local businesses so they can get more leads, save time, and stop losing customers in messy texts, calls, and DMs.

The 30-Second Explanation

Shawcliffe Digital helps owner-operated businesses set up practical digital systems. That might be a website, quote request form, booking request system, live inventory/status page, review request system, owner dashboard, or customer follow-up system. The point is not just to look good online — it is to make it easier for customers to take action and easier for the owner to manage the business.

The “Not Just Apps” Explanation

We do build apps and websites, but we do not think of it as just selling apps. A local business usually needs a system: a way for customers to find them, understand what they offer, request service, book, send details, get updates, leave reviews, and come back. That is what we build.

The DIY Objection Explanation

You can piece some of this together yourself with tools like Wix, Google Forms, Calendly, or Facebook. The hard part is usually designing the whole customer flow so it actually fits your business and does not become another thing you ignore. We set up the system around how you actually work.

7.14 Selling Value Without Being Pushy

Sales Mindset

Do not think:

“How do I convince this person?”

Think:

“Can I clearly show them where a better system would save time, reduce missed opportunities, or help them get more business?”

Ethical Value Selling Questions

Ask:

  • What happens when you miss a call?
  • How many inquiries do you get in a normal week?
  • How many are incomplete?
  • How many do you forget to follow up on?
  • How often do customers ask the same questions?
  • How often do happy customers leave reviews?
  • How much is one good customer worth?
  • What would one extra booking/job/order per month be worth?
  • What admin task would you gladly stop doing manually?
  • What would make your business look more professional?

Value Framing Examples

Instead of:

This system costs $1,500.

Say:

If this saves you a few hours a month, helps you catch missed inquiries, and turns even one extra serious lead into a booked job, it can pay for itself pretty quickly.

Instead of:

You need a CRM.

Say:

You need a simple way to see who contacted you, what they asked for, and who still needs a follow-up.

Instead of:

You need automation.

Say:

You are doing the same follow-up manually over and over. Once the basic process is clear, we can automate parts of it.

7.15 Handling Price Objections

Price objections are normal.

Do not panic, apologize, or instantly discount.

First understand the objection.

Common Price Objections

ObjectionWhat It Might Mean
“That’s more than I expected.”They did not understand the scope/value
“I can build a website myself.”They see it as a website, not a system
“Another person is cheaper.”They are comparing different levels of service
“I’m just starting out.”Budget may be real constraint
“Can we do it for less?”Need smaller scope
“I don’t need all that.”Scope may be too large
“Will this guarantee customers?”Needs expectation setting
“I need to think about it.”Could be budget, trust, timing, spouse/partner approval

Price Objection Responses

“That’s more than I expected.”

I understand. The reason it is priced that way is because this is more than a basic online brochure. It includes [components], which are meant to help customers actually [book/request a quote/check availability/follow up]. We can also look at a smaller starter version if that makes more sense right now.

“Can we do it cheaper?”

Possibly, but we would need to reduce scope rather than quietly cut corners. The clean way to lower the price is to decide which components are essential for launch and which ones can wait for a future phase.

“I can build a website myself.”

You might be able to. The bigger question is whether you want to spend your time figuring out the customer flow, forms, notifications, updates, review requests, and follow-up. We are not just selling pages — we are setting up a system around how your business gets customers.

“Someone else is cheaper.”

That may be true. The important thing is comparing what is included. Some providers are building a simple page. We are usually building the customer path, lead capture, notifications, owner updates, review requests, and support around it. If you only need a basic page, a cheaper option might be fine.

“Will this guarantee more customers?”

No honest person should guarantee that a website or system alone will produce a specific number of customers. What we can do is remove friction: make you easier to contact, make inquiries more organized, help you follow up, improve professionalism, and support reviews. Those things improve your chances, but they still depend on your offer, reputation, follow-up, and market.

“I’m just starting out.”

That makes sense. In that case, I would not recommend overbuilding. A starter system with your business profile, services, inquiry form, notifications, and review link may be enough to begin professionally. More advanced pieces can be added once there is more demand.

7.16 Professional Follow-Up

Follow-up is not pestering.

Follow-up is professional closure.

Many owners are busy. Silence does not always mean no.

Follow-Up Rules

RuleReason
Always follow up after a meaningful conversationPeople are busy
Keep follow-ups shortRespect time
Reference their specific problemShows you listened
Give a clear next stepReduces friction
Stop after a reasonable numberAvoid desperation
Track follow-up datesPrevents lost leads

Recommended Follow-Up Sequence

Follow-UpTimingPurpose
11–2 days after proposalFriendly check-in
25–7 days laterClarify questions/offer smaller scope
310–14 days laterFinal polite follow-up
NurtureMonthly or occasionalStay in touch if good fit

Follow-Up Message 1

Hi [Name], just checking in to see if you had any questions about the proposal. The main thing we were trying to solve was [specific problem], and the recommended system was built around making it easier for customers to [specific action].

Follow-Up Message 2

Hi [Name], I know things get busy. If the full version feels like too much right now, we can also talk about a smaller starter version focused only on [core outcome]. That would let you launch the most important piece first and add more later.

Final Follow-Up Message

Hi [Name], I do not want to keep bothering you, so I’ll leave this here for now. I still think the biggest opportunity is [specific problem/opportunity]. If it becomes a priority later, I’d be happy to revisit it.

7.17 When to Walk Away From a Lead

Walking away is part of good sales.

Bad clients are expensive even when they pay.

Walk Away When

  • Client refuses written scope
  • Client refuses reasonable payment terms
  • Client is rude or disrespectful
  • Client expects guaranteed results
  • Client wants illegal, dishonest, or misleading work
  • Client wants major custom software at starter pricing
  • Client will not answer basic questions
  • Client keeps changing the project before it starts
  • Client wants sensitive data workflows beyond Shawcliffe’s current ability
  • Client pressures for a launch timeline that would require unsafe shortcuts
  • Client does not trust Shawcliffe but still wants to proceed

Walk-Away Message

Thanks for the conversation. After thinking it through, I do not think Shawcliffe Digital is the right fit for this project. We focus on practical websites, lead systems, booking systems, quote request systems, and simple owner dashboards for local businesses. I would rather be honest now than take on something that is not a good fit.

7.31 Sales Scripts by Situation

First Call Opening

Thanks for taking the time. I’ll keep this practical. I want to understand how customers currently find you, contact you, book or request service, and where things get messy. Then I can recommend whether you need a simple website, a lead system, booking system, quote request system, or something else.

Explaining Archetypes

Internally, we group local businesses into common patterns. Some businesses mostly need bookings. Some need quote requests. Some need live inventory or status updates. Some need intake forms or customer profiles. Once we know which pattern your business fits, we can recommend the right system without reinventing everything from scratch.

Explaining Components

We build systems from reusable components. For example, a contractor might need a quote request form, photo upload, notifications, CRM Lite, and review requests. A barber might need services, booking requests, rebooking, and reviews. The components change based on the business problem.

Explaining Monthly Support

After launch, the system still needs to be maintained. Forms, notifications, updates, review requests, dashboards, and small changes all need a support process. Monthly support gives you a clear way to get help without everything becoming random one-off messages.

Explaining Phase 2

That is a good idea, but I would not put it in the first version. The first version should solve the main problem and launch cleanly. Once it is working, we can add that as a Phase 2 improvement.

7.32 Sales Objection Cheat Sheet

ObjectionResponse
“I just need a basic website.”“That may be true. The question is what you need the website to do — generate inquiries, explain services, collect quote requests, book appointments, or support reviews?”
“I already have Facebook.”“Facebook is useful, but it is not the same as having a clear customer path you control.”
“I get enough customers already.”“That is good. Then the value may be saving time, organizing inquiries, getting reviews, or reducing repetitive messages.”
“I’m not techy.”“That is exactly why we keep the owner side simple.”
“I don’t want an app.”“You may not need one. You may just need a simple system customers can use from their phone.”
“I don’t have time.”“The system is meant to save time, but we would need your basics upfront: services, prices, photos, and business info.”
“Can this be cheaper?”“We can reduce scope, but I do not want to quietly cut corners.”
“I need to ask my spouse/partner.”“Of course. I can send a clear summary of the problem, recommended system, price, and next steps.”
“Will this get me leads?”“It will make you easier to contact and help reduce missed opportunities. No honest system can guarantee a specific number of leads.”
“I’m too small for this.”“Then we start small. A starter system may be enough until demand grows.”

7.36 Common Sales Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Selling Too Technically

Do not sell “CRM Lite.”

Sell:

“A simple way to track who contacted you and who still needs follow-up.”

Mistake 2: Pitching Before Understanding

The more you listen, the easier the sale becomes.

Mistake 3: Giving Free Consulting Forever

Be helpful, but do not build the whole strategy for free before they become a client.

Mistake 4: Chasing Bad Leads

A bad lead can waste more time than a good client pays for.

Mistake 5: Discounting Instead of Reducing Scope

If price is too high, remove components.

Do not quietly do the same work for less.

Mistake 6: Forgetting Monthly Support

Every proposal should explain what happens after launch.

Mistake 7: Overpromising Results

Do not promise:

  • Guaranteed leads
  • Guaranteed Google ranking
  • Guaranteed revenue
  • Guaranteed reviews
  • Guaranteed customer behaviour

Promise professional setup, clear systems, practical improvements, and support.
