7.38 Key Takeaways

  • Shawcliffe should sell business systems, not apps.
  • The best sales conversations start with the owner’s real pain: missed leads, time waste, messy messages, unclear booking, weak follow-up, no reviews, or poor customer clarity.
  • Every lead should be classified by archetype.
  • Every recommendation should be built from reusable components.
  • The sales process should be friendly, local, direct, and honest.
  • Price objections should be handled by clarifying value or reducing scope, not by panicked discounting.
  • Bad leads should be declined early.
  • Follow-up is professional, but chasing forever is not.
  • Referrals and case studies will become one of Shawcliffe’s strongest growth channels.

Before creating detailed discovery templates, Shawcliffe should answer:

Section 08

Client Discovery Templates

8.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Discovery Questionnaires

1. Purpose of This Section

This section gives Shawcliffe Digital practical discovery templates for local owner-operated business leads.

Discovery is where we figure out:

  • What the business actually does
  • How customers currently find them
  • Where leads get missed
  • Where the owner loses time
  • Where money is being left on the table
  • What customers repeatedly ask
  • What manual admin tasks are draining the owner
  • Which archetype the business fits
  • Which reusable components are needed
  • What should be included now
  • What should wait until later
  • Whether the client is a good fit

The internal rule:

Discovery is not about asking random questions. Discovery is about finding the business problem that justifies the system.

8.2 How Shawcliffe Should Use Discovery

Discovery should produce enough information to write a clear proposal.

A good discovery process should answer:

QuestionWhy It Matters
What archetype is this business?Determines template direction
What is the main customer action?Book, request quote, preorder, check status, contact, upload, review
What is currently messy?Reveals pain
Where is time being wasted?Supports value argument
Where is money being lost?Supports pricing/value
What components are needed?Defines scope
What can wait?Prevents overbuilding
Is the client realistic?Prevents bad projects
Is monthly support likely?Supports recurring revenue

8.3 Discovery Formats

Discovery can happen through:

  • Phone call
  • Video call
  • In-person conversation
  • Short intake form
  • Email questionnaire
  • Combination of call + form

For early Shawcliffe Digital, the best format is usually:

  • Short initial conversation
  • Discovery call
  • Follow-up form for missing details

Do not send a giant questionnaire before trust is built. Busy owner-operators may ignore it.

8.4 Universal Discovery Form

For Any Local Owner-Operated Business

Use this when the business does not clearly fit an archetype yet, or as the first-pass discovery form for all leads.

A. Business Basics

  • What is your business name?
  • Who is the main contact person?
  • What do you sell or provide?
  • What city/area do you serve?
  • Are you solo, family-run, or do you have staff?
  • How long have you been in business?
  • What kind of customer do you want more of?
  • What service/product makes you the most money?
  • What service/product do you most want to promote?
  • Do you have a busy season?

B. Current Customer Flow

  • How do customers usually find you?
    • Google
    • Facebook
    • Instagram
    • Word of mouth
    • Referrals
    • Signs
    • Markets/events
    • Existing customers
    • Other
  • After customers find you, what do they usually do?
    • Call
    • Text
    • Email
    • DM
    • Fill out a form
    • Walk in
    • Book online
    • Other
  • Where do most inquiries currently come from?
  • How quickly do you usually respond?
  • What happens after someone contacts you?
  • Where do leads get lost or forgotten?
  • What would make the customer path easier?

C. Time-Wasting Problems

  • What questions do customers ask over and over?
  • What information do you repeatedly type or explain?
  • What admin task do you hate doing?
  • What do you often forget to update?
  • What do customers fail to tell you upfront?
  • What part of booking, quoting, ordering, or follow-up takes too much time?
  • What would you like customers to do themselves before contacting you?

D. Missed-Money Problems

  • Do you miss calls or messages while working?
  • Do customers ever fail to follow through after asking?
  • Do you forget to follow up with leads?
  • Do you lose business because customers do not know prices, availability, or process?
  • Do you ask for reviews consistently?
  • Do you have a way to encourage repeat business?
  • Do you have a way to contact past customers?
  • What is one good customer/job/order worth to you?
  • What would one extra booking/job/order per month be worth?
  • What kind of customer inquiry is usually not worth your time?

E. Current Tools

  • Do you have a website?
  • Do you use Facebook or Instagram for business?
  • Do you have a Google Business Profile?
  • Do you use booking software?
  • Do you use forms?
  • Do you use spreadsheets?
  • Do you use a CRM or customer list?
  • Do you use email marketing or SMS?
  • Do you currently ask for Google reviews?
  • Do you have business cards, signs, flyers, or QR codes?

F. Project Goals

  • What are you hoping Shawcliffe Digital can help with?
  • Do you mainly need:
    • More leads?
    • Better quote requests?
    • Easier booking?
    • Fewer repeated questions?
    • Better follow-up?
    • More reviews?
    • Better customer updates?
    • More professional appearance?
    • A dashboard you can update yourself?
    • Something else?
  • If this project worked well, what would be easier?
  • What would make this worth the money?
  • What would you want working first?
  • What can wait until later?

G. Budget and Urgency

  • Is this urgent or exploratory?
  • Do you have a target launch date?
  • Do you have a budget range in mind?
  • Are you looking for a small starter version or a more complete system?
  • Are you open to monthly support after launch?
  • Who else needs to approve the project?
  • What would prevent you from moving forward?

H. Likely Components to Consider

Based on answers, consider:

  • Business Profile
  • Service / Product Menu
  • Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
  • Notifications
  • Admin Dashboard
  • CRM Lite
  • Review Request System
  • Booking Request System
  • Photo / File Upload
  • Payments / Deposits
  • Status Tracker
  • Product Inventory / Limited Batch
  • Location / Pop-Up Tracker
  • Resource Library
  • Relevant profile component if needed

Universal Discovery Output

After the universal discovery form, Shawcliffe should know:

  • Primary archetype
  • Main customer action
  • Main pain point
  • Missed-money opportunity
  • Recommended starter system
  • Components needed now
  • Components for later
  • Budget fit
  • Urgency
  • Red flags
  • Proposal direction

  • Do customers forget appointments?
  • Do you require deposits?
  • Do you have no-shows?
  • Do you rebook clients before they leave?

D. Repeated Customer Questions

Ask which questions they answer repeatedly:

  • What services do you offer?

  • How long does it take?

  • Where are you located?

  • Do you do kids/men/women/specific styles?
  • What is your cancellation policy?
  • Can I send inspiration photos?

E. Manual Admin Tasks

  • What do you manually type repeatedly?
  • Do you manually confirm appointments?
  • Do you manually remind people?
  • Do you manually follow up for rebooking?
  • Do you manually ask for reviews?
  • Do you track client notes anywhere?
  • Do you track allergies, preferences, formulas, or style notes?
  • Do you manually update service prices online?

F. Missed-Money Opportunities

  • Do you lose leads because you reply late?

  • Could packages increase repeat visits?
  • Could a QR code at your chair/station help reviews or rebooking?

G. Budget, Urgency, and Value

  • What problem do you want fixed first?
  • What would make this system worth it?
  • How many extra bookings per month would matter?
  • How much is one regular client worth over a year?
  • Are you looking for a starter system or a fuller booking/review setup?
  • Are you open to monthly support for updates, reviews, and booking support?

8.17 Discovery Answer Scoring

After discovery, score the opportunity.

Business Problem Score

ScoreMeaning
1Problem is vague
2Problem exists but not urgent
3Clear problem
4Clear painful problem
5Clear painful problem with money/time impact

Component Fit Score

ScoreMeaning
1Mostly custom/unclear
2Some reusable components
3Good component fit
4Strong archetype template fit
5Excellent reusable template opportunity

Client Fit Score

ScoreMeaning
1Difficult, unclear, or disrespectful
2Many concerns
3Reasonable but needs guidance
4Good fit
5Excellent fit, responsive, practical

Budget Fit Score

ScoreMeaning
1No budget
2Budget likely too low
3Possible with starter scope
4Good budget fit
5Strong budget and monthly potential

Urgency Score

ScoreMeaning
1No urgency
2Someday/maybe
3Useful soon
4Clear timeline
5Urgent and realistic

Total Score

TotalRecommendation
21–25Strong lead. Prepare proposal.
16–20Good lead. Clarify scope/budget.
11–15Maybe. Keep starter scope only.
6–10Weak. Nurture or decline.
1–5Do not pursue.

8.18 Discovery-to-Proposal Summary Template

Use this after every discovery call.

Client

Business name and contact.

Archetype

Primary archetype and optional secondary archetype.

Current Customer Flow

How customers currently find/contact/book/order/request.

Main Problem

The biggest time, money, customer, or communication issue.

Missed-Money Opportunity

Where leads, bookings, orders, reviews, or repeat business are being lost.

Recommended System

Example:

  • Contractor Quote Request System
  • Barber Booking & Review System
  • Roadside Seller Live Status System
  • Professional Intake System

Components Included

List recommended Phase 1 components.

Components for Later

List future upgrades.

Monthly Support Opportunity

What ongoing support makes sense?

Budget / Timeline

Known budget clues and urgency.

Red Flags

Any concerns.

Proposal Recommendation

  • Send proposal
  • Ask more questions
  • Offer starter scope only
  • Decline
  • Nurture for later

8.19 Must-Have Now vs Nice-to-Have Later

Must-Have Now

Shawcliffe should immediately create:

  • Universal discovery form
  • Discovery call notes template
  • Archetype-specific discovery questions for the first 3 target archetypes
  • Discovery-to-proposal summary template
  • Discovery scoring system
  • Pain-to-component map
  • Budget/urgency question bank
  • Red flag checklist

Nice-to-Have Later

Do not delay selling because these are not perfect:

  • Fully automated discovery form
  • Separate online form for all 12 archetypes
  • Fancy CRM integration
  • Auto-generated proposals
  • Long industry-specific intake packets
  • Video discovery process
  • Automated lead scoring
  • Client portal for discovery documents

Start with simple call notes and a checklist.

8.20 Common Discovery Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Asking Too Many Questions Too Early

A busy owner may not want to fill out a giant form before they trust Shawcliffe.

Start conversationally.

Mistake 2: Asking Feature Questions Instead of Business Questions

Do not start with:

Do you want SMS, CRM, dashboard, or automation?

Start with:

Where are customers getting stuck?
What are you tired of doing manually?
Where are leads being lost?

Mistake 3: Accepting “I Need a Website” at Face Value

A website may be the delivery method.

The real need may be:

  • Lead capture
  • Booking
  • Quote requests
  • Reviews
  • Status updates
  • Preorders
  • Intake
  • Follow-up

Mistake 4: Ignoring Budget Until the Proposal

Ask about budget before writing a detailed proposal.

Otherwise, Shawcliffe may waste time designing the wrong scope.

Mistake 5: Not Identifying the Decision Maker

Especially with churches, clinics, partnerships, shops, and family businesses.

Ask:

Who else needs to approve this?

Mistake 6: Not Listening for Support Burden

If the client needs constant updates, dashboards, SMS, payments, inventory, or automations, monthly support must be part of the conversation.

Mistake 7: Letting Discovery Become Free Consulting

Give enough value to build trust.

Do not design the whole system for free before agreement.

8.21 Definition of Done for Section 8

This section is complete when Shawcliffe Digital has:

  • A short universal discovery form
  • Detailed discovery templates for all 12 archetypes
  • Questions that uncover customer acquisition
  • Questions that uncover time loss
  • Questions that uncover money loss
  • Questions that uncover repeated customer questions
  • Questions that uncover manual admin tasks
  • Questions that uncover booking/inquiry/quote problems
  • Questions that uncover marketing gaps
  • Questions that uncover communication/follow-up problems
  • Questions that uncover review/testimonial problems
  • Questions that uncover budget and urgency
  • Questions that identify what would make the project worth it
  • Likely reusable components mapped to each archetype
  • Proposal direction for each archetype
  • Discovery scoring system
  • Discovery-to-proposal summary template

8.22 Key Takeaways

  • Discovery should find the business problem before recommending technology.
  • Every discovery should identify the archetype, customer flow, pain, missed-money opportunity, likely components, budget, urgency, and red flags.
  • Most owner-operators do not need a huge questionnaire at first. They need a practical conversation.
  • The universal form works for any local business.
  • The archetype-specific forms help Shawcliffe go deeper once the business type is clear.
  • Discovery should lead directly into a proposal built around reusable components.
  • The best questions reveal time waste, missed leads, repeated questions, poor follow-up, weak reviews, and customer confusion.
  • Good discovery prevents bad scope.

Section 09

Proposal and Pricing Process

9.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Proposal & Pricing Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains how Shawcliffe Digital should create proposals and price projects in a repeatable, practical way.

The goal is to avoid random pricing, vague scope, awkward money conversations, and projects that quietly turn into unpaid custom software.

Shawcliffe Digital should price around:

  • Business problem solved
  • Archetype
  • Reusable components included
  • Complexity
  • Client readiness
  • Support burden
  • Timeline pressure
  • Customization level
  • Recurring value

The internal rule:

Do not price “a website” or “an app.” Price the business system, the components, the complexity, and the support responsibility.

9.2 Shawcliffe Pricing Philosophy

We Are Not Selling Hours

Hourly thinking can trap a small agency.

A client does not care that something took 6 hours, 20 hours, or 40 hours.

They care whether it helps them:

  • Get more leads
  • Save time
  • Reduce missed calls/messages
  • Look professional
  • Book more customers
  • Get better quote requests
  • Sell more products
  • Collect reviews
  • Follow up properly
  • Reduce chaos

Shawcliffe should understand internal time, but proposals should focus on outcomes and scope.

We Price Based On Four Things

Pricing FactorMeaning
Business valueWhat problem does this solve for the client?
Build complexityHow difficult is it to design, build, test, and launch?
Reusable valueCan this improve a Shawcliffe template/component?
Support burdenHow much ongoing responsibility does this create?

Internal Pricing Rule

A simple-looking feature can still be expensive if it creates support, risk, integrations, notifications, payments, or client confusion.

Examples:

FeatureLooks SimpleHidden Work
SMS notification“Send a text”Consent, cost, deliverability, support, failed sends
Payment deposit“Add payment”Provider setup, policy wording, test payments, refunds responsibility
Owner dashboard“Let me edit it”Auth, permissions, validation, training, support
CRM Lite“Save leads”Data model, status flow, privacy, search, follow-up
File upload“Upload photos”Storage, file size, access, security, mobile testing
Inventory updates“Show what’s available”Dashboard, sold-out states, stale data, training

9.3 Proposal Goals

A good Shawcliffe proposal should make the client feel:

  • Understood
  • Confident
  • Clear on what they are buying
  • Clear on what is not included
  • Clear on what happens next
  • Clear on price and monthly support
  • Clear that Shawcliffe is practical, not bloated

A proposal should not be a giant corporate document.

It should be simple, specific, and professional.

9.4 Repeatable Proposal Structure

Every proposal should follow this structure.

Proposal Sections

SectionPurpose
1. Opening / Thank YouFriendly introduction
2. Problem SummaryShow that Shawcliffe understands the business issue
3. Business ArchetypeClassify the client into a repeatable pattern
4. Recommended SystemName the system being proposed
5. Components IncludedDefine exactly what is included
6. Components Not IncludedPrevent assumptions and scope creep
7. TimelineSet expectations
8. Client ResponsibilitiesExplain what the client must provide
9. Project PriceState the build/setup price
10. Monthly SupportExplain ongoing plan options
11. Optional Add-OnsGive upgrade choices
12. Future Upgrade PathShow this can grow later
13. Next StepsTell the client how to proceed

9.5 Proposal Template

Use this as Shawcliffe’s basic proposal structure.

Proposal Title

Proposal for [Client Business Name]
Prepared by Shawcliffe Digital
Date: [Date]

1. Opening

Hi [Client Name],

Thanks for taking the time to talk with us about [Business Name]. Based on our conversation, we do not think the main need is just “a website.” The bigger opportunity is to create a simple system that helps customers [book / request a quote / check availability / preorder / contact you / upload details / leave reviews] without everything getting scattered across texts, calls, DMs, and manual follow-up.

2. Problem Summary

What We Heard

Right now, customers are [describe current messy process]. This creates problems like [missed leads, repeated questions, incomplete quote requests, booking back-and-forth, no review follow-up, unclear availability, etc.].

Why This Matters

When this process is unclear or manual, it can cost you time, create customer confusion, and cause missed opportunities.

3. Business Archetype

Primary Archetype: [One of the 12 archetypes]
Secondary Archetype if applicable: [Optional]

Why This Matters

We group businesses into common operating patterns so we can recommend a practical system instead of reinventing everything from scratch. Your business fits closest to our [archetype] pattern, which usually needs [booking / quote request / live status / recurring client / intake / product availability] tools.

4. Recommended System

Recommended System: [System Name]

Examples:

  • Contractor Quote Request System
  • Roadside Seller Live Status System
  • Barber Booking & Review System
  • Cleaner Recurring Client System
  • Food Maker Menu & Preorder System
  • Dog Groomer Booking & Pet Profile System
  • Tutor Student Progress System
  • Professional Intake System

One-Sentence Promise

This system will help [Business Name] [specific outcome].

Example:

This system will help customers send job details, location, and photos upfront so you can respond to quote requests faster and avoid wasting time on incomplete inquiries.

5. Components Included

List only what is included.

ComponentWhat It Means for This Project
Business ProfileBusiness name, contact info, location/service area, hours, basic identity
Service / Product MenuClear list of services/products/packages
Lead Capture / Inquiry FormCustomer form to collect structured inquiries
NotificationsOwner receives email/SMS alerts when a lead comes in
Photo / File UploadCustomers can upload job photos or files
Review Request SystemSimple process/link/QR to request reviews
Admin DashboardOwner can update agreed fields
CRM LiteLeads/customers can be tracked in a simple database

6. Components Not Included

This section is important.

It prevents assumptions.

To keep this first version focused, the following are not included unless added separately:

Not IncludedNotes
Full ecommerce checkoutCan be discussed later
Advanced AI receptionistPossible future upgrade
Paid ad managementSeparate service
Unlimited content updatesCovered only under monthly support terms
Complex calendar syncAdd-on if needed
Custom mobile app store releaseSeparate larger project
Advanced analytics dashboardFuture Growth/Premium option
Multi-user staff permissionsAdd-on if needed
Ongoing daily updates by ShawcliffeRequires support plan

7. Timeline

Example:

StageApproximate Timeline
Onboarding / asset collection3–7 days depending on client readiness
Design/build1–3 weeks depending on scope
Client review2–5 business days
Revisions2–7 business days
LaunchAfter approval and final checks

Timeline Note

Timeline depends on receiving required content, assets, access, and approvals on time. Delays in client-provided materials may delay launch.

8. Client Responsibilities

The client must provide:

  • Business name and contact info
  • Services/products and descriptions
  • Prices or starting prices
  • Hours/location/service area
  • Photos/logo/brand assets if available
  • Policies, booking rules, cancellation terms, deposit terms if relevant
  • Google Business Profile/review link if included
  • Domain/hosting/access if needed
  • Payment provider info if payments are included
  • Approval/feedback within agreed review windows

Client Responsibility Language

Shawcliffe will build and configure the system, but we need accurate business information from you. We cannot responsibly guess your prices, policies, services, or legal/industry-specific language.

9. Project Price

Project Build Price: $[Amount]

This includes the components listed above.

Payment structure example:

  • [Amount] due to begin
  • [Amount] due before launch

Or:

  • Full setup/build fee due before project starts for smaller projects

10. Monthly Support

Recommended:

Monthly Support Plan: $[Amount]/month

Includes:

  • Hosting/maintenance if applicable
  • Small updates within plan limits
  • Bug fixes for included system
  • Form/notification monitoring
  • Review request support
  • Dashboard support
  • Monthly check-in depending on tier

Not included unless specified:

  • New features
  • New pages
  • Major redesign
  • Ad management
  • Daily content updates
  • Complex automation changes
  • Third-party tool fees unless explicitly bundled

11. Optional Add-Ons

Add-OnPrice / RangeNotes
SMS notifications$[amount] setup + monthly usage/supportUseful for urgent leads
CRM Lite$[amount]Track leads and follow-up
Review request system$[amount]Helps grow reputation
Admin dashboard$[amount]Owner can update content/status
Payment/deposit setup$[amount]Helps reduce no-shows/cancellations
QR code cards/signage setup$[amount]Connect physical customers to digital system
Local SEO basics$[amount]Service/location basics
Analytics/campaign tracking$[amount]Track sources and conversions

12. Future Upgrade Path

Possible future improvements:

  • CRM Lite
  • SMS/email follow-up
  • Payments/deposits
  • Review automation
  • Advanced dashboard
  • Product/status updates
  • Recurring schedule
  • Customer profiles
  • Loyalty/referral system
  • Analytics/reporting
  • AI receptionist or automated follow-up

Upgrade Path Language

The first version should solve the most important problem clearly. Once it is live and being used, we can add more advanced features based on what the business actually needs.

13. Next Steps

To move forward:

  • Approve the proposal
  • Confirm scope and payment terms
  • Complete onboarding checklist
  • Provide required content/assets/access
  • Shawcliffe begins build
  • Review draft
  • Approve launch
  • Move into support plan

9.6 Proposal Rules

Rule 1: Always Include “Not Included”

This protects Shawcliffe from accidental scope creep.

Do not assume the client knows.

If it is not included, write it.

Rule 2: Never Hide Monthly Support

Every proposal should mention support.

Even if the client declines, the expectation is set.

Rule 3: Price Components, Not Vibes

Avoid random pricing based on nervousness.

Use:

  • Package level
  • Component count
  • Complexity
  • Support burden
  • Customization
  • Urgency
  • Reusability

Rule 4: Reduce Scope Before Reducing Price

If the client cannot afford the full version, remove components.

Do not quietly do the same work for less.

Rule 5: Do Not Start Build Without Scope and Payment

A small agency needs boundaries.

No clear scope + no payment = future resentment.

9.7 Pricing Ladder

These ranges are practical internal starting points for a small early-stage agency. They should be adjusted as Shawcliffe gains proof, confidence, demand, and better templates.

All examples are in Canadian dollars.

Basic Pricing Ladder

Offer TypeExample RangeNotes
Simple landing page$500–$1,500Very limited scope, few sections
Starter website$1,000–$3,000Basic pages, business profile, service/menu, contact
Website + lead capture$1,500–$4,000Adds structured inquiry and notifications
Booking/inquiry system$2,000–$5,000Includes forms/workflow and owner notifications
Quote request system$2,000–$6,000Often includes photo upload and CRM Lite
Roadside live status system$2,500–$7,500Dashboard, status, inventory, location
Custom business system$4,000–$12,000+Multi-component system
Premium custom system$10,000+Advanced workflows, automation, integrations
Monthly maintenance$75–$250/monthBasic upkeep
Monthly care plan$250–$750/monthSupport, updates, monitoring
Growth support/marketing$750–$2,500+/monthMore active improvement and reporting

Important Internal Note

At the beginning, Shawcliffe may choose lower introductory pricing to build proof and case studies.

But do not underprice support-heavy features.

Low intro pricing should be intentional, limited, and explained internally as a portfolio/case-study decision.

9.10 Pricing Adjustments

Pricing should change based on real project factors.

A. Number of Components

More components = higher price.

Component CountTypical Project Type
3–4 componentsStarter
5–7 componentsGrowth
8–12 componentsCustom business system
12+ componentsPremium or phased build

Rule

Do not sell 10 components at Starter pricing.

B. Complexity of Components

Not all components are equal.

Component TypeComplexity
Static business infoLow
Simple formMedium
Dashboard-editable form/menu/statusMedium/High
SMS/payment/CRM/profile logicHigh
Automation/AI/integrationsVery high

Rule

A project with 5 hard components may cost more than a project with 10 simple pieces.

C. Amount of Custom Design

Price increases when the client needs:

  • Custom brand direction
  • Multiple page layouts
  • Heavy visual polish
  • Custom illustrations
  • Complex galleries
  • Before/after portfolios
  • Copywriting from scratch
  • Multiple design revisions
  • Committee approval

Rule

If they need heavy design, price it. Do not bury design work inside build pricing.

D. Client Content Readiness

Content readiness has a huge effect on timeline and pricing.

Client ReadinessPricing Effect
Has logo, photos, services, prices, copyNormal
Has some info but needs cleanupSlight increase
Has no content and needs Shawcliffe to create itIncrease
Does not know services/prices/policiesDelay or strategy fee
Keeps changing contentChange request or support plan

Rule

Clients who are unprepared need either a smaller scope or paid content/strategy help.

E. Integrations

Integrations increase price and risk.

Examples:

  • SMS platform
  • Email marketing platform
  • Payment provider
  • Booking calendar
  • Google Analytics/Search Console
  • CRM
  • Google Business Profile
  • Automation tools
  • AI receptionist/call routing tools

Rule

Any third-party tool adds setup, testing, and support risk.

Price accordingly.

F. Support Needs

Support-heavy systems should include or require monthly support.

High-support components:

  • Admin Dashboard
  • Notifications
  • SMS
  • Payments
  • CRM Lite
  • Status Tracker
  • Inventory
  • Recurring Schedule
  • Profile Systems
  • Analytics
  • Automation/AI

Rule

Do not sell support-heavy systems without a support plan unless the client clearly accepts paid support as needed.

G. Urgency

Rush timelines should cost more.

Rush work creates:

  • Schedule disruption
  • Higher stress
  • More mistakes
  • Less flexibility
  • Evening/weekend pressure

Internal Rush Rule

If a client needs a faster-than-normal timeline, add a rush fee or reduce scope.

Example:

Timeline PressurePricing Action
Normal timelineStandard price
Mild rushAdd 15–25% or reduce scope
Serious rushAdd 25–50% or decline
Unrealistic rushDecline or offer limited starter version

H. Reusable Template vs Highly Custom Work

Reusable template work can be priced more competitively because it helps Shawcliffe build assets.

Highly custom work should cost more.

Project TypePricing Approach
Reuses existing templateStandard package pricing
Improves a target templatePossible strategic discount if case-study value
New reusable componentPrice normally, document for reuse
Highly custom one-offPremium pricing
Complex feature not reusableAdd-on or decline

Rule

Custom work that does not improve Shawcliffe’s reusable system should not be cheap.

9.11 Package Structures

Shawcliffe should offer simple packages.

Do not offer too many options.

Three build packages plus monthly support is enough.

9.12 Starter System

Best For

  • New owner-operators
  • Businesses with no real website

9.16 Build-and-Support Plan

What It Is

A package that includes:

  • Initial system build
  • Monthly support for a set period
  • Ongoing updates and improvement rhythm

This is useful when the client wants both launch and continued help.

Example Structure

Build-and-Support Plan

  • Setup/build: $[amount]
  • Monthly support: $[amount]/month
  • Minimum initial support period: [example: 3 months or 6 months]
  • Includes: build + support + training + small improvements

Best For

  • Clients who need help after launch
  • Dashboard systems
  • Notification systems
  • CRM Lite systems
  • Roadside/status systems
  • Booking systems
  • Review request systems

Internal Note

This is often better than selling a build and hoping they keep paying later.

9.17 System Subscription

What It Is

A monthly system package where the client pays for access, hosting, maintenance, support, and ongoing use of a Shawcliffe-built system.

Use this carefully.

It works best when Shawcliffe has a reusable template and can support it efficiently.

Best For

  • Roadside Seller Live Status System
  • Review Request System
  • Simple booking/request systems
  • QR campaign systems
  • Seasonal seller systems
  • Very standardized archetype templates

Example Structure

PlanSetupMonthly
Starter SubscriptionLower setupHigher monthly
Standard SubscriptionModerate setupModerate monthly
Premium SubscriptionHigher setupHigher monthly with support

Good Subscription Candidates

  • Fruit stand live status page
  • Food truck location/status page
  • Simple review request system
  • QR promo page for retail
  • Simple lead capture landing page
  • Basic booking request system

Be Careful

Subscriptions require Shawcliffe to define:

  • What happens if client cancels
  • What client owns
  • What Shawcliffe owns
  • What happens to data
  • What happens to domain
  • What happens to dashboard access
  • What support is included
  • What customization is allowed

This needs lawyer-reviewed language later.

9.22 Support Pricing Rules

Rule 1: Dashboard Means Support

If the client has an owner dashboard, they will likely need help.

Include support or clearly define paid support.

Rule 2: SMS Means Monthly

SMS has usage costs and troubleshooting.

Do not include SMS casually.

Rule 3: CRM Means Monthly Value

CRM Lite becomes more valuable over time, but also needs support.

Rule 4: Inventory/Status Means Ongoing Use

If a client updates inventory/status regularly, support and training matter.

Rule 5: Automation Means Premium Support

Automation is not “set it and forget it.”

It needs monitoring, updates, and clear boundaries.

9.24 Handling Low-Budget Clients

Some clients will have real needs but limited budget.

Do not shame them.

Do not overbuild.

Offer a smaller system.

Low-Budget Response

That budget makes sense for a simpler first version. I would not recommend trying to build the full system right away. We can start with the essentials: your business profile, services, a clear inquiry form, notifications, and a review link. Then you can add dashboard, CRM, SMS, or automation later.

Starter Scope Reduction Options

To reduce price, remove:

  • Admin Dashboard
  • CRM Lite
  • SMS
  • Payments
  • Advanced design
  • Extra pages
  • Automations
  • Analytics
  • Profile systems
  • Multiple forms
  • Custom integrations

Do not remove:

  • Clear business info
  • Clear customer action
  • Mobile usability
  • Basic testing
  • Scope clarity

9.25 Handling Custom Requests

Custom Request Decision Table

RequestResponse
Fits existing componentInclude if in scope or add price
Reusable new componentConsider building if priced properly
Client-specific but simpleAdd-on
Client-specific and complexPremium add-on or Phase 2
Not useful to business goalRecommend against
High-risk/compliance-heavyDecline or require specialist review
Vague ideaClarify before pricing

Custom Request Language

That is possible, but it is outside the base system. The question is whether it is important for launch or better as a Phase 2 improvement. If it is important now, I can price it as an add-on.

9.26 Payment Structure

Shawcliffe should keep payment simple.

Recommended Options

Small Projects

  • Full payment before build starts

Best for:

  • Landing pages
  • Starter websites
  • Small review/QR systems
  • Very small add-ons

Medium Projects

  • Initial payment to begin
  • Remaining balance before launch

Best for:

  • Starter/Growth systems
  • Booking systems
  • Quote systems
  • Dashboard systems

Larger Projects

  • Setup/payment milestones based on stages
  • Final balance before launch
  • Monthly support begins at launch

Best for:

  • Premium systems
  • Custom business systems
  • Multi-component builds

Payment Rules

  • Do not begin serious build without agreed payment.
  • Do not launch with unresolved payment.
  • Do not add unpaid features.
  • Do not allow unclear monthly support expectations.
  • Track every invoice and payment status.

9.27 Proposal Follow-Up Process

After Sending Proposal

Day 1–2

Hi [Name], just checking that you received the proposal. The main focus is helping customers [specific action] and giving you a simpler way to manage [specific problem]. Let me know what questions come up.

Day 5–7

Hi [Name], I know things get busy. If the full version feels like too much right now, we can also look at a smaller first phase focused on [core outcome].

Day 10–14

Hi [Name], I do not want to keep chasing you, so I’ll leave this here for now. I still think the biggest opportunity is [specific problem]. If it becomes a priority later, I’d be happy to revisit it.

9.30 Common Pricing Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Pricing From Fear

Do not lower price because saying the real number feels awkward.

If the system has real value, price it clearly.

Mistake 2: Selling Components Without Boundaries

If you include dashboard, CRM, SMS, payments, or automation, define exactly what that means.

Mistake 3: Discounting Instead of Reducing Scope

Lower scope before lowering price.

Mistake 4: Forgetting Support Burden

A feature that creates future requests should affect monthly pricing.

Mistake 5: Hiding What Is Not Included

This creates conflict later.

Always list exclusions.

Mistake 6: Treating Reusable Templates as Worthless

Just because Shawcliffe can build something quickly does not mean it has low value.

Speed is a strength, not a reason to undercharge.

Mistake 7: Custom Work at Template Price

Highly custom work should cost more.

Do not let custom complexity sneak into a starter package.

9.32 Key Takeaways

  • Shawcliffe should price systems, not just websites or apps.
  • Every proposal should include the problem, archetype, recommended system, included components, excluded components, timeline, client responsibilities, price, support, add-ons, and next steps.
  • Starter projects should stay simple.
  • Growth projects should include the core workflow and owner support.
  • Premium projects should be priced for complexity, support, and risk.
  • Dashboards, CRM, SMS, payments, inventory, profiles, analytics, and automation should not be casually included for free.
  • If the client needs a lower price, reduce scope.
  • Monthly support should be part of almost every serious proposal.
  • Reusable templates are valuable because they solve real business problems faster.

9.35 Questions to Answer Before Moving to Section 10

Before creating archetype-specific offers, Shawcliffe should answer:

  • What is our minimum acceptable project price?
  • What monthly support tier do we want most clients on?
  • Which 3 offers do we want to sell first?
  • Which components are included in each offer?
  • Which components are always add-ons?
  • Which components require monthly support?
  • Are we willing to offer introductory case-study pricing?
  • What do we need in exchange for case-study pricing?
  • How do we handle clients who want only a website?
  • How do we explain that fast build speed does not mean low value?

This section turns Shawcliffe Digital’s 12 owner-operated business archetypes into practical starter offers.

“For your type of business, the best starter system is probably this.”

Every archetype should have a simple starter offer that solves one obvious business problem.

11Local Retail / Boutique ShopsLocal Shop Promo Starter SystemPromote hours, products, events, reviews
12Professional Local ServicesProfessional Intake Starter SystemQualify leads and collect intake details

10.3 Package Philosophy

Each starter offer should be:

  • Simple enough to sell
  • Clear enough for the client to understand
  • Narrow enough to scope
  • Useful enough to justify real pricing
  • Built from reusable components
  • Easy to upgrade later

A starter offer should not include every possible feature.

The goal is:

Launch the first useful system, then improve from there.

10.4 Common Starter Offer Structure

Most archetype-specific starter offers should include some version of:

ComponentWhy It Usually Matters
Business ProfileMakes the business clear and professional
Service / Product MenuShows what the business offers
Lead Capture / Inquiry / Booking FormTurns interest into action
NotificationsAlerts the owner when something comes in
Basic Review RequestHelps build trust and reputation
Simple Customer ConfirmationLets customer know their request was received

Some offers also need:

  • Admin Dashboard
  • Photo / File Upload
  • Status Tracker
  • Product Inventory
  • Location Tracker
  • CRM Lite
  • Profile component
  • Resource Library
  • Document Checklist
  • Payments / Deposits

10.24 How to Present Offers in Sales Calls

Simple Sales Flow

  • Listen to the business problem.
  • Identify archetype.
  • Name the likely offer.
  • Explain the promise.
  • List only the core components.
  • Mention optional upgrades.
  • Ask what would make it worth it.
  • Confirm budget/timeline fit.
  • Offer proposal or starter scope.

Example

From what you described, you fit our Home Service Trades pattern. I would not start with a giant custom app. I would start with our Quote Request Starter System.

That means customers can choose the job type, send location, describe the issue, upload photos, and you get the request in one organized place. Later, we can add CRM tracking, SMS, review requests, or local SEO if those become priorities.

Must-Have Now

Shawcliffe should immediately create one-page offer sheets for:

Nice-to-Have Later

10.26 Common Offer Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Making Every Offer Too Big

A starter offer should not solve every future problem.

It should solve the first important problem.

Mistake 2: Using Technical Names

Do not sell:

CRM Lite + notification workflow + form logic.

Sell:

A simple way to collect leads and remember who needs follow-up.

Mistake 3: Giving Away Add-Ons

SMS, dashboards, payments, CRM, profiles, and automation create support.

Charge for them.

Mistake 4: Selling the Same Offer to Everyone

A barber does not need the same first system as a fruit stand.

A fruit stand does not need the same first system as a tax preparer.

Use archetypes.

Mistake 5: Underestimating Monthly Support

The more useful the system is, the more likely the client will need ongoing support.

That is not a problem.
That is part of the business model.

Section 11

Scope of Work and Project Boundaries

11.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Scope Control Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains how Shawcliffe Digital should define project scope, protect boundaries, prevent scope creep, and keep projects profitable.

Scope is where a small agency either becomes calm and professional or chaotic and resentful.

A good scope of work protects:

  • Shawcliffe Digital
  • The client
  • The development timeline
  • The project budget
  • The client relationship
  • The final launch
  • Monthly support expectations

The internal rule:

If it is not written in the scope, it is not included.

That does not mean Shawcliffe should be rigid or unhelpful. It means changes should be handled clearly, priced properly, and placed in the right phase.

11.2 Why Scope Matters So Much

Owner-operated business clients often speak casually:

  • “Can we just add this?”
  • “Would it be easy to also include…”
  • “While you’re in there…”
  • “I forgot I also need…”
  • “Can you make it like this other site?”
  • “Can we change the whole layout?”
  • “Can you add text messaging too?”
  • “Can customers pay through it?”
  • “Can it also track all my clients?”

Most clients are not trying to be difficult. They simply do not know what is simple, complex, included, excluded, reusable, custom, or support-heavy.

That is Shawcliffe’s job to clarify.

Bad Scope Creates

  • Unpaid work
  • Delayed launches
  • Confused clients
  • Overwhelmed developers
  • Vague expectations
  • Frustration between Curtis and Cassandra
  • Pricing regret
  • Support chaos
  • Projects that never feel finished

Good Scope Creates

  • Clear expectations
  • Faster builds
  • Easier proposals
  • Better client trust
  • Better pricing
  • Better handoffs
  • Cleaner launches
  • More profitable projects
  • Easier monthly support
  • More reusable templates

11.3 Core Scope Principle

Scope Is Built From Components

Shawcliffe should not define scope as:

“Build a website.”

That is too vague.

Define scope as:

“Build a [system name] using these included reusable components.”

Example:

“Build a Contractor Quote Request Starter System including Business Profile, Service Menu, Quote Request Form, Photo Upload, Owner Notifications, Customer Confirmation, and Basic Review Request.”

This makes the project easier to understand, price, test, and finish.

11.4 What Belongs in a Scope of Work

Every Shawcliffe SOW should include these sections.

SectionPurpose
Project nameNames the system being built
Client/business nameIdentifies who the project is for
Project goalExplains the business problem being solved
Business archetypeConnects project to Shawcliffe’s framework
Included componentsLists exactly what is included
Excluded componentsLists what is not included
Pages/screensDefines public-facing and admin pages
Forms/workflowsDefines customer actions and data collected
NotificationsDefines who gets notified and how
Dashboard/admin accessDefines what the owner can edit
Client responsibilitiesLists what client must provide
Revision roundsDefines number and type of revisions
Timeline assumptionsExplains timing and dependency on client assets
Payment termsDefines when payments are due
Change request policyExplains how new requests are handled
Launch requirementsDefines what must happen before launch
Support termsDefines what happens after launch
Ownership/access notesClarifies practical access and third-party tools
Approval processDefines when work is considered approved

Use this as Shawcliffe’s internal base scope template.

11.6 How to List Included Components

Included components should be specific.

Do not write:

“Includes dashboard.”

Write:

“Includes a simple owner dashboard allowing the client to update open/closed status, product availability, product prices, and current location.”

Weak vs Strong Scope Language

Weak ScopeStrong Scope
WebsiteOne-page mobile-friendly website with business profile, service list, inquiry form, and review link
BookingBooking request form for customers to request preferred appointment date/time; does not include live calendar sync
DashboardOwner dashboard to update open/closed status, today’s products, prices, and sold-out state
NotificationsEmail notification to owner when a customer submits the quote request form
CRMBasic lead list with name, contact info, requested service, status, notes, and date submitted
PaymentsExternal payment/deposit link added to confirmation message; does not include full checkout system

Included Component Table Template

ComponentIncludedNot Included

11.7 How to List Excluded Components

The “not included” section is not negative. It is professional.

It prevents misunderstanding.

Every proposal and SOW should include excluded items.

Common Exclusions

Unless specifically included, these should usually be excluded:

  • Full ecommerce
  • Full calendar booking/sync
  • Custom mobile app store release
  • Paid ad management
  • Ongoing daily updates
  • Unlimited revisions
  • Unlimited content writing
  • Full CRM
  • Advanced automation
  • AI receptionist
  • Advanced analytics dashboard
  • Complex staff permissions
  • Secure document portal
  • Legal/medical/financial policy writing
  • Logo design/branding package
  • Photography/videography
  • Social media management
  • Search engine ranking guarantees
  • Guaranteed leads or revenue
  • Third-party subscription fees
  • Complex integrations
  • Multiple languages
  • Accessibility compliance audit
  • Copywriting beyond agreed scope

Exclusion Language

To keep the first version focused, this scope does not include the following unless separately quoted.

Strong Exclusion Example

This project includes a booking request form. It does not include full live calendar booking, automatic appointment approval, staff scheduling, cancellation/rescheduling workflows, or third-party calendar integration unless added as a separate paid feature.

11.8 Revision Rounds

Revision rounds must be defined before the project starts.

A revision round is a structured set of client feedback on the agreed work.

It is not an unlimited invitation to rethink the entire project.

Suggested Revision Rounds by Package

PackageSuggested Included Revisions
Starter System1 structured revision round
Growth System2 structured revision rounds
Premium System2–3 structured revision rounds
Custom/Premium BuildDefined by milestone

What Counts as an Included Revision

Usually included:

  • Correcting spelling
  • Correcting phone/email/address
  • Adjusting approved wording
  • Replacing a photo
  • Minor layout adjustment
  • Updating service descriptions
  • Correcting a form field within agreed workflow
  • Adjusting button text
  • Clarifying instructions
  • Fixing obvious mistakes

What Does Not Count as an Included Revision

Usually not included:

  • New page
  • New component
  • New dashboard feature
  • New payment workflow
  • New booking workflow
  • New form
  • Full redesign
  • Changing the business model
  • Changing the primary offer
  • Adding SMS
  • Adding CRM
  • Adding automation
  • Adding ecommerce
  • Adding new service area pages
  • Rewriting all copy from scratch
  • Repeated changes after approval

Revision Language

This project includes [number] structured revision round(s). Revisions include corrections and adjustments within the agreed scope. New features, new pages, new workflows, or major changes to the approved direction will be treated as change requests.

Client Review Instruction

Please send feedback in one organized message where possible. This helps us keep the revision round clear and avoids missed changes. New ideas are welcome, but they may be moved to Phase 2 or quoted separately if they are outside the agreed scope.

11.9 Client Content Responsibilities

Client content is one of the biggest project blockers.

Shawcliffe must clearly define what the client provides.

Client Must Provide

Depending on the project, client may need to provide:

  • Business name
  • Owner/contact name
  • Phone number
  • Email
  • Address/location/service area
  • Hours
  • Services/products
  • Prices or starting prices
  • Service/product descriptions
  • Photos
  • Logo
  • Brand colors if available
  • Social links
  • Google Business Profile link
  • Google review link
  • Policies
  • Booking rules
  • Cancellation rules
  • Deposit rules
  • Intake questions
  • Legal/medical/financial/professional wording
  • Domain access
  • Payment provider access/link
  • SMS/email sender details if needed

Client Content Rule

Shawcliffe can organize, polish, and structure client-provided information, but the client is responsible for the accuracy of business details, prices, services, policies, and industry-specific claims.

Content Readiness Levels

LevelDescriptionPricing / Timeline Impact
ReadyClient has services, prices, photos, infoNormal timeline
Mostly ReadySome cleanup neededSlight delay or light copy fee
MessyInfo scattered, missing piecesDelay and possible content fee
Not ReadyClient cannot define offer/prices/policiesStrategy/content phase required
Changing ConstantlyClient revises core info repeatedlyChange requests or extended timeline

Client-Facing Content Language

We can help organize and polish the wording, but we need the core facts from you. That includes services, prices or starting prices, hours, location, policies, and any industry-specific wording. We do not want to guess at anything that affects your customers or your business.

Missing Content Policy

If required content is missing, the project timeline may pause until the content is received. Placeholder content may be used for structure, but final launch requires approved business information.

11.10 Change Requests

A change request is any client request outside the approved scope.

Change requests are normal.

They are not bad.

They simply need to be handled properly.

Change Request Categories

CategoryExampleResponse
Minor in-scope adjustmentChange button wordingInclude in revision
Out-of-scope add-onAdd SMS notificationsQuote separately
Future improvementAdd loyalty system laterAdd to Phase 2 list
Scope replacementChange quote system into booking systemRe-scope project
Risky requestCollect sensitive documents insecurelyDecline or require proper setup
Unclear idea“Make it more interactive”Clarify before pricing

Change Request Process

  • Client makes request.
  • Curtis captures it.
  • Curtis identifies if it is in scope.
  • Cassandra reviews technical complexity if needed.
  • Decision is made:
    • Include
    • Quote add-on
    • Save for later
    • Decline
  • Client approves price/timeline if add-on.
  • Work is scheduled.

Change Request Language

That is outside the original scope, but it may be a good addition. I can either add it to the future improvements list or price it as an add-on before we build it.

Change Request Mini-Template

Change Request

Requested by: [Client]
Date: [Date]
Request: [Description]
Reason: [Business reason]
Category: In-scope / Add-on / Phase 2 / Decline
Estimated cost: $[Amount]

Approved by client: Yes / No

11.11 How to Prevent Scope Creep

Scope creep happens when new work is added without changing price, timeline, or expectations.

Common Scope Creep Phrases

Watch for:

  • “Can we just…”
  • “Would it be easy to…”
  • “While you’re in there…”
  • “I forgot we also need…”
  • “This should be quick…”
  • “Can you add one more thing…”
  • “Can we change the whole direction…”
  • “My friend said we should add…”
  • “Can we make it like this other company…”

Scope Creep Prevention Rules

Rule 1: Always Refer Back to Components

That sounds like adding [component]. It was not part of the starter scope, but we can price it as an add-on.

Rule 2: Keep a Future Improvements List

Do not reject every idea. Capture it.

Rule 3: Do Not Let Development Receive Raw Client Requests

Client requests go to Curtis first.

Rule 4: Do Not Build Before Clarifying

No “quick” changes without understanding the effect.

Rule 5: Protect Launch Scope

The closer the project gets to launch, the harder it should be to add new features.

Rule 6: Reduce Ambiguity

Write what is included and excluded.

Rule 7: Use Paid Change Requests

If it adds value, it can have a price.

Scope Creep Response

That is a good idea, but it is outside the first launch scope. The cleanest way to handle it is to either save it for Phase 2 or quote it as an add-on. I do not want to casually add it and delay the launch or create confusion.

11.12 How to Say No Politely

Saying no is part of professional service.

The goal is to be clear without sounding rude.

No to Out-of-Scope Feature

That feature is not included in the current scope. We can price it as an add-on or save it for a future phase.

No to Rush Timeline

I do not want to promise that timeline and then cut corners. We can either reduce the launch scope or set a more realistic date.

No to Unlimited Revisions

We need to keep revisions structured so the project can actually launch. This round can cover corrections and adjustments within the agreed scope. Larger changes can be quoted separately.

No to Free Add-On

That would add extra build and testing time, so it would need to be treated as an add-on rather than included for free.

No to Unsupported Work

That is outside what we support right now. I would rather be honest than take on something we cannot responsibly maintain.

No to Risky/Regulated Content

We can help structure and display the information, but we cannot write or approve legal, medical, financial, or regulated claims for you. That wording needs to come from you or the appropriate professional.

No to Bad-Fit Project

After thinking it through, I do not think this is the right fit for Shawcliffe Digital. We focus on practical websites, lead systems, booking systems, quote request systems, and simple owner dashboards. This project seems to need a different kind of provider.

11.13 How to Price Add-Ons

Add-ons should be priced based on:

  • Build time
  • Testing time
  • Support burden
  • Business value
  • Complexity
  • Whether it is reusable
  • Whether it requires integrations
  • Whether it changes launch timeline

Add-On Pricing Categories

Add-On TypeExample RangeNotes
Small content/page adjustment$100–$500Depends on scope
Additional page$250–$750+More if custom design/copy
Additional form$250–$1,000+More if conditional logic
Photo/file upload$500–$1,500+Storage/testing needed
SMS notifications$250–$1,500 setup + monthlyUsage/support applies
Payment/deposit flow$500–$2,000+Testing/policy needed
Admin dashboard feature$500–$3,000+Depends on field/workflow
CRM Lite upgrade$1,000–$4,000+Data/workflow/support
Review workflow$250–$1,500+Manual vs automated
Resource library$500–$3,000+Depends on content
Profile system$1,500–$5,000+Property/pet/vehicle/student
Analytics tracking$250–$1,500+Basic vs campaign tracking
Automation/AI workflow$1,500–$10,000+Premium and support-heavy

Add-On Pricing Rule

If an add-on requires testing, support, training, or third-party setup, it is not “just a small change.”

Add-On Language

We can add that. Based on the extra setup, testing, and support involved, it would be an add-on of $[amount]. It may also add [timeline] to the project.

11.14 Protecting Development Time

Development time is one of Shawcliffe’s most valuable resources.

Because Shawcliffe is a husband-and-wife agency, protecting development time also protects work-life balance and business sanity.

Development Protection Rules

Rule 1: Curtis Triages Client Requests

Clients should not send build requests directly to Cassandra unless agreed.

Curtis filters:

  • Bug
  • Revision
  • Add-on
  • Future idea
  • Support request
  • Not recommended

Rule 2: No Unapproved Features Enter Build

If it is not in the SOW or approved change request, it does not enter development.

Rule 3: Use a Build Queue

Cassandra should work from a clear list, not scattered messages.

Rule 4: Batch Questions

Do not interrupt development for every tiny client question.

Collect questions and batch them.

Rule 5: Separate Bugs From Feature Requests

A broken included feature is different from a new desired feature.

Rule 6: Protect Deep Work

Development requires focused time. Constant interruptions increase mistakes.

Internal Request Triage Table

Request TypeExampleCurtis ActionCassandra Action
BugForm not sendingConfirm and prioritizeFix
Included revisionChange service wordingAdd to revision listUpdate
New featureAdd depositsQuote add-onBuild after approval
Future ideaAdd loyalty laterSave to Phase 2No action now
Training issueClient forgot dashboardExplain or schedule trainingOnly if technical
Not recommendedAdd unnecessary featureAdvise againstNo action

11.16 Project Boundary Rules

These are the rules Shawcliffe should follow on every project.

Boundary 1: No Build Without Approved Scope

A conversation is not scope.

A text message is not scope.

A vague “website” is not scope.

Boundary 2: No Launch Without Final Checks

Launch requires:

  • Client approval
  • Payment status checked
  • Forms tested
  • Notifications tested
  • Mobile tested
  • Dashboard tested if included

Boundary 3: No Unlimited Revisions

Every project needs a revision limit.

Boundary 4: No Free Support Forever

After launch, support must be tied to:

  • Monthly plan
  • Warranty/bug-fix period
  • Paid support request

Boundary 5: No Guessing Client Policies

Client provides:

  • Pricing
  • Services
  • Cancellation terms
  • Refund terms
  • Health/legal/financial/professional wording
  • Deposit rules
  • Warranty/service policies

Boundary 6: No Unsupported Complexity

Decline or postpone features Shawcliffe cannot responsibly support yet.

11.21 Support Boundaries in the SOW

Every SOW should explain what happens after launch.

Basic Support Language

After launch, support is handled according to the selected monthly support plan. If no support plan is selected, future updates, changes, troubleshooting, or feature requests may be quoted separately.

Bug Fix Language

Bugs related to the included system will be reviewed and fixed according to the support terms. A bug means an included feature is not working as intended. A new feature, new workflow, or changed business requirement is not considered a bug.

Monthly Update Language

Monthly support may include small updates within the plan limits. Larger changes, new pages, new features, new components, or major redesigns are quoted separately.

Third-Party Tool Language

Third-party tools such as payment processors, SMS providers, email platforms, domain registrars, hosting providers, analytics tools, or booking platforms may have their own costs, limits, outages, rules, or support processes. These are not controlled by Shawcliffe Digital.

11.23 Must-Have Now vs Nice-to-Have Later

Must-Have Now

Shawcliffe should immediately create:

  • Basic SOW template
  • Included components table
  • Excluded components table

  • Client content responsibility policy
  • Change request process
  • Add-on pricing menu
  • Scope creep response scripts
  • Launch requirements checklist
  • Support boundary language

Nice-to-Have Later

Do not delay selling while waiting for:

  • Lawyer-polished master services agreement
  • Advanced e-signature workflow
  • Automated change request portal
  • Complex client portal
  • Full legal contract library
  • Automated project scoping calculator
  • Detailed compliance templates

However, once Shawcliffe is taking regular paid work, formal legal agreement review should become a priority.

11.24 Common Scope Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Saying “Website” Instead of Defining the System

A website can mean almost anything.

Define the business system and components.

Mistake 2: Forgetting the “Not Included” Section

This is one of the biggest scope protections.

Mistake 3: Starting Work Before Content Is Ready

Missing content delays projects and creates frustration.

Mistake 4: Treating Revisions as Unlimited

Unlimited revisions destroy timelines and profit.

Mistake 5: Letting Clients Add Features During Review

Client review is for reviewing agreed work.

New features are add-ons or Phase 2.

Mistake 6: Letting Development Be Interrupted Directly

Protect build time.

Requests should go through triage.

Mistake 7: Not Pricing Support Burden

Dashboards, SMS, CRM, payments, inventory, and automation create ongoing support.

Charge accordingly.

Mistake 8: Being Afraid to Say No

A clear no is better than a resentful yes.

11.26 Key Takeaways

  • Scope protects both Shawcliffe and the client.
  • Every scope should be built around the business problem, archetype, and included components.
  • Every proposal should clearly say what is included and what is not included.
  • Revision rounds must be limited and structured.
  • Client content responsibilities must be written down.
  • Change requests are normal, but they must be approved and priced.
  • Scope creep usually starts with casual language like “can we just…”
  • Development time must be protected from scattered client requests.
  • Dashboards, SMS, CRM, payments, inventory, profiles, analytics, and automation should never be casually included.
  • A clear, professional no protects the relationship better than an unclear yes.

Section 12

Client Onboarding Process

12.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Onboarding Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains what happens after a client accepts a proposal and before Shawcliffe Digital begins the serious build.

Onboarding is the bridge between:

“Yes, we want to work with you.”

and:

“Shawcliffe has everything needed to build this properly.”

Most small agency projects do not stall because the build is impossible.

They stall because:

  • The client does not send photos
  • Prices are unclear
  • Services are not defined
  • Domain access is missing
  • The client sends assets across five platforms
  • Nobody knows the review link
  • Policies are unwritten
  • Dashboard users are not confirmed
  • Payment provider access is not ready
  • The client expects Shawcliffe to guess business details
  • Build starts before the client is actually ready

The internal rule:

Do not begin full build until the client is onboarded enough to build responsibly.

Client onboarding should confirm:

Business informationNeeded for website/system identity
Services/products/pricesNeeded for customer clarity
Photos/logo/assetsNeeded for visual trust

Access/loginsNeeded for domain, hosting, Google, payment tools, etc.
Notification contactsNeeded so leads go to the right person
Dashboard usersNeeded if owner dashboard is included
Review linksNeeded for review request systems
Payment providerNeeded if deposits/payments are included
Client responsibilitiesNeeded to prevent delays

12.4 Onboarding Rule

No Random Asset Collection

Client materials should not be scattered across:

  • Text messages
  • Facebook Messenger
  • Instagram DMs
  • Email attachments
  • Verbal conversations
  • Random screenshots
  • Notes apps
  • Personal phones

Shawcliffe needs one organized place for client assets.

Use something simple:

  • Shared Google Drive folder
  • Airtable/Notion form
  • Google Form
  • Project folder
  • Email thread only for small projects

The exact tool matters less than the rule:

Everything important must end up in the client record or project folder.

12.10 Access and Login Collection

Access collection must be organized and handled carefully.

Do not casually ask clients to text passwords.

Access Needed by Project Type

Access TypeNeeded For
Domain registrarConnecting website/system to domain
Hosting accountExisting site migration or hosting update
Existing website platformRebuild, content transfer, redirects
Google Business ProfileReview link, business info, local SEO support
Google Analytics/Search ConsoleTracking/analytics if included

Email platformEmail notifications/campaigns
SMS platformSMS notifications

Booking platformIntegration if included

Access Collection Rules

Do

  • Ask what access is needed
  • Use secure sharing methods where possible
  • Prefer adding Shawcliffe as a user/admin instead of sharing passwords
  • Document what access was received
  • Remove access if project ends and appropriate
  • Keep access limited to what is needed

Do Not

  • Ask clients to text passwords casually
  • Store passwords in random notes
  • Share access broadly
  • Use personal accounts when business accounts are needed
  • Accept responsibility for tools not included in scope

Client-Facing Access Language

For any tools we need access to, the safest option is usually to add Shawcliffe as a user or admin rather than texting passwords. If that is not possible, we will agree on the safest practical way to share access.

Domain access missingBuild on staging, launch delayed
Review link missingAdd review system later
Payment provider missingPayment feature delayed

Hi [Client Name],

We have enough to begin some parts of the project, but the following items are still missing:

  • [Missing item]
  • [Missing item]

These items are needed for [reason]. If we do not receive them, we can either:

Curtis

Do not blame the client aggressively.

But do not absorb the cost of disorganization for free.

12.26 Common Onboarding Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Starting Build Before Services and Prices Are Clear

If services/products are unclear, the customer-facing system will be unclear.

Mistake 2: Letting Assets Arrive Everywhere

Random texts, DMs, emails, and screenshots create chaos.

Everything must end up in the client folder.

Mistake 3: Guessing Policies

Do not invent cancellation, refund, deposit, legal, health, food, or professional wording.

Mistake 4: Forgetting Notification Recipients

A lead form is useless if nobody receives the lead.

Mistake 5: Forgetting Dashboard Users

Dashboard setup requires knowing who will use it and what they should edit.

Mistake 6: Ignoring Domain Email Risk

Changing domain settings can break email if handled carelessly.

Mistake 7: Treating Missing Content as Shawcliffe’s Problem for Free

Help the client, but do not absorb unlimited content creation.

Mistake 8: Not Confirming Ready-to-Build

Build should begin after a readiness check, not just because the client sent “some stuff.”

Must-Have Now

Shawcliffe should create immediately:

  • General onboarding checklist
  • Client homework checklist
  • Business information form
  • Services/products/pricing table
  • Content/assets checklist
  • Access collection checklist
  • Notification contact form
  • Dashboard user form
  • Missing content email template
  • Development handoff template

Nice-to-Have Later

Do not delay selling while waiting for:

  • Automated onboarding portal
  • Perfect client portal
  • Branded upload system
  • Fully automated access manager
  • Fancy CRM onboarding pipeline
  • Video onboarding series
  • Full content strategy workbook
  • Automated reminders

Start with a clean checklist, folder, and email templates.

  • Logo/photo collection process
  • Services/products/pricing collection process
  • Access/login collection process
  • Google Business Profile/review link collection
  • Domain/hosting collection process
  • Payment provider collection process

  • Dashboard user collection

  • Ready-to-build definition
  • Offer-specific onboarding templates for:
    • Live Status Starter System
    • Quote Request Starter System
    • Booking & Review Starter System
  • Client onboarding email templates
  • Client folder structure
  • Development handoff template
  • Onboarding quality control checklist

12.29 Key Takeaways

  • Onboarding is where Shawcliffe turns a sale into a buildable project.
  • Do not start full build from scattered messages.
  • Every client needs a business information form.
  • Every project needs services/products/prices or an approved pricing approach.
  • Photos and logo matter, but missing photos should not always block launch.
  • Policies must come from the client.
  • Notification recipients must be confirmed before forms go live.
  • Dashboard users and editable fields must be confirmed before dashboard build.
  • Domain and hosting access must be handled carefully, especially if email is connected to the domain.
  • Missing content should be documented, not ignored.
  • A project is ready to build only when the required information, assets, access, and scope details are clear enough to proceed responsibly.

Section 13

Project Management and Build Workflow

13.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Delivery Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section defines how Shawcliffe Digital should manage a project after onboarding is complete and before the project launches.

This is the delivery system.

It answers:

  • Where does the project live?
  • Who owns each task?
  • What happens after onboarding?
  • How does Curtis hand off work to Cassandra?
  • How does Cassandra build from reusable components?
  • How does Shawcliffe review internally before the client sees it?
  • How does client feedback get collected?
  • How are revisions tracked?
  • How is QA handled?
  • What must happen before launch?
  • How does the client move into support?

The internal rule:

A project should never live only in someone’s head, a text thread, or a scattered pile of messages.

13.2 Core Delivery Philosophy

Shawcliffe Digital is a lean husband-and-wife agency.

That means the process needs to be:

  • Clear
  • Lightweight
  • Repeatable
  • Practical
  • Visible
  • Not corporate
  • Not overcomplicated
  • Strong enough to prevent chaos

The goal is not to create paperwork for its own sake.

The goal is to make sure:

  • Curtis knows what the client expects
  • Cassandra knows exactly what to build
  • The client knows what to review
  • Scope does not drift
  • Bugs are caught before launch
  • Launch does not happen in a panic
  • Support starts cleanly after launch

13.6 Project Status Rules

Every project card should always answer:

  • What stage is this project in?
  • What is the next action?
  • Who owns the next action?
  • What is blocking progress?
  • Is the client waiting on us?
  • Are we waiting on the client?
  • Is payment current?
  • Is scope still controlled?
  • Is there anything that should become an add-on?
  • Is the project ready to move to the next stage?

If the project card cannot answer those questions, the project is not being managed clearly.

Curtis

13.24 Managing Client Communication During Build

Communication Rules

Rule 1: Curtis Is the Client Contact

The client should not send random build requests directly to Cassandra.

Rule 2: Updates Should Be Calm and Predictable

Clients should not wonder if the project disappeared.

Rule 3: Do Not Over-Explain Technical Details

Explain what affects the client, not every technical step.

Rule 4: Keep Scope Visible

When client asks for extras, refer back to scope.

Rule 5: Put Decisions in Writing

If price, scope, features, or launch timing changes, write it down.

Simple Client Update Template

Hi [Client Name],

Quick update on your [system name]:

  • Current stage: [Build / Review / Revisions / QA / Launch Prep]
  • What we completed: [Item]
  • What we are working on now: [Item]
  • What we still need from you: [Item, if any]
  • Next step: [Item]

Thanks,
Curtis

Missing Item Follow-Up

Hi [Client Name],

We are at the point where we need [missing item] to keep moving.

This affects [specific part of project].

Please send it when you can, or let me know if you want us to use a simpler placeholder approach for now.

Thanks,
Curtis

13.25 Managing Internal Communication

Because Shawcliffe is a husband-and-wife agency, internal communication needs boundaries.

Business stress should not become vague household stress.

Internal Rules

  • Use the project board, not memory.
  • Use project cards, not scattered verbal instructions.
  • Batch client requests before sending to development.
  • Separate client urgency from true urgency.
  • Do not promise timelines without checking build workload.
  • Do not accept features without checking technical complexity.
  • Discuss scope changes before building them.
  • Document decisions after discussing them.
  • Protect deep work time.
  • Keep future ideas separate from current build tasks.

Daily Internal Check-In During Active Build

Keep this short.

Questions

  • What project is active?
  • What stage is it in?
  • What is blocked?
  • What does Curtis owe?
  • What does Cassandra owe?
  • Is the client waiting?
  • Are we waiting on the client?
  • Has scope changed?
  • Is launch still realistic?
  • What is the next task?

13.29 Common Project Management Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: No Single Source of Truth

If the project lives in texts, emails, memory, and screenshots, it will get messy.

Use the project card.

Mistake 2: Sending Raw Client Feedback Straight to Development

Curtis should sort feedback first.

Not every client comment is a development task.

Mistake 3: Letting Client Review Become Strategy

Client review is for reviewing agreed work.

New business ideas go to Phase 2 or add-ons.

Mistake 4: Skipping Internal Review

The client should not be the first person to discover obvious issues.

Mistake 5: Skipping Mobile Testing

Most customers will interact from their phone.

Mistake 6: Launching Without Payment Check

Do not launch major work with unresolved payment terms.

Mistake 7: Launching Without Support Handoff

If support expectations are unclear, every future request becomes awkward.

Mistake 8: Not Documenting Future Ideas

Good ideas should not disappear, but they should not hijack the launch.

13.30 Minimum Viable Project Management System

If Shawcliffe wants the simplest possible system, use this.

For Every Project, Maintain

  • Project card
  • Client folder
  • Approved scope
  • Build task list
  • Revision list
  • QA checklist
  • Launch checklist
  • Support handoff notes
  • Future improvements list

That is enough to run professionally at the beginning.

13.32 Key Takeaways

  • Shawcliffe needs a lightweight project management system, not a bloated corporate one.
  • Curtis should own client communication, project board, scope, feedback, and support handoff.
  • Cassandra should own technical build, component assembly, technical QA, and deployment.
  • The project board should always show the current stage and next action.
  • Build should not begin until onboarding is complete enough.
  • Every project should be built from reusable components where possible.
  • Internal review should happen before client review.
  • Client feedback must be sorted before it becomes development work.
  • QA must test the real customer and owner workflows.
  • Launch requires approval, payment check, technical readiness, and support clarity.
  • Support handoff is part of the project, not an afterthought.

Section 14

QA, Testing, and Launch Checklist

14.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Quality Assurance Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section defines Shawcliffe Digital’s QA, testing, and launch process.

QA means quality assurance.

In plain English:

QA is the process of checking that the system works, makes sense, looks professional, and is ready for real customers before launch.

For Shawcliffe Digital, QA is not optional.

A small agency can lose trust quickly if:

  • Forms do not send
  • Notifications go to the wrong person
  • A phone number is wrong
  • A dashboard update does not save
  • A QR code points to the wrong page
  • A payment link fails
  • A review link is broken
  • Mobile layout is awkward
  • The client finds obvious mistakes
  • Customers submit requests that disappear

The internal rule:

The client should not be the first tester, and the public should never be the first tester.

14.2 QA Philosophy

Shawcliffe should test every system from three viewpoints.

ViewpointQuestion
CustomerCan a real customer understand and complete the intended action?
OwnerCan the business owner receive, use, update, and respond to the system?
TechnicalDoes the system work reliably enough to launch?

All three matter.

A system can technically work but still confuse customers.

A system can look good but fail to notify the owner.

A system can be easy for customers but impossible for the owner to manage.

14.3 QA Ownership

QA should be shared, but not vague.

Curtis Owns

AreaResponsibility
Customer path testingDoes the customer know what to do?
Business accuracyAre services, prices, hours, location, and policies correct?
Owner usabilityWould a busy owner understand this?
Client approvalHas the client approved launch?
Scope checkAre we accidentally launching extras or missing included items?
Support readinessDoes the client know what happens after launch?

Cassandra Owns

AreaResponsibility
Technical functionalityDo forms, dashboards, uploads, links, and workflows work?
Notification testingDo alerts go where they should?
Data handlingIs information saved correctly if storage/CRM is included?
DeploymentIs the system technically ready to go live?
Domain/SSL/hostingDoes the live setup work?
Technical limitationsAre known issues documented?
Technical launchIs the public version live and stable?

Shared Ownership

AreaResponsibility
Final launch approvalBoth agree the project is ready
Bug severity decisionsDecide what blocks launch
Client-facing limitationsDecide what must be explained
Post-launch smoke testBoth verify the live system
Support handoffConfirm support expectations are clear

14.4 QA Stages

QA should happen in stages, not only at the end.

QA Timeline

StageWhen It HappensPurpose
Build QADuring buildCatch obvious technical issues early
Internal Business ReviewBefore client reviewCurtis checks customer/owner clarity
Internal Technical ReviewBefore client reviewCassandra checks functionality
Client ReviewBefore final QAClient confirms business accuracy
Revision QAAfter revisionsRetest anything changed
Final Pre-Launch QABefore launchConfirm ready for public use
Launch Day QAImmediately after launchTest live system
Post-Launch Smoke TestWithin 24–72 hoursConfirm system still works after launch
