14.6 Mobile Testing

Most customers will interact from a phone.

For Shawcliffe’s clients, mobile testing is essential.

A fruit stand customer, homeowner, pet owner, parent, or event client is likely using the system while busy, standing somewhere, or multitasking.

Mobile Testing Standards

At minimum, test:

  • iPhone-sized screen
  • Android-sized screen if available
  • Narrow browser width
  • Portrait orientation
  • Form completion by thumb
  • Button tapping
  • Image loading
  • Dashboard use on phone if owner will update from phone

Mobile QA Checklist

ItemPass?Notes
Page loads quickly enough
Text is readable without zooming
Buttons are easy to tap
Forms are usable on phone
Required fields are not frustrating
Keyboard does not cover key fields
Images do not break layout
Navigation is simple
Main call-to-action is visible
Contact buttons work
Map/location links work
Dashboard works on phone if included
QR code opens correct page on phone

Mobile Testing Rule

If the customer action is hard on a phone, the system is not ready.

14.7 Form Testing

Forms are central to Shawcliffe’s systems.

A broken form is a serious launch blocker.

Universal Form QA Checklist

ItemPass?Notes
Form loads

Optional fields can be skipped
Dropdowns/radio buttons/checkboxes work
Phone/email fields accept proper input
Error messages are understandable
Submit button works
Duplicate submissions are considered
Spam protection works if included
Customer confirmation appears
Owner notification sends
Submission data is stored if included
Test submission can be identified
Test data removed before launch if needed

Use realistic test data.

FieldTest Value
NameTest Customer

Form Testing Rule

A form is not tested until Shawcliffe confirms what the customer sees and what the owner receives.

14.8 Notification Testing

Notifications are where many systems fail silently.

A form that submits but does not notify the owner can lose real leads.

Notification Types

Review requestPost-service review message

ItemPass?Notes

Notification includes useful details
Notification subject line is clear

Multiple recipients receive it if included

Notification does not expose sensitive info unnecessarily
Failed notification risk considered
Client has confirmed who responds

Owner Notification Should Include

For most lead/booking/quote systems:

  • Customer name
  • Customer phone
  • Customer email
  • Requested service/product
  • Message/details
  • Date/time submitted
  • Uploaded files link if included
  • Urgency if included

  • Reminder that urgent issues should call if applicable
  • Policy note if relevant

Notification Testing Rule

Never assume notifications work. Trigger them and verify receipt.

Thanks,
Curtis

Final Approval Language

Approved for launch.

Ask the client to reply with something clear like that.

14.20 Bug Severity Levels

Not every issue has the same seriousness.

Use severity levels to decide what blocks launch.

Bug Severity Table

SeverityMeaningExampleLaunch?
Severity 1 — CriticalCore system broken or serious riskForm does not submit, payment broken, site downDo not launch
Severity 2 — MajorImportant feature broken or confusingOwner notification missing, dashboard not savingUsually do not launch
Severity 3 — ModerateIssue affects usability but workaround existsMinor layout issue, non-critical link wrongMaybe launch after discussion
Severity 4 — MinorCosmetic or small content issueSlight spacing issue, minor typoCan launch if documented
Severity 5 — Future ImprovementNot a bug, improvement ideaAdd SMS laterDoes not block launch

Critical Launch Blockers

Do not launch if:

  • Website/system does not load
  • Main form does not submit
  • Owner notification does not send
  • Payment link is broken if payments included
  • Dashboard cannot update critical fields
  • Customer receives wrong information
  • Business phone/email/address is wrong
  • Review link points to wrong business
  • Domain/SSL broken
  • Client has not approved
  • Payment terms unresolved
  • Required policy missing for booking/payment/order

Known Limitation Examples

Some issues can launch if documented:

  • Client has not supplied all photos
  • Gallery is smaller than desired
  • Review automation saved for Phase 2
  • SMS alerts not included yet
  • CRM Lite not included yet
  • Advanced analytics not configured because not in scope
  • Some future dashboard fields saved for add-on

14.30 Common QA Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Only Testing as the Builder

The builder knows how it is supposed to work.

Customers do not.

Test like a confused customer.

Mistake 2: Testing Only on Desktop

Most local-business customer actions happen on phones.

Mistake 3: Not Testing Notifications

The most dangerous failure is a lead that silently disappears.

Mistake 4: Not Testing the Live Version

A staging version working does not guarantee the live version works.

Mistake 5: Not Testing QR Codes Before Print

A printed broken QR code is embarrassing and expensive.

Mistake 6: Forgetting Client Approval

The client must approve facts, prices, services, policies, and launch.

Mistake 7: Treating Payment Links Casually

Payments require extra testing and approved policies.

Mistake 8: Skipping Post-Launch Smoke Test

Launch is not done until the live system is tested.

14.33 Key Takeaways

  • QA is not optional.
  • Curtis should test the customer and business experience.
  • Cassandra should test the technical functionality.
  • The client should approve all business facts before launch.
  • Forms must be tested end-to-end.
  • Notifications must be verified by receipt, not assumed.
  • Dashboards must be tested on the device the owner will actually use.
  • QR codes must be scanned before printing.
  • Payment links must not launch without approved payment/refund/deposit wording.
  • No Severity 1 issue should launch.
  • Launch is not done until the live system has been tested.
  • Post-launch smoke testing catches problems before they become client frustration.

Section 15

Client Support and Maintenance Process

15.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Support Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains what happens after Shawcliffe Digital launches a client system.

Launch is not the end of the relationship.

After launch, clients may need:

  • Bug fixes
  • Small updates
  • Training reminders
  • Dashboard help
  • Form changes
  • Service or price updates
  • Review request support
  • Notification troubleshooting
  • Seasonal updates
  • New features
  • Add-ons
  • Monthly improvements
  • Emergency help

Without a support process, every client message becomes stressful.

The internal rule:

Support must be clear, trackable, and bounded.

Support should help clients, but it should not become unlimited free work.

15.2 Support Philosophy

Shawcliffe Digital should treat support as part of the product.

A good business system is not just built and abandoned.

However, support must be defined.

Support is not:

  • Unlimited revisions forever
  • Free new features
  • Free marketing work
  • Instant replies at all hours
  • Endless dashboard retraining
  • Manual daily updates unless paid
  • A replacement for the owner running their business

Support is:

  • Keeping the included system working
  • Helping the client use what was built
  • Making small agreed updates
  • Fixing real bugs
  • Explaining what counts as extra
  • Identifying useful future upgrades
  • Keeping the client relationship healthy

15.3 Support Ownership

Curtis Owns

AreaResponsibility
Support intakeReceives and logs support requests

TriageDecides whether request is bug, update, training, add-on, emergency

Change request handlingQuotes or sends to Phase 2

Is this urgent?Affects priority and work schedule
Is monthly support enough?Client may need higher tier

Should this client be retained?Some clients may be too demanding

15.4 Official Support Channels

Support should come through one official channel.

This prevents requests from getting lost in:

  • Texts
  • Instagram DMs
  • Facebook messages
  • Personal phone calls
  • Casual conversations
  • Random emails
  • Verbal comments
  • Screenshots with no context

Recommended Early Support Channel

At the beginning, keep it simple.

Use:

One dedicated support email address

Example:

support@shawcliffedigital.ca

If not ready yet, use a clearly named email or one organized thread.

Acceptable Support Channels

ChannelUse Case
Support emailBest default

Phone callOnly for scheduled support or urgent issues
Text messageAvoid except trusted emergency clients

Support Channel Rule

All support requests must end up in the support log, even if they arrive by text, phone, or in-person conversation.

Client-Facing Support Channel Language

To keep support organized, please send requests through [support email/form]. That way we can track what was requested, what was done, and whether it is included in your support plan or needs to be quoted separately.

15.5 Support Request Intake

Every support request should be captured before action is taken.

Do not jump straight into fixing unless it is clearly urgent.

Support Intake Questions

Ask:

  • What is the issue or request?
  • Is something broken, or are you asking for a change?
  • What page, form, dashboard, or feature is affected?
  • When did you notice it?
  • Is it affecting customers right now?
  • Can you send a screenshot or example?
  • What were you trying to do?
  • What happened instead?
  • Is this urgent, or can it wait for normal support?
  • Is this part of the original system or a new request?

15.7 Bug vs Update vs New Feature

This distinction is critical.

Clients may call everything a “fix.”

Shawcliffe needs to classify it correctly.

Bug

A bug means:

An included feature is not working the way it was supposed to work.

Examples:

  • Form does not submit
  • Owner notification does not arrive
  • Dashboard save button fails
  • Review link goes to wrong page
  • QR code points to wrong system
  • Payment link is broken
  • Site is down
  • Public page does not reflect dashboard update

Small Update

A small update means:

A minor change to existing content or settings within the existing system.

Examples:

  • Update hours
  • Change phone number
  • Swap photo
  • Edit service description
  • Update product price
  • Change announcement text
  • Add one new service to an existing list
  • Update seasonal wording

New Feature

A new feature means:

New functionality, workflow, page, component, integration, automation, or business process not included in the original scope.

Examples:

  • Add SMS notifications
  • Add payment deposits
  • Add CRM Lite
  • Add customer accounts
  • Add full inventory tracking
  • Add calendar sync
  • Add loyalty program
  • Add advanced analytics
  • Add AI receptionist
  • Add new dashboard section
  • Add second business/location workflow

Classification Table

RequestCategory
“The form stopped working.”Bug
“Can you change my Saturday hours?”Small Update
“How do I update today’s products?”Training Issue
“Can customers pay deposits now?”New Feature / Add-On
“Can we add SMS alerts?”New Feature / Add-On
“The QR code opens the wrong page.”Bug
“Can you add a new service?”Small Update or Add-On depending on size
“Can you build a full booking calendar?”New Feature / Larger Add-On
“Can you rewrite all my service copy?”Content Add-On
“Can you add Google ads?”New Service / Marketing Plan

Client-Facing Explanation

A bug means something we already built is not working properly. A small update is a minor change to existing content. A new feature is new functionality that was not part of the original build. Bugs and small updates may be covered by your plan, while new features are quoted separately.

15.20 Avoiding Unlimited Free Support

Support creep is like scope creep after launch.

It often starts with small friendly requests.

Common Support Creep Phrases

  • “Can you quickly…”
  • “This should only take a second…”
  • “While you’re in there…”
  • “Can you just add one thing…”
  • “I thought this was included…”
  • “It used to be fine, but now I want…”
  • “Can you show me again?”
  • “Can you update this every week?”
  • “Can you post this for us?”
  • “Can you make a new page?”

Support Creep Prevention Rules

Rule 1: Log Every Request

If it is not logged, it becomes invisible work.

Rule 2: Name the Category

Bug, update, training, new feature, add-on.

Rule 3: Tie Work to Plan

Is it included in their support tier?

Rule 4: Quote Before Building

No unpaid add-ons.

Rule 5: Watch Repetition

Repeated training questions may mean:

  • Client needs cheat sheet
  • Dashboard is confusing
  • Support plan should increase
  • System needs improvement
  • Client is not a good fit

Rule 6: Do Not Reward Chaos

Clients who send scattered messages should be redirected to support channel.

Friendly Boundary Script

I can help with that. I want to keep support organized, so please send it through the support channel and I’ll log it properly. If it is included in your plan, we’ll handle it there. If it is outside the plan, I’ll quote it before we do the work.

15.21 Handling Clients Without a Monthly Plan

Some clients will decline support.

That is allowed.

But Shawcliffe must not accidentally provide support anyway.

No-Plan Rules

Clients without monthly support:

  • Do not get included monthly updates
  • Do not get monitoring
  • Do not get priority support
  • Do not get routine checks
  • Do not get free training forever
  • Do not get free new features
  • Do not get ongoing troubleshooting unless agreed

Paid Support Options

For no-plan clients, offer:

OptionUse
One-time support quoteSpecific task
Hourly support blockMultiple small tasks
Monthly care planOngoing support
Upgrade projectNew feature/system
Training sessionHelp using dashboard/system

No-Plan Client Response

Since there is no active monthly support plan, this would be handled as a paid support request. I can review what is needed and send a quote before we do anything.

No-Plan Emergency Response

If the issue is a true emergency, Shawcliffe may help, but still clarify billing.

This looks urgent, so we can look at it as soon as possible. Since there is no active monthly support plan, emergency troubleshooting may be billed separately. I’ll let you know what we find.

15.27 Support Boundary Language for Contracts/Proposals

Use this language in proposals or support agreements.

General Support Boundary

Support includes help with the system as defined in the selected support plan. New features, new pages, new workflows, major design changes, integrations, automations, or work outside the original system are quoted separately.

Bug Definition

A bug means an included feature is not working as intended. A change in business needs, a new desired feature, or a request to expand the system is not considered a bug.

Update Definition

A small update means a minor change to existing content or settings, such as hours, prices, wording, photos, or service details, within the limits of the selected support plan.

No Monthly Plan Boundary

If no monthly support plan is active, future updates, troubleshooting, training, or changes are handled as paid support requests.

Emergency Boundary

Emergency support is prioritized for issues that prevent customers from accessing the system, submitting inquiries, making payments if included, or receiving accurate critical information. Emergency response availability depends on the support agreement.

  • Client refuses to pay for support
  • Client blames Shawcliffe for their own business disorganization
  • Client requests misleading or unethical changes
  • Client creates more support burden than their plan covers
  • Client refuses to learn basic dashboard use
  • Client repeatedly changes direction

Options

SituationResponse
Client needs more helpRecommend higher plan
Client wants lots of new workQuote Phase 2
Client is disorganizedRequire support channel and written requests
Client is abusiveEnd relationship
Client has outgrown systemPropose rebuild or upgrade
Client refuses support planMove to paid support only

Ending Support Language

Based on the level and type of support being requested, I do not think the current arrangement is working well. We can either move to a support plan that matches the level of help needed, or we can limit future work to separately quoted requests.

15.32 Common Support Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Not Logging Requests

Invisible support becomes unpaid work.

Mistake 2: Letting Text Messages Become the Support System

Texts are easy, but they are hard to track.

Mistake 3: Treating Every Request as Urgent

Urgency must be defined.

Mistake 4: Letting Clients Without Plans Get Plan-Level Support

This trains clients not to pay for support.

Mistake 5: Sending Raw Requests Straight to Development

Curtis should triage first.

Mistake 6: Calling New Features “Fixes”

A feature the client wants now is not automatically a bug.

Mistake 7: Not Offering an Upgrade

Repeated support requests often reveal the next logical paid improvement.

Mistake 8: Overpromising Response Times

Do not promise 24/7 priority support unless priced and planned.

Mistake 9: Forgetting Training

Some support issues are actually training issues.

A one-page cheat sheet may save hours later.

Mistake 10: Not Updating Components After Support Issues

If the same issue appears twice, improve the component or checklist.

15.35 Key Takeaways

  • Support must be clear, tracked, and bounded.
  • Curtis should triage all support requests before Cassandra gets involved.
  • Bugs, small updates, training issues, and new features are different things.
  • Clients without monthly support should not receive ongoing free support.
  • Emergency issues should be defined carefully.
  • Dashboards, forms, notifications, CRM, payments, QR codes, inventory, and automation all create support responsibilities.
  • Support requests often reveal future paid upgrades.
  • Repeated support problems should improve Shawcliffe’s templates, QA checklists, onboarding, and pricing.
  • A support log is essential.
  • Monthly support is one of Shawcliffe’s most important recurring revenue opportunities.

Section 16

Monthly Recurring Revenue and Support Plan Strategy

16.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Recurring Revenue Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains how Shawcliffe Digital should build monthly recurring revenue after launching client projects.

Monthly recurring revenue, or MRR, is the money Shawcliffe earns every month from ongoing support, maintenance, hosting, care plans, marketing support, system updates, and long-term client relationships.

This matters because one-time builds are unpredictable.

One month may have sales.

Another month may be slow.

Recurring revenue helps create stability.

The internal rule:

Every serious project should have a clear post-launch support or recurring revenue path.

16.2 Why Monthly Recurring Revenue Matters

A one-time project brings money once.

A support client brings stability every month.

One-Time Revenue

Examples:

  • Website build
  • App prototype
  • Quote request system
  • Live status system
  • Booking system
  • Dashboard setup

One-time revenue is useful, but it can create a feast-or-famine business.

Recurring Revenue

Examples:

  • Maintenance plan
  • Care plan
  • Hosting/support bundle
  • Review request plan
  • Seasonal support
  • Dashboard support
  • CRM Lite support
  • Google Business Profile support
  • Analytics/reporting
  • SMS/email customer list support
  • Automation monitoring
  • Higher-touch marketing support

Recurring revenue helps Shawcliffe:

  • Predict income
  • Maintain client relationships
  • Improve systems over time
  • Catch bugs early
  • Create upsell opportunities
  • Keep clients from drifting away
  • Build long-term business value

16.3 Recurring Revenue Philosophy

Shawcliffe should not sell monthly support as a guilt add-on.

Do not say:

“Do you want to pay us monthly too?”

Say:

“Once this system is live, it still needs to be maintained, updated, tested, and improved. The monthly plan makes sure it keeps working and gives you a clear way to get help.”

Monthly support should feel like part of the business system, not an afterthought.

What Monthly Support Is Really For

Client Thinks It IsWhat It Actually Provides
“Website maintenance”Peace of mind, updates, fixes, support
“Hosting”System stability and access
“Support”Help when something breaks or changes
“Updates”Keeping business info current
“Review help”Reputation building
“Dashboard support”Owner confidence using the system
“Analytics”Understanding what is working
“Marketing support”Ongoing improvement
“Automation support”Monitoring workflows that can fail quietly

16.4 The Monthly Value Stack

A good monthly plan should combine several kinds of value.

Monthly Value Categories

CategoryValue to Client
Technical maintenanceKeeps system working
Small updatesKeeps business info current
Support accessGives client a clear help path
Monitoring/checksCatches issues before customers do

System complexityStatic siteForms/dashboardCRM/automation

16.23 How to Explain Monthly Value to Clients

Clients may say:

“Why do I need to pay monthly?”

Shawcliffe needs simple explanations.

General Explanation

The monthly plan keeps the system supported after launch. It gives you a clear place to go when something needs updating, breaks, changes, or needs improvement. Without a plan, future work is just quoted as needed.

Lead System Explanation

If your system is capturing leads, we need to make sure forms and notifications keep working. A broken form or missed notification can cost real money.

Dashboard Explanation

Since you’ll be updating parts of the system yourself, the support plan gives you help if you get stuck, need changes, or something stops saving properly.

Review Plan Explanation

Reviews are not a one-time task. The value comes from asking consistently and making it easy for customers to review you over time.

Seasonal Seller Explanation

Your business changes day to day during the season. Support helps keep products, locations, statuses, QR codes, and customer updates working when they matter most.

CRM Explanation

The CRM becomes useful when you actually use it to follow up. Monthly support helps keep the lead process organized and lets us improve it based on how leads are coming in.

Marketing Explanation

The first build creates the system. Monthly marketing support helps improve results over time by adjusting pages, offers, follow-up, reviews, and campaigns.

16.24 Handling “I Don’t Want Monthly”

Not every client will want monthly support.

That is fine.

But Shawcliffe must protect itself.

Response

That is okay. If you do not want a monthly plan, future updates, support, troubleshooting, or changes can be quoted as needed. The main difference is that there is no ongoing monitoring, included update time, or priority support.

Offer a Middle Option

Another option is starting with Basic Maintenance so there is at least a support path for small fixes and updates, without committing to a larger care plan.

When No Monthly Is Fine

No monthly may be acceptable for:

  • Static landing page
  • Very simple website
  • No dashboard
  • No SMS
  • No payments
  • No CRM
  • No active inventory/status
  • Client truly does not need updates

When No Monthly Is Risky

No monthly is risky for:

  • Live status systems
  • Product inventory
  • Dashboards
  • CRM Lite
  • SMS
  • Payments
  • Quote systems with important notifications
  • Booking systems
  • Seasonal sellers
  • Clients who need frequent updates
  • Any system central to daily operations

16.25 Avoiding Underpriced Support

Underpriced support is dangerous because it feels small at first.

Then, after 10 clients, it becomes a second unpaid job.

Signs Support Is Underpriced

  • Client sends frequent requests
  • Requests take longer than expected
  • Cassandra is pulled in often
  • Client expects instant help
  • Client needs repeated training
  • Monthly fee does not cover time spent
  • You avoid replying because the plan feels unfair
  • Client asks for strategy but pays maintenance pricing
  • Client’s system is business-critical but plan is tiny

What To Do

Options:

  • Raise support tier at renewal
  • Quote recurring requests separately
  • Move client to Growth Support
  • Simplify system
  • Train client better
  • Create dashboard cheat sheet
  • Improve component
  • End support if not profitable

Support Repricing Language

Based on the level of support and updates being requested, the current plan is no longer the right fit. We can either move to a higher support plan that matches the work needed, or handle future requests as separately quoted work.

16.27 Post-Launch Check-In Strategy

Post-launch check-ins help retain clients.

First 7-Day Check-In

Ask:

  • Have customers used it yet?
  • Did any forms/bookings/requests come through?
  • Did notifications arrive properly?
  • Did anything confuse you?
  • Do any details need updating?

30-Day Check-In

Ask:

  • What has worked so far?
  • What have customers asked about?
  • Have you received leads/bookings/orders?
  • Are you using the dashboard?
  • Are you asking for reviews?
  • Is there anything you are still doing manually?
  • What would be the next useful improvement?

90-Day Review

Ask:

16.33 MRR Sales Scripts

During Proposal

For this kind of system, I recommend monthly support because it includes forms, notifications, and customer-facing information. If those break or go stale, you can lose leads or confuse customers.

After Launch

Now that the system is live, monthly care gives you a clear way to request updates, get help, and keep the system working properly.

For a Dashboard System

Since you’ll be updating this yourself, support matters. If you get stuck or your business changes, you have a clear place to go instead of trying to figure it out alone.

For Review Support

Reviews are one of the simplest ways to build local trust, but most businesses do not ask consistently. We can help you make that part of the process.

For No Monthly Plan

You do not have to choose a monthly plan. It just means future support, changes, and troubleshooting are quoted as needed rather than included.

16.34 MRR Objection Handling

“I don’t want another monthly bill.”

I understand. The monthly plan is not mandatory for every project. The trade-off is that without it, updates and support are handled as separate paid requests. For simple websites, that may be fine. For active systems with forms, notifications, dashboards, or inventory, monthly support usually makes more sense.

“Can I just call you if something breaks?”

Yes, but if there is no monthly plan, it would be treated as paid support as needed. A monthly plan gives you included support and clearer priority.

“What if I don’t use the support every month?”

The plan is partly about access and readiness, not just tasks. It keeps a support path open, covers checks and small updates, and gives us a way to help quickly when something changes or breaks.

“Can we start without support?”

For a very simple system, yes. For systems with dashboards, notifications, SMS, payments, CRM, inventory, or live status, I strongly recommend at least a basic care plan because those systems are more active.

“Is hosting included?”

Hosting can be included depending on the plan. If Shawcliffe manages hosting or technical maintenance, that responsibility needs to be covered by the monthly plan.

16.39 Common MRR Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Treating Monthly Support as Optional for Every System

Some systems need support.

If a client has SMS, dashboard, inventory, CRM, payments, or automation, support should be strongly recommended or required.

Mistake 2: Underpricing Support to Make the Sale

Cheap support feels easier to sell but becomes painful later.

Mistake 3: Including Too Much

Do not make Standard Care include Growth Support work.

Mistake 4: Failing to Explain Value

Clients will not pay monthly if they think it is just “keeping the website online.”

Explain forms, notifications, updates, reviews, dashboards, and customer flow.

Mistake 5: Letting No-Plan Clients Consume Time

If they declined support, future work is paid as needed.

Mistake 6: Not Reviewing MRR Monthly

Recurring revenue only becomes strategic if tracked.

Mistake 7: Promising Fast Response for Low Plans

Response expectations must match price.

Mistake 8: Selling Automation Without Support

Automation needs monitoring.

Mistake 9: Forgetting Seasonal Plans

Seasonal businesses may be great clients if pricing matches their business cycle.

Section 17

Reusable Component and Template Documentation

17.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Product Library Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains how Shawcliffe Digital should document reusable components and archetype templates.

This is one of the most important systems in the business.

Shawcliffe Digital should not rebuild every client project from scratch.

The goal is to gradually build a library of:

  • Reusable components
  • Reusable field sets
  • Reusable form patterns
  • Reusable dashboards
  • Reusable customer flows
  • Reusable QA checklists
  • Reusable support notes
  • Reusable sales explanations
  • Reusable proposal language
  • Reusable archetype templates

The internal rule:

Every client project should either reuse an existing component or improve the component library.

17.2 Why Component Documentation Matters

Without documentation, reusable work becomes hidden in Cassandra’s head or buried in old projects.

That creates problems:

  • Every project feels custom
  • Curtis cannot confidently sell components
  • Cassandra has to remember how things were built
  • Bugs repeat
  • QA is inconsistent
  • Pricing is guessed
  • Support is harder
  • Future upgrades are unclear
  • Templates do not improve over time

Good component documentation lets Shawcliffe:

  • Build faster
  • Price better
  • Sell more clearly
  • Reduce mistakes
  • Train future helpers
  • Improve QA
  • Improve support
  • Turn client work into product assets
  • Build template systems for many archetypes

17.3 Component vs Template

Shawcliffe needs to distinguish between components and templates.

Component

A component is one reusable piece of a system.

Examples:

  • Business Profile
  • Service Menu
  • Lead Capture Form
  • Notifications
  • Admin Dashboard
  • Review Request System
  • CRM Lite
  • Status Tracker
  • Product Inventory
  • Photo Upload
  • Booking Request
  • Payment/Deposit Flow

A component answers:

“What reusable feature or workflow does this provide?”

Template

A template is a reusable package made from multiple components for a specific archetype or offer.

Examples:

  • Live Status Starter System
  • Quote Request Starter System
  • Booking & Review Starter System
  • Pet Booking & Intake Starter System
  • Professional Intake Starter System

A template answers:

“What complete starter system do we sell to this kind of business?”

Simple Difference

ItemMeaningExample
ComponentReusable building blockPhoto Upload
TemplateReusable offer/system made from componentsContractor Quote Request Starter System

17.7 Component Readiness Levels

Not every component is equally ready.

Use readiness levels.

Component Readiness Scale

LevelMeaning
IdeaConcept exists, not built
PrototypeBuilt once or partly built
UsableCan be used in client work with care
ReusableDocumented and reliable enough to reuse
ProductizedStandardized, priced, tested, support documented
MatureUsed many times, improved, stable, easy to sell

Readiness Definitions

Idea

  • Exists in strategy
  • Not built
  • Not priced
  • Not tested
  • No documentation

Prototype

  • Built experimentally
  • May work in one context
  • Not fully reusable
  • Needs technical cleanup
  • QA not standardized

Usable

  • Can be used in a client project
  • Needs developer attention
  • Some docs exist
  • Scope must be carefully controlled

Reusable

  • Has standard fields/options
  • Has setup steps
  • Has QA checklist
  • Has pricing notes
  • Has support notes
  • Can be used without reinventing

Productized

  • Has sales language
  • Has proposal language
  • Has support plan guidance
  • Has upgrade paths
  • Has examples
  • Can be sold repeatedly

Mature

  • Used across multiple projects
  • Bugs and support issues addressed
  • Strong documentation
  • Clear pricing
  • Easy to configure
  • Reliable template asset

Internal Rule

Do not sell an Idea as if it is Mature.

It is okay to sell newer components, but price and timeline should reflect risk.

Template Name

Purpose

This template helps mobile, seasonal, and pop-up sellers keep customers informed about current status, location, product availability, prices, and sold-out updates.

One-Sentence Promise

Customers can check whether you are open, where you are, what you have today, and what is sold out before they come.

Ideal Client

Good fit if the business:

Poor-Fit Client

17.25 Component Improvement Loop

Every project should improve the library.

Improvement Loop

  • Build project.
  • Use components/template.
  • QA system.
  • Launch.
  • Support client.
  • Notice bugs, friction, or repeated requests.
  • Update component documentation.
  • Improve component if needed.
  • Update pricing/support notes.
  • Use improved version next time.

Internal Review After Each Project

Ask:

  • Which components were used?
  • Which components worked well?
  • Which components were confusing?
  • What did the client ask for that was not included?
  • What bugs appeared?
  • What support issues appeared?
  • What should be added to QA?
  • What should be added to onboarding?
  • What should be added to scope exclusions?
  • What should become a future upgrade?

17.33 How Support Feeds Component Improvement

Support is not just a cost.

Support teaches Shawcliffe what to improve.

Support-to-Component Examples

Support IssueComponent Improvement
Client keeps forgetting how to update dashboardAdd dashboard cheat sheet
Booking clients confused about confirmationImprove booking confirmation language
Quote clients ask for SMS after launchAdd SMS upgrade to proposal
Live status clients want customer alertsCreate alert upgrade path
Clients miss review requestsAdd review campaign option
Product updates too frequentRecommend dashboard or higher support
Form notifications failImprove notification QA checklist
Clients ask same setup questionsImprove onboarding template

Monthly Improvement Question

At monthly review, ask:

What support request happened more than once, and how do we stop it from happening again?

17.34 Avoiding One-Off Custom Chaos

Shawcliffe will be tempted to say yes to custom requests.

Some are useful.

Some create chaos.

Custom Request Filter

Before building custom work, ask:

  • Does this fit an existing component?
  • Can this become a reusable variation?
  • Does this help one of our 12 archetypes?
  • Will future clients want this?
  • Can we support it?
  • Does it require monthly support?
  • Is the client paying enough?
  • Is this better as Phase 2?
  • Is this outside our current ability?
  • Will this distract from the core business?

Decision Table

Request TypeDecision
Fits existing componentUse component
Small reusable variationBuild and document
Strong new reusable componentPrice properly and document
One-off but profitableConsider if support manageable
One-off and low valueDecline or postpone
Too riskyDecline
Too vagueClarify before pricing
Support-heavyRequire monthly plan

Internal Rule

Custom work is not bad. Undocumented custom work is bad.

17.35 First 12 Component Quick Cards

These should be created first.

1. Business Profile

Purpose

Shows who the business is, what they do, where they are, and how to contact them.

Used In

All templates.

Required Inputs

Business name, phone, email, location/service area, hours, description, social links.

QA

Check accuracy, mobile display, links.

Support

Low, unless business info changes often.

Pricing

Foundation component included in most projects.

Upgrade

Google Business Profile/local SEO support.

2. Service / Product Menu

Purpose

Shows what the business offers.

Used In

All templates.

Required Inputs

Services/products, prices, descriptions, categories, durations if relevant.

QA

Check names, prices, descriptions, visibility.

Support

Medium if prices/products change often.

Pricing

Foundation component; more expensive if large or dashboard-editable.

Upgrade

Dashboard-editable menu, inventory, packages.

3. Lead Capture / Inquiry Form

Purpose

Collects structured customer inquiries.

Used In

Trades, professional services, food makers, events, property services.

Required Inputs

Fields, notification recipient, confirmation message.

QA

Submit form, test validation, test notification.

Support

Medium; forms and notifications must keep working.

Pricing

Core paid component.

Upgrade

CRM Lite, SMS, analytics, automation.

4. Notifications

Purpose

Sends alerts or confirmations when something happens.

Used In

Most systems.

Required Inputs

Recipients, channel, trigger, message content.

QA

Trigger and verify receipt.

Support

Medium/high if SMS included.

Pricing

Email may be included; SMS is add-on/monthly.

Upgrade

SMS, routing, reminders, automation.

5. Review Request System

Purpose

Helps businesses ask for reviews consistently.

Used In

Most local businesses.

Required Inputs

Google review link, message wording, QR need.

QA

Test link and QR.

Support

Low to medium; campaigns need monthly support.

Pricing

Easy add-on or support plan feature.

Upgrade

Review campaign, SMS/email request, tracking.

6. Admin Dashboard

Purpose

Lets the owner update agreed fields.

Used In

Live Status, food makers, retail, dashboards, CRM.

Required Inputs

Dashboard user, editable fields, access rules.

QA

Login, save, public update, mobile.

Support

High.

Pricing

Growth/Premium component.

Upgrade

Advanced dashboard, multi-user permissions, reporting.

7. Status Tracker

Purpose

Shows current status such as open, closed, sold out, closing soon.

Used In

Live Status, mobile sellers, food trucks, pop-ups.

Required Inputs

Status labels, dashboard update rules.

QA

Update status and verify public display.

Support

Medium/high because accuracy matters.

Pricing

Growth component; requires support for active use.

Upgrade

Customer alerts, automation, QR tracking.

8. Product Inventory / Limited Batch

Purpose

Shows what products are available, limited, or sold out.

Used In

Mobile sellers, food makers, retail.

Required Inputs

Products, categories, prices, availability states.

QA

Check product display, availability updates, sold-out states.

Support

High if updated often.

Pricing

Growth/Premium depending on complexity.

Upgrade

Preorders, customer alerts, payments.

9. Location / Pop-Up Tracker

Purpose

Shows current location, market schedule, or pop-up route.

Used In

Mobile sellers, food trucks, market vendors, event businesses.

Required Inputs

Locations, schedules, map links.

QA

Test map links, schedule display, mobile.

Support

Medium if locations change often.

Pricing

Growth component.

Upgrade

Multi-location, QR tracking, alerts.

10. Booking Request System

Purpose

Lets customers request appointments or consultations.

Used In

Personal care, pet services, education, wellness, professional services.

Required Inputs

Services, availability rules, notification recipient, confirmation wording, policies.

QA

Submit request, test notification, test confirmation.

Support

Medium/high if services/prices change often.

Pricing

Growth component.

Upgrade

Deposits, reminders, rebooking, CRM, calendar sync.

11. Photo / File Upload

Purpose

Lets customers submit photos/files with inquiry.

Used In

Trades, events, vehicles, pet services, custom orders.

Required Inputs

File purpose, allowed file types, max files, owner access.

QA

Test uploads on phone and desktop.

Support

Medium.

Pricing

Add-on/Growth component.

Upgrade

CRM-connected files, secure portal.

12. CRM Lite

Purpose

Tracks leads/customers and follow-up status.

Used In

Trades, property services, pet services, vehicles, education, professional services.

Required Inputs

Lead statuses, fields, owner workflow.

QA

Create lead, update status, add notes, test search/filter if included.

Support

High.

Pricing

Growth/Premium component, usually needs monthly support.

Upgrade

Automation, reminders, reporting.

17.36 Minimum Viable Component Library

At the beginning, Shawcliffe does not need perfect documentation.

Minimum viable library:

  • Component name

  • Used in which offers
  • Required inputs
  • Setup steps
  • QA checklist
  • Support notes
  • Pricing impact
  • Upgrade path
  • Known limitations

That is enough to start.

17.37 Must-Have Now vs Nice-to-Have Later

Must-Have Now

Shawcliffe should immediately create documentation for:

  • Business Profile
  • Service / Product Menu
  • Lead Capture / Inquiry Form
  • Notifications
  • Review Request System
  • Admin Dashboard
  • Status Tracker
  • Product Inventory / Limited Batch
  • Location / Pop-Up Tracker
  • Booking Request System
  • Photo / File Upload
  • CRM Lite

And template documentation for:

  • Live Status Starter System
  • Quote Request Starter System
  • Booking & Review Starter System

Nice-to-Have Later

Do not delay selling while waiting for:

  • Perfect internal wiki
  • Full automated component catalog
  • Screenshots for every component
  • Full video walkthroughs
  • Formal technical diagrams
  • Version control system for documentation
  • Client-facing product pages for all components
  • Fully mature templates for all 12 archetypes

Start with practical docs and improve them after each project.

17.38 Common Component Documentation Mistakes

Mistake 1: Documenting Only Technical Details

Curtis also needs sales, pricing, support, and proposal language.

Mistake 2: Documenting Only Sales Details

Cassandra also needs setup steps, dependencies, QA, and limitations.

Mistake 3: Not Updating Docs After Bugs

If a bug happens twice, the component documentation failed.

Mistake 4: Treating Every Client Build as Unique

Most local businesses share patterns.

Look for reuse.

Mistake 5: Not Documenting Limitations

Limitations prevent overselling and support conflict.

Mistake 6: Not Documenting Pricing Impact

If a component creates support or testing burden, pricing should reflect it.

Mistake 7: Letting Templates Become Bloated

A starter template should stay focused.

Add-ons and upgrades belong in upgrade paths.

Mistake 8: Not Creating Examples

Examples make selling and building easier.

17.40 Key Takeaways

  • Shawcliffe’s long-term strength comes from reusable components and templates.
  • Every project should improve the component library.
  • Components are building blocks.
  • Templates are complete archetype-specific starter systems.
  • Documentation must serve both sales and development.
  • Curtis needs sales, pricing, support, and proposal language.
  • Cassandra needs setup steps, dependencies, QA, and technical notes.
  • Component docs should include purpose, archetypes, fields, configuration, dependencies, setup, testing, support, pricing, upgrades, limitations, version history, and examples.
  • Templates should include ideal client, poor-fit client, included components, exclusions, required inputs, QA, support, pricing, and upgrade paths.
  • Support issues should feed back into component improvement.
  • Custom work is acceptable only if it is priced, documented, and supportable.
  • The first templates to document deeply are:
    • Live Status Starter System
    • Quote Request Starter System
    • Booking & Review Starter System

Section 18

Marketing and Lead Generation System

18.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Marketing & Sales Pipeline Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains how Shawcliffe Digital should attract leads, create interest, follow up, and turn conversations into paid projects.

The goal is not to become a flashy marketing agency pretending to be bigger than it is.

The goal is to become known as a practical local husband-and-wife digital agency that helps owner-operated businesses get more organized, get more leads, save time, and communicate better with customers.

The internal rule:

Marketing should make it easy for the right local business owner to understand what Shawcliffe does and why it matters.

18.2 Shawcliffe’s Core Positioning

Shawcliffe Digital should not position itself as just another “web design agency.”

That sounds generic.

Shawcliffe should position itself as a builder of practical business systems for local owner-operators.

Plain-English Positioning

Shawcliffe Digital helps local owner-operated businesses build simple websites, apps, forms, dashboards, and customer systems that turn interest into organized leads, bookings, quote requests, reviews, and repeat business.

Shorter Positioning

We build simple digital systems for local businesses so customers can book, request quotes, check availability, leave reviews, and take action without everything getting lost in texts and DMs.

Even Shorter Positioning

We help local businesses turn customer interest into organized action.

What Shawcliffe Is

Shawcliffe IsMeaning
PracticalFocused on useful systems, not vanity tech
Local-business focusedBuilt for owner-operators, not giant companies
Systems-mindedWebsites, forms, dashboards, notifications, reviews, follow-up
LeanHusband-and-wife team with low overhead
HonestClear scope, no fake guarantees
ReusableUses components/templates to build efficiently
Long-termSupports clients after launch when needed

What Shawcliffe Is Not

Shawcliffe Is NotWhy
Just a website shopThe goal is business workflow, not just pages
A fake “guaranteed leads” agencyLead guarantees are risky and often dishonest
A bloated corporate firmOwner-operators need practical help
A cheap unlimited labor serviceSupport and changes must be priced
A social media posting factoryThat may be a future service, but not the core
A full enterprise software companyStart with simple systems
A magic marketing solutionSystems help, but owners still must respond and operate well

18.3 One-Sentence Pitch Options

Curtis should memorize several versions.

Different situations require different levels of detail.

General One-Sentence Pitch

Shawcliffe Digital helps local owner-operated businesses build simple websites and customer systems so people can book, request quotes, check availability, leave reviews, and contact them without everything getting buried in texts, DMs, and missed calls.

Casual Pitch

We help small local businesses get their customer requests organized — things like quote forms, booking requests, review links, live availability updates, and simple owner dashboards.

Very Short Pitch

We build practical websites and customer systems for local businesses.

More Personal Pitch

My wife and I run Shawcliffe Digital. She handles the technical build, and I work with local business owners to figure out what system would actually save them time or help them get more organized.

Sales Conversation Pitch

A lot of small businesses do not need a giant app. They need a clearer customer path. We build simple systems so customers can take the next step — request a quote, book, check availability, submit photos, leave a review, or get updates — without the owner chasing everything manually.

18.4 Core Marketing Message

Shawcliffe’s main marketing message should be:

Your customers are already interested. We help make it easier for them to take the next step.

This works because many owner-operators already have some demand.

Their problem is often not total invisibility.

Their problem is:

  • Missed calls
  • Scattered texts
  • Unanswered DMs
  • Repeated questions
  • No quote details
  • No review process
  • No booking structure
  • No customer list
  • No follow-up
  • No live availability
  • No simple owner dashboard

Marketing Message Variations

ProblemMessage
Missed leadsStop losing customer requests in scattered messages
Quote chaosGet better quote requests with photos and details upfront
Booking chaosLet customers request appointments without endless back-and-forth
Sold-out confusionLet customers check what is available before they come
Review weaknessMake it easier for happy customers to leave reviews
Repeated questionsPut common answers in one clear place
Owner overwhelmGive the owner a simple dashboard instead of manual posting
Follow-up problemsTrack leads and customers before they disappear

18.5 Primary Offers to Market First

Shawcliffe should not market all 12 archetype offers equally at the beginning.

Start with the first three.

1Live Status Starter SystemFruit stands, roadside sellers, food trucks, pop-up vendorsDistinctive, demo-friendly, tied to existing prototype

If Shawcliffe tries to market everything at once, the message becomes muddy.

Than:

Small business tip: If customers ask for quotes by text, make sure you collect at least service type, location, urgency, photos, and contact info. A lot of back-and-forth happens because the first message is missing basic details.

If you sell from a stand, market, truck, or pop-up, a simple QR code that shows “open/closed, today’s products, location, and sold-out status” can save customers from guessing before they come.

If you run an appointment business, make sure customers can quickly see services, prices or starting prices, booking instructions, and a review link. A lot of bookings get lost when everything depends on DMs.

18.37 How to Explain “Business Systems”

Some business owners will not understand “business systems.”

Use plain examples.

Explanation

A business system is a simple digital setup that helps customers take action and helps the owner manage what comes in.

Examples:

  • A contractor gets quote requests with photos instead of vague texts.
  • A barber gets appointment requests and review links in one place.
  • A fruit stand lets customers check if they are open and what is available today.
  • A cleaner collects property details before quoting.
  • A baker collects custom order requests with pickup dates.
  • A pet groomer collects pet information before booking.

Simple Analogy

A website is like a sign. A business system is like a sign plus a front desk, intake form, notebook, reminder, and follow-up process.

18.38 Objection Handling in Marketing

“I already have Facebook.”

Facebook is useful, but posts get buried and customers may not find the exact information they need. A simple system gives customers one stable place to take action.

“I already get enough work.”

That is great. In that case, the goal may not be more leads. It may be better leads, fewer repeated questions, easier reviews, or less admin.

“I do not need an app.”

You may not. Most businesses do not need a full app first. A simple website, form, dashboard, or QR-linked system may solve the problem more cheaply and faster.

“I do not have time for this.”

That is exactly why the first version should be simple. We collect the key information, build the system, and keep the customer path focused.

“That sounds expensive.”

It depends on scope. We can start with the essential system first and add dashboard, SMS, CRM, payments, or automation later if they are worth it.

“Will this guarantee more customers?”

No honest agency should guarantee that. What we can do is make it easier for interested customers to take action and easier for you to manage those requests.

18.44 Common Marketing Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Marketing “Websites” Too Generically

Lots of people build websites.

Shawcliffe should market practical business systems.

Mistake 2: Trying to Sell All 12 Archetypes at Once

Focus first on Live Status, Quote Request, and Booking & Review.

Mistake 3: Talking Too Technically

Owner-operators care about leads, bookings, quotes, reviews, time, and customer confusion.

Mistake 4: Not Showing Demos

A demo is more powerful than a long explanation.

Mistake 5: Not Following Up

Many deals happen after follow-up.

Mistake 6: Chasing Bad Fits

Not every business is worth pursuing.

Mistake 7: Forgetting Referrals

Referrals may be the strongest early channel.

Mistake 8: Overpromising Results

Do not guarantee leads, rankings, revenue, or reviews.

Mistake 9: Hiding Price Too Much

Starting ranges help filter bad-fit clients.

Mistake 10: Waiting Until Everything Is Perfect

The best early learning comes from real conversations.

Section 19

Sales Scripts, Conversations, and Objection Handling

19.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Sales Conversation Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section gives Curtis practical scripts and conversation frameworks for selling Shawcliffe Digital’s services honestly and confidently.

The goal is not to become pushy, fake, or manipulative.

The goal is to help local business owners understand:

  • What Shawcliffe Digital does
  • Why it matters
  • What problem Shawcliffe can solve
  • Whether their business is a good fit
  • What kind of system makes sense
  • What it may cost
  • What happens next

The internal rule:

Sales is not convincing someone to buy something they do not need. Sales is helping the right person understand the value of solving a real problem.

19.2 Shawcliffe Sales Philosophy

Shawcliffe should sell like a trusted local advisor, not a high-pressure agency.

Curtis should sound:

  • Practical
  • Honest
  • Curious
  • Local
  • Clear
  • Calm
  • Helpful
  • Not desperate
  • Not corporate
  • Not overly technical

The sales style should be:

“Let’s understand what is actually happening in your business and see if a simple system would help.”

Not:

“You need our revolutionary digital transformation solution.”

What Shawcliffe Should Avoid

AvoidWhy
Fake urgencyDamages trust
Guaranteed lead promisesRisky and often dishonest
Overly technical languageConfuses owner-operators
Criticizing their current setup harshlyMakes people defensive
Acting bigger than you areInauthentic
Underpricing out of fearCreates resentment
Saying yes to everythingCauses scope creep
Pretending every business is a fitWastes time
Talking too much before asking questionsMisses the real problem

What Shawcliffe Should Do Instead

DoWhy
Ask about their customer flowReveals real problems
Use plain examplesMakes systems understandable
Offer starter versionsReduces overwhelm
Name what is included/excludedBuilds trust
Explain monthly support earlyAvoids surprise
Be honest about limitationsPrevents bad-fit expectations
Focus on value, not featuresHelps client understand price
Follow up respectfullyMany owners are busy
Let bad fits walk awayProtects the business

19.3 Core Sales Message

The basic Shawcliffe message:

We help local owner-operated businesses turn customer interest into organized action.

That means:

  • Customers can request a quote
  • Customers can book or request appointments
  • Customers can check availability
  • Customers can submit photos/details
  • Customers can leave reviews
  • Customers can join a list
  • Owners can receive organized information
  • Owners can update simple dashboards
  • Owners can stop relying only on scattered messages

19.4 Elevator Pitches

Curtis should memorize several versions.

Different situations need different lengths.

5-Second Pitch

We build practical websites and customer systems for local businesses.

10-Second Pitch

Shawcliffe Digital helps local businesses set up simple systems for quote requests, booking requests, reviews, live availability updates, and customer follow-up.

20-Second Pitch

My wife and I run Shawcliffe Digital. We help local owner-operated businesses build practical websites and customer systems, so customers can request quotes, book appointments, check availability, leave reviews, or contact them without everything getting lost in texts, DMs, and missed calls.

30-Second Pitch

Shawcliffe Digital is a husband-and-wife digital agency. My wife handles the technical build, and I work with local business owners to figure out what kind of system would actually save them time or help them get more organized. We build things like quote request forms, booking request systems, live status pages, owner dashboards, review request systems, and simple websites that help customers take action.

More Personal Pitch

We’re a small husband-and-wife team. Cassandra is the developer, and I handle the client side. Our focus is helping local owner-operated businesses with practical digital systems — not bloated tech, not fake marketing promises, just useful tools that help customers book, request quotes, check availability, leave reviews, and communicate better.

19.5 Casual Explanations

These are useful when someone asks:

“So what do you actually do?”

Casual Explanation 1

We help small businesses organize how customers contact them. A lot of businesses have leads coming in through texts, calls, DMs, Facebook, Instagram, and random messages. We build simple systems so customers can send the right information in one place.

Casual Explanation 2

It is like web design, but more practical. Instead of just making a nice-looking site, we ask what customers need to do. Do they need to request a quote? Book? Check if something is available? Upload photos? Leave a review? Then we build the system around that.

Casual Explanation 3

A lot of small businesses do not need a giant app. They need a clearer customer path. We build that path.

Casual Explanation 4

We build websites, forms, dashboards, and customer systems for local businesses. The goal is to reduce chaos: fewer missed messages, fewer repeated questions, better quote requests, easier bookings, and more reviews.

19.6 How to Explain “Business Systems”

Some clients understand “website.”
Fewer understand “business system.”

Use examples.

Simple Explanation

A business system is a website or app setup that helps customers do something and helps the owner manage what comes in.

Example Explanation

For a contractor, that might mean a quote request form where customers send job details and photos.

For a barber, it might mean a booking request and review system.

For a fruit stand, it might mean a live page showing whether they are open, where they are, and what is sold out.

For a cleaner, it might mean a form that collects property details and recurring service needs.

Analogy

A regular website is like a sign. A business system is like a sign plus a front desk, intake form, notebook, reminder, and follow-up process.

Very Plain Version

We build the thing that helps your customer take the next step.

19.7 In-Person Conversation Starters

Curtis should not open by pitching.

Open by asking about the business.

General Business Owner Starter

How do customers usually find you right now?

Customer Flow Starter

When someone wants to book or ask about your service, what do they usually do? Call, text, DM, email?

Pain Starter

Does that work pretty well, or do things ever get missed?

Repeated Question Starter

What questions do customers ask you over and over?

Quote-Based Business Starter

When someone asks for a quote, do they usually send enough information, or do you have to chase them for details?

Appointment Business Starter

Do most bookings come through a booking system, or are they still mostly texts and DMs?

Seasonal Seller Starter

Do customers ever message asking if you are open or what you have available that day?

Review Starter

Do you have a regular way of asking happy customers for reviews?

Soft Transition to Shawcliffe

That is the kind of thing we help with. We build simple systems so customers can send the right information or take the next step without everything being scattered.

19.8 Natural Sales Conversation Flow

Use this flow in casual conversations, networking, and discovery.

Step 1: Ask About Their Business

What kind of work do you mostly do?

Step 2: Ask How Customers Contact Them

When someone wants to hire you or buy from you, how does that usually happen?

Step 3: Ask What Gets Messy

Where does that process get annoying or time-consuming?

Step 4: Identify the Customer Action

So ideally, would you want customers to request a quote, book, check availability, order, or just send better information?

Step 5: Connect to a System

That sounds like something a simple [quote request / booking / live status] system could help with.

Step 6: Give a Plain Example

For example, instead of someone texting “how much?” they fill out a form with job type, location, urgency, and photos. Then you get everything in one organized message.

Step 7: Ask Permission

Would it be useful if I sent you an example?

Step 8: Next Step

If it looks helpful, we can do a short discovery call and I can recommend a simple first version.

19.9 Cold Call Script

Cold calls should be short and respectful.

The goal is not to close on the call.

The goal is to start a conversation or get permission to send an example.

General Cold Call Script

Hi, is this [Name]?

Hi [Name], my name is Curtis from Shawcliffe Digital. My wife and I run a small digital agency helping local owner-operated businesses set up practical websites and customer systems.

I’ll be brief. We build things like quote request forms, booking request systems, live availability pages, review request systems, and simple owner dashboards.

I noticed [specific observation about their business], and I thought there may be a simple way to help customers [request quotes / book / check availability / send better details].

Is that something you handle pretty smoothly already, or is it sometimes a bit scattered?

If They Engage

That makes sense. For businesses like yours, we often start with a simple [system name]. It helps customers [specific action] and gives you the information in a more organized way.

Would it be okay if I sent you a quick example by text or email?

If They Are Busy

If They Say Not Interested

No worries. I appreciate your time. If customer requests, quotes, bookings, or reviews ever become something you want to organize better, feel free to reach out.

If They Ask Price Immediately

It depends on the scope. Simple starter systems usually begin in the low thousands, and more involved systems with dashboards, SMS, payments, or CRM cost more. I would not want to quote properly without understanding what you actually need.
