19.13 Discovery Call Script

The discovery call should not be a sales monologue.

It should uncover:

  • Business type
  • Customer flow
  • Current mess
  • Missed money
  • Useful system
  • Budget/timeline fit
  • Client fit

Discovery Call Opening

Thanks for taking the time to talk.

The goal of this call is not for me to pressure you into anything. I want to understand how customers currently find you, contact you, book, request quotes, or buy from you. Then I can tell you honestly whether a simple system would help, what kind of first version would make sense, and whether Shawcliffe is a good fit.

Discovery Question Section 1: Business Basics

  • Can you give me the quick version of what your business does?
  • Who are your typical customers?
  • What services or products do you most want more of?
  • Are there any jobs or requests you do not want more of?
  • What area do you serve?
  • Is this seasonal or year-round?

Discovery Question Section 2: Customer Flow

  • How do customers usually find you?
  • What do they usually do next?
  • Do they call, text, email, DM, use a website, or walk in?
  • Where do most inquiries come from?
  • What happens after someone reaches out?
  • Do you have a system for tracking leads or requests?

Discovery Question Section 3: The Mess

  • What part of that process gets annoying?
  • Do customers ask the same questions repeatedly?
  • Do people send incomplete information?
  • Do you ever forget to follow up?
  • Do inquiries get buried?
  • Do you miss calls or messages while working?
  • Do customers ever get confused about what to do?

Discovery Question Section 4: Missed Money

  • What is a good customer, booking, order, or job worth to you?
  • How often do you think leads slip through the cracks?
  • Do you ask for reviews consistently?
  • Do repeat customers matter in your business?
  • Would one or two extra good customers per month matter?
  • Would better-qualified inquiries save you time?

Discovery Question Section 5: Current Tools

  • Do you have a website?
  • Do you use Facebook or Instagram?
  • Do you have a Google Business Profile?
  • Do you have online booking?
  • Do you have a review link?
  • Do you use any forms, spreadsheets, CRM, or booking software?
  • What is working okay right now?

Discovery Question Section 6: Ideal Outcome

  • What would you like customers to be able to do more easily?
  • What would make your life easier?
  • What would save time?
  • What would help you look more professional?
  • What would help customers come prepared?
  • What would make this worth paying for?

Discovery Question Section 7: Budget and Timing

  • Are you looking to do something soon, or just exploring?
  • Do you have a rough budget in mind?
  • Would you rather start simple and upgrade later, or build a more complete system upfront?
  • Would monthly support be helpful after launch?
  • Is there a date this needs to be ready by?

Discovery Call Closing

Based on what you’ve told me, I think the most practical first version would be [system name].

That would focus on [main customer action] and include [core components].

I would not start with [unnecessary bigger feature] unless we decide it is worth it later.

The next step would be for me to put together a simple proposal showing:

  • What problem we are solving
  • What system we recommend
  • What is included
  • What is not included
  • Starting price
  • Monthly support option
  • Next steps

Does that sound reasonable?

19.14 Explaining the First Three Offers

Curtis should explain each offer in plain business language.

A. Live Status Starter System

Simple Explanation

This is for businesses where customers need current information before they come. It lets customers check whether you are open, where you are, what you have today, prices, and whether anything is sold out.

Problem Explanation

If customers have to guess whether you are open or stocked, some will not bother coming. If they come and you are closed or sold out, they may be frustrated. This system gives them one simple place to check.

Owner Benefit

You can update the important information from your phone instead of posting manually everywhere or answering the same questions repeatedly.

Customer Benefit

Customers can scan a QR code or open a link and know whether it is worth coming today.

Example

For a fruit stand, it could show open, closed, closing soon, corn available, peaches sold out, today’s prices, and the current location.

B. Quote Request Starter System

Simple Explanation

This is for businesses that quote jobs. Customers send the job type, location, urgency, description, and photos through one organized form.

Problem Explanation

A lot of quote requests start with “how much?” but you cannot answer properly without basic details. This system collects the details upfront.

Owner Benefit

You spend less time chasing information and can decide faster whether the job is worth quoting.

Customer Benefit

Customers know what to send and feel like they took the right first step.

Example

For a welder or contractor, the form could ask what they need done, where the job is, how urgent it is, and let them upload photos.

C. Booking & Review Starter System

Simple Explanation

This is for appointment businesses. Customers can see services, prices or starting prices, request an appointment, and leave a review.

Problem Explanation

Appointment requests often get buried in DMs, texts, calls, and comments. Reviews also get forgotten unless there is a simple process.

Owner Benefit

You get booking requests in a more organized way and make it easier to ask happy clients for reviews.

Customer Benefit

Customers know what you offer, how to request an appointment, and how to review you afterward.

Example

For a barber, the page could show services, prices, booking request form, and a Google review QR code.

19.15 Handling “I Just Need a Website”

This is one of the most important objections.

Many clients will say:

“I just need a website.”

Do not argue.

Use it as a doorway.

Response 1: Agree and Reframe

Absolutely, we can start with a website. The main question is: what should the website help customers do?

Response 2: Explain the Difference

A website can be just information, or it can help the customer take action. For example, request a quote, book, check availability, upload photos, leave a review, or join a customer list.

Response 3: Keep It Simple

We do not need to overcomplicate it. We can build a simple first version that looks professional and gives customers one clear next step.

Response 4: Discovery Question

When someone lands on your website, what do you most want them to do?

Response 5: Sales Bridge

If the answer is “contact me,” we should make that contact useful. Instead of a vague contact form, we can ask the right questions so you get better inquiries.

19.16 Handling Price Objections

Price objections are normal.

Do not panic.

Do not immediately discount.

First, clarify whether it is:

  • Too expensive for them
  • More than expected
  • Unclear value
  • Too much scope
  • Bad timing
  • Lack of trust
  • No budget

Objection: “That Sounds Expensive”

Response

I understand. It is more than just a page on the internet. The price reflects the system: the customer flow, forms, notifications, dashboard if included, testing, launch, and support setup.

That said, we can adjust scope. The best way to reduce price is to start with the essentials and save add-ons for later.

Objection: “Can You Do It Cheaper?”

Response

Possibly, but I would rather reduce the scope than quietly cut corners. We can look at what is essential for the first version and what can wait.

Objection: “I Was Thinking More Like $500”

Response

That budget is more in the range of a very simple landing page or DIY setup. A proper business system with forms, notifications, testing, and support is more involved.

If $500 is the budget, I would recommend starting with the simplest possible online presence and waiting on the larger system until it makes sense.

Objection: “Another Company Can Do a Website Cheaper”

Response

They probably can. If you only need a basic website, that may be fine. What we focus on is the customer system behind it — quote requests, booking requests, dashboard updates, review flows, notifications, and follow-up.

It depends whether you want a basic site or a system that helps organize customer action.

Objection: “Can You Match Their Price?”

Response

I do not want to match a price without knowing whether we are offering the same thing. If their scope is simpler, we can reduce our scope too. But I would rather be clear than pretend two very different projects are the same.

Objection: “I Don’t Have the Budget Right Now”

Response

That is completely fair. We can either start with a smaller first version, or I can give you a future roadmap so you know what to build toward when the timing is better.

Internal Rule

Reduce scope before reducing price.

19.17 Handling “I Already Have Facebook”

Many small businesses rely on Facebook or Instagram.

Do not insult it.

Response

Facebook is useful. I would not tell you to stop using it. The issue is that posts get buried, and customers may not find the exact information they need when they need it.

Continue

A simple system gives customers one stable place to take action. Facebook can still send people there.

Example

For a fruit stand, Facebook is great for posting updates, but a QR code or live status page lets customers instantly check open/closed, products, prices, and sold-out status without scrolling.

For Appointment Businesses

Instagram is great for showing your work. But if booking requests are buried in DMs, a simple booking request page can make the next step clearer.

For Contractors

Facebook recommendations are great, but once someone is interested, they still need a clear way to send job details and photos.

19.18 Handling “I Can Do It Myself”

Some clients can do parts themselves.

Respect that.

Response

You might be able to. There are good DIY tools out there. The question is whether you want to spend the time figuring it out, setting it up, testing it, and maintaining it.

Continue

What we bring is not just the tool. It is the structure: what customers should do, what information you need, what gets sent where, what happens after submission, and how it fits your business.

If They Are Handy

If you enjoy doing that kind of thing and have time, DIY may be a good option. If you want it done properly and want a clear system, that is where we can help.

If They Say Wix/Squarespace

Those tools can be useful. A lot of the value is not the platform, though. It is the customer flow: quote questions, booking request, review link, notifications, dashboard, and follow-up.

19.19 Handling “I Need to Think About It”

This is normal.

Do not pressure.

Clarify what they need to think about.

Response

Of course. Is there anything specific you are unsure about — the price, the scope, whether you need it, or timing?

If Price

That makes sense. We can look at a smaller first version if that helps.

If Timing

No problem. I can leave you with the recommendation and we can revisit when the timing is better.

If Value

The main question is whether the system would save you time, reduce missed opportunities, or make the customer path clearer. If it does not do that, it is probably not worth building yet.

Follow-Up Permission

Would it be alright if I followed up once next week?

19.20 Handling “Will This Get Me More Customers?”

Be very careful.

Do not guarantee customers.

Response

I cannot honestly guarantee more customers. No agency should promise that.

What this can do is make it easier for interested customers to take the next step and make it easier for you to manage those requests.

Continue

If people are already finding you but getting lost in texts, DMs, vague quote requests, unclear booking, or no review process, this can help.

If nobody knows your business exists yet, then we may also need marketing, local SEO, referrals, or ads.

Practical Version

The system does not magically create demand. It helps capture and organize the demand you already have, and it gives future marketing somewhere useful to send people.

19.21 Handling “I Don’t Need More Leads”

This may be true.

Shift the conversation.

Response

That is a good problem to have. In that case, the goal may not be more leads. It may be better leads, fewer repeated questions, easier scheduling, more reviews, or less admin.

Follow-Up Question

Is there any part of customer communication that still wastes your time?

Possible Direction

  • Better qualified inquiries
  • Review process
  • Customer list
  • Fewer repeated questions
  • Seasonal updates
  • Dashboard control
  • Customer prep information
  • Filtering bad-fit customers

19.22 Handling “My Friend/Relative Can Build a Website”

Do not attack the friend.

Response

That may be a good option, especially if you only need a basic site. The important thing is making sure the site has a clear customer action and is easy for you to maintain.

Continue

What we focus on is the business system: what customers should do, what information you need, how requests are organized, how reviews happen, and what support looks like after launch.

If Appropriate

If your friend builds the site, we could still potentially help later with forms, quote requests, review systems, QR code flows, or dashboards.

19.23 Handling “I Already Have a Website”

Do not assume their website is bad.

Response

Great. Then the question is whether the current website is doing what you need it to do.

Follow-Up Questions

  • Are customers using it?
  • Are you getting inquiries from it?
  • Are the inquiries useful?
  • Can customers take the right action?
  • Does it save you time?
  • Does it connect to reviews, booking, quote requests, or follow-up?

Sales Bridge

If the website already looks fine, we may not need to replace it. We might just add a better customer action, like a quote form, booking request, review page, or QR-linked landing page.

19.24 Handling “I Already Use Booking Software”

This may be good.

Do not replace tools unnecessarily.

Response

That may already solve the booking part. The question is whether customers can find it easily and whether the rest of the customer flow is clear.

Follow-Up

Do people actually use the booking link, or do they still DM/text you?

Possible Direction

  • Better landing page
  • Review request flow
  • Service explanation
  • Google Business Profile support
  • QR code to booking
  • Rebooking campaigns
  • Customer list
  • Website cleanup

19.25 Handling “I Don’t Want Monthly Support”

Respect it, but set boundaries.

Response

That is okay. Monthly support is not mandatory for every project. It just means future updates, troubleshooting, changes, or support would be quoted separately as needed.

For Active Systems

For systems with dashboards, notifications, SMS, inventory, booking, or quote forms, I do recommend support because those are active parts of your business. If something breaks or changes, you want a clear support path.

Simple Option

We can start with a basic maintenance plan instead of a larger care plan if you just want light support.

19.26 Handling “Can We Start Small?”

This is usually good.

Response

Yes. That is often the best way. We can build the essential first version, then add CRM, SMS, payments, dashboards, automation, or marketing later if they prove worth it.

Continue

The important thing is choosing the right first version — the one that solves the main problem without overbuilding.

19.27 Handling “Can You Build an App?”

Many clients say “app” when they mean “system.”

Response

Possibly, but I would first ask whether you truly need an app or whether a mobile-friendly web system would solve the problem.

Explain

A lot of businesses do not need customers to download an app. They need customers to scan a QR code, open a link, request a quote, book, check availability, or leave a review.

Continue

We can always discuss an app later, but the first question is: what should the customer be able to do?

19.28 Handling “Can You Do AI?”

Do not overpromise.

Response

AI can be useful in some cases, but I would not start there unless the basic customer flow is clear. First we need to know what information customers need, where it goes, and what the business owner does with it.

Continue

Once the basic system is working, AI might help with message drafting, routing, FAQs, follow-up, or receptionist-style workflows. But I would treat that as a later upgrade unless there is a strong reason to start there.

19.29 Handling “Can You Guarantee Results?”

Be honest.

Response

No, and I would be cautious of anyone who guarantees leads or revenue. What we can do is build a clearer customer path and measure whether more people are taking action.

Continue

The system can help capture interest, reduce confusion, improve follow-up, and make review requests easier. But the business still needs demand, good service, and follow-through.

19.30 Closing Without Being Pushy

Closing should feel like a natural next step.

Do not pressure.

Ask for a clear decision or next step.

Soft Close After Discovery

Based on what you told me, I think a [system name] would be the most practical first step. Would you like me to put together a proposal?

Fit-Based Close

I think this is a good fit if your priority is [main problem]. If that is not the priority right now, we can wait.

Scope Close

We can keep the first version focused: [included components]. Then if it works well, we can add [future upgrades] later. Would you like me to price that first version?

Proposal Close

The proposal would show what is included, what is not included, timeline, price, and monthly support option. Should I prepare that for you?

Next-Step Close

The next step would be a short discovery form so I can confirm the details and avoid guessing. Would you like me to send that?

Budget Close

If the budget is around [range], I can shape the scope around a realistic first version. If that range is too high right now, I would rather say that honestly before we waste time.

19.31 Closing Phrases to Avoid

Avoid:

  • “So, are you ready to buy today?”
  • “This price is only good now.”
  • “You’ll definitely make the money back.”
  • “Everyone needs this.”
  • “Your current setup is terrible.”
  • “Trust me, this will work.”
  • “It is cheap.”
  • “It is easy.”
  • “We can do anything.”

These create pressure or unrealistic expectations.

19.32 Ethical Follow-Up

Follow-up is part of sales.

Harassment is not.

Follow-Up Rule

Follow up clearly, then move on.

Ethical Follow-Up Sequence

  • Send proposal or demo.
  • Follow up after a few days.
  • Follow up one more time.
  • Leave the door open.
  • Move to nurture or closed-lost.

Proposal Follow-Up 1

Hi [Name], just checking whether you had a chance to review the proposal.

The main thing to consider is whether the first version solves the main problem we discussed: [problem].

Happy to answer questions.

Proposal Follow-Up 2

Hi [Name], I do not want to keep chasing you, so I’ll leave this here.

If the timing is not right, no worries. If you want a smaller first version or want to revisit later, just let me know.

Thanks,
Curtis

19.33 Sales Red Flags

Curtis should watch for bad-fit signals.

Client Red Flags

Red FlagWhy It Matters
“This should be easy”They may undervalue work
“I need it tomorrow”Rush/scope risk
“I have no budget, but…”Likely not ready
“Can you guarantee leads?”Unrealistic expectation
“My last developer was terrible”Could be true, but investigate
Refuses to define services/pricesBuild blocker
Wants unlimited revisionsScope risk
Wants everything but cheapBad economics
Disrespectful communicationBad relationship
Wants misleading claimsEthical risk
Avoids payment termsFinancial risk
Changes idea constantlyProject risk
Wants complex app immediatelyOverbuild risk

Red Flag Response

I want to be honest. I am not sure this is the right fit for Shawcliffe as currently described. We work best when the first version is clear, practical, and focused. If we can narrow the scope, there may be a fit. If not, another provider may be better.

19.34 When to Walk Away

Walking away is sometimes the right sales decision.

Walk Away If

  • Client is rude
  • Client wants dishonest marketing
  • Client demands guarantees
  • Client refuses clear scope
  • Client refuses payment terms
  • Client wants high complexity at low price
  • Client will not provide content
  • Client expects unlimited support
  • Client ignores boundaries
  • Client is outside Shawcliffe’s ability to support

Walk-Away Script

Thanks for the conversation. After thinking it through, I do not think Shawcliffe Digital is the right fit for this project as currently described.

We focus on practical websites, customer systems, quote request systems, booking request systems, live status pages, and simple owner dashboards for local businesses.

I would rather be honest now than take on something that is not a good fit.

19.35 Sales Scripts by Offer

A. Live Status Starter System Sales Script

Opening

I noticed your business depends on customers knowing current information — whether you are open, where you are, what you have today, and whether anything is sold out.

Problem

That can be hard to manage through Facebook posts, texts, signs, and repeated messages.

Offer

We build a Live Status Starter System. Customers can scan a QR code or open a link to check your current status, products, prices, and location.

Owner Benefit

You can update agreed fields from your phone.

Close

Would it be useful if I showed you a quick example?

B. Quote Request Starter System Sales Script

Opening

For quote-based businesses, one of the biggest time-wasters is customers reaching out without the details you need.

Problem

They ask “how much?” but do not send photos, location, measurements, urgency, or enough context.

Offer

We build a Quote Request Starter System so customers send the right details through one organized form.

Owner Benefit

You get better information upfront and can decide faster whether the job is worth quoting.

Close

Would it be useful if I showed you a quick example?

C. Booking & Review Starter System Sales Script

Opening

For appointment businesses, bookings and reviews often happen in scattered places — texts, DMs, calls, comments, and social media.

Problem

That can lead to missed appointments, repeated questions, and forgotten reviews.

Offer

We build a Booking & Review Starter System so customers can see services, request an appointment, and leave a review through a simple customer path.

Owner Benefit

You get more organized requests and a simple way to build reviews.

Close

Would it be useful if I showed you a quick example?

19.36 Sales Call Structure

Use this for a more formal sales call.

30-Minute Sales Call Agenda

TimeSection
0–3 minFriendly opening
3–8 minBusiness overview
8–15 minCustomer flow and problems
15–20 minCurrent tools and missed opportunities
20–25 minRecommend possible system
25–28 minBudget/timeline/support
28–30 minNext step

Opening

Thanks again for taking the time. I will ask a few questions about your business and how customers currently contact you. Then I can recommend whether a system makes sense and what kind of first version would be practical.

Recommendation

Based on what you told me, I would not start with a huge custom app. I would start with [system name], focused on [main customer action]. That gives you the core benefit first, and we can add [upgrades] later if it makes sense.

Next Step

The next step would be a proposal with the exact scope, price, timeline, and support option. Would you like me to put that together?

19.37 Discovery-to-Recommendation Phrases

Use these to connect what the client said to the offer.

For Scattered Messages

Since customer requests are coming from several places, the main opportunity is to give people one clearer path.

For Missing Details

Since customers often leave out important information, the system should ask for those details upfront.

For Repeated Questions

Since you answer the same questions repeatedly, those answers should be built into the page, form, or confirmation message.

For Missed Reviews

Since happy customers are not being asked consistently, review requests should become part of the customer flow.

For Seasonal Updates

Since your availability changes often, customers need a simple way to check current status.

For Follow-Up Problems

Since follow-up is hard to track manually, CRM Lite may be a good Phase 2 upgrade after the starter system is working.

19.38 Explaining Scope During Sales

Scope should be introduced early.

Scope Explanation

The proposal will be very clear about what is included and what is not included. That protects both of us. If you want to add things later, we can quote them as add-ons or Phase 2.

Starter Scope Explanation

The starter version should solve the main problem first. We do not need to add every possible feature right away.

Add-On Explanation

Things like SMS, payments, CRM, automation, and advanced dashboards are valuable, but they add build and support time, so I would treat them as add-ons rather than quietly including them.

19.39 Explaining Monthly Support During Sales

Do not wait until after launch to mention support.

General Support Explanation

After launch, the system may need updates, form checks, notification checks, dashboard help, review support, or improvements. That is what the monthly support plan is for.

No Monthly Option

If you do not want monthly support, that is okay. Future requests would just be quoted as needed.

Active System Support

For active systems with forms, dashboards, notifications, inventory, or SMS, I usually recommend support because those are important customer-facing workflows.

Support Value

The support plan is not just “paying for nothing.” It gives you a clear support path and helps keep the system useful after launch.

19.40 Explaining Timeline

Avoid overpromising.

Timeline Language

Timeline depends on scope and how quickly we receive the required content, access, and approvals.

If Client Wants Rush

We may be able to move faster by reducing scope, but I do not want to promise a rushed launch and cut corners.

If Client Delays Content

The build timeline depends on receiving your services, prices, policies, photos, and access. Missing content can pause the project or move features to a later phase.

19.41 Explaining Fast Build Speed

Because Cassandra can build quickly, clients may think it should be cheap.

Response

Speed comes from having good systems, reusable components, and experience. The value is not just the hours spent. It is knowing what to build, how to structure it, how to test it, and how to make it useful for the business.

Simpler Version

Fast does not mean low value. It means we have a repeatable process.

Analogy

A mechanic may fix something quickly because they know exactly what they are doing. You are paying for the result and expertise, not just the minutes.

19.42 Closing Scripts

Close for Proposal

I think there is enough here to put together a practical proposal. It would show the recommended system, included components, what is not included, pricing, timeline, and support option. Would you like me to prepare that?

Close for Smaller Starter Version

If the full version feels like too much, we can start with the essential version first. That would focus on [main action] and leave [upgrades] for later.

Close for Discovery Form

To avoid guessing, I’ll send a short discovery form. Once I have that, I can recommend the cleanest first version.

Close for Demo

I can send you a quick example so you can see what I mean. If it looks useful, we can talk about whether it fits your business.

Close for Not Now

No problem. I’ll leave the idea with you. If the timing is better later, or if customer requests start getting messy, feel free to reach out.

19.43 Post-Call Follow-Up Template

Send after a discovery or sales call.

Follow-Up After Discovery

Hi [Name],

Thanks for taking the time to talk today.

Here is what I heard:

  • Your business: [summary]
  • Current customer flow: [summary]
  • Main issue: [problem]
  • Best first system: [system name]
  • Main goal: [customer action]
  • Possible future upgrades: [upgrades]

I think the practical first version would be [recommendation].

The next step would be a proposal showing scope, price, timeline, what is included, what is not included, and monthly support options.

Thanks,
Curtis

19.44 Proposal Send Script

Proposal Email

Hi [Name],

Thanks again for the conversation.

I put together a proposal for a [system name] based on what we discussed.

The proposal includes:

  • The main problem we are solving
  • The recommended system
  • Included components
  • Items not included
  • Timeline
  • Client responsibilities
  • Project price
  • Monthly support option
  • Future upgrade path

The goal is to keep the first version practical and focused, without overbuilding.

Please take a look and let me know what questions you have.

Thanks,
Curtis

19.45 Proposal Objection Responses

“Can We Remove Monthly Support?”

Yes, if the system is simple enough. If monthly support is removed, future support and updates would be quoted as needed. For systems with forms, dashboards, notifications, inventory, or SMS, I strongly recommend keeping some support in place.

“Can We Add This Feature?”

Yes, potentially. That feature is outside the current proposal, so I can either add it as a priced add-on or save it for Phase 2.

“Can We Lower the Price?”

We can look at reducing the first version. The best way to lower price is to remove or postpone features, not quietly cut corners.

“Can We Start Next Week?”

Possibly, as long as scope, payment, and onboarding materials are ready. The main thing that delays projects is missing content, access, or approvals.

19.46 Language for Ethical Confidence

Curtis can be confident without being arrogant.

Confidence Phrases

  • “The practical first step would be…”
  • “I would not start with the complicated version.”
  • “That sounds like a Phase 2 feature.”
  • “I would treat that as an add-on.”
  • “I do not want to overbuild this.”
  • “I do not want to promise something we cannot responsibly support.”
  • “The value here is the customer path.”
  • “The goal is fewer missed opportunities and less back-and-forth.”
  • “Let’s keep the first version focused.”
  • “If this does not solve a real problem, I would not recommend building it yet.”

Trust-Building Phrases

  • “I want to be honest.”
  • “That may not be worth building yet.”
  • “You may not need a full app.”
  • “A simpler version may be enough.”
  • “I do not want to guess at your business details.”
  • “We should not add that unless it is worth the extra cost.”
  • “That is outside the current scope, but it could be a future upgrade.”
  • “I would rather be clear now than surprise you later.”

19.47 Mistakes Curtis Should Avoid in Sales Conversations

Mistake 1: Talking Too Much

Ask more questions.

Mistake 2: Leading With Technology

Do not start with:

“We build React apps with dashboards and automations.”

Start with:

“How do customers contact you right now?”

Mistake 3: Apologizing for Price

Say the price calmly.

Mistake 4: Offering Discounts Too Quickly

Reduce scope instead.

Mistake 5: Saying Yes to Every Idea

Some ideas are Phase 2.

Some are bad ideas.

Some are not worth building.

Mistake 6: Avoiding Budget

Budget matters. Ask respectfully.

Mistake 7: Skipping Next Step

Every good conversation should end with a clear next step or clear close.

Mistake 8: Continuing With Bad Fits

Bad-fit clients cost more than they pay.

Curtis can use these to practice.

19.51 Key Takeaways

  • Curtis should sell through curiosity, not pressure.
  • The best first question is often: “How do customers contact you right now?”
  • Shawcliffe sells practical customer systems, not generic websites.
  • Most objections are opportunities to clarify scope, value, timing, or fit.
  • Do not guarantee leads, revenue, rankings, or reviews.
  • Do not discount quickly. Reduce scope instead.
  • “I just need a website” should become “What should the website help customers do?”
  • Monthly support should be explained early.
  • Bad-fit clients should be politely declined.
  • Closing should feel like a helpful next step, not a trap.

Section 20

Contracts, Agreements, and Payment Terms

20.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Client Agreement Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains how Shawcliffe Digital should handle client agreements, payment terms, scope attachments, ownership, delays, cancellations, support terms, and legal boundaries.

This is not legal advice.

This is a practical internal guide to help Shawcliffe understand what should be covered in a client agreement before getting a lawyer to review and improve the final version.

The internal rule:

No serious project should begin without written agreement on scope, payment, responsibilities, ownership, support, and boundaries.

A good agreement protects:

  • Shawcliffe Digital
  • The client
  • The project timeline
  • The payment process
  • Cassandra’s development time
  • Curtis’s client relationship
  • Reusable components
  • Monthly support revenue
  • Future dispute handling

20.2 Why Agreements Matter

A written agreement prevents confusion like:

  • “I thought that was included.”
  • “I thought I paid after launch.”
  • “I thought revisions were unlimited.”
  • “I thought you would write all the content.”
  • “I thought you handled hosting forever.”
  • “I thought I owned the whole software system.”
  • “I thought monthly support included new features.”
  • “I thought you guaranteed leads.”
  • “I thought you would update this every day.”
  • “I thought you were responsible for my Google account.”

Most conflict comes from vague expectations.

A good agreement makes expectations visible.

20.3 Agreement Philosophy

Shawcliffe’s agreement should be:

  • Plain-English
  • Clear
  • Fair
  • Professional
  • Not overly scary
  • Strong enough to protect the business
  • Specific enough to avoid scope creep
  • Flexible enough for small local clients
  • Lawyer-reviewed before serious use

The tone should be:

“Here is how we work together clearly.”

Not:

“Here is a terrifying 40-page contract.”

20.4 Important Disclaimer

Every Shawcliffe agreement template should include an internal note like this:

This document is a practical starting point only and is not legal advice. Shawcliffe Digital should have its client agreement reviewed by a qualified Alberta lawyer before relying on it for paid client work, especially for larger projects, subscriptions, privacy/data handling, payment terms, liability limitations, and regulated industries.

Client-facing contracts should not include “we got this from ChatGPT.”

Internal docs can say it.

20.5 Core Agreement Structure

Every client agreement should have two main parts:

  • Master Client Agreement
  • Scope of Work Attachment

A. Master Client Agreement

This covers the general business/legal relationship.

It should include:

  • Who the parties are
  • General services
  • Payment terms
  • Client responsibilities
  • Revisions
  • Change requests
  • Cancellation
  • Late payment
  • Ownership
  • Reusable components
  • Third-party tools
  • Hosting/domain responsibilities
  • Privacy/data handling basics
  • Support terms
  • Warranty/bug-fix period
  • Portfolio/case study permission
  • Liability limitations
  • Dispute handling
  • Governing law
  • Signatures

B. Scope of Work Attachment

This covers the specific project.

It should include:

  • Project name
  • Business archetype
  • Recommended system
  • Included components
  • Excluded components
  • Pages/screens
  • Forms/workflows
  • Dashboard fields
  • Notifications
  • Timeline
  • Client homework
  • Price
  • Payment schedule
  • Monthly support plan
  • Revision rounds
  • Launch requirements
  • Add-ons
  • Future upgrades

Internal Rule

The Master Agreement explains the relationship.
The Scope of Work explains the project.

20.6 What Belongs in Every Agreement

Every Shawcliffe agreement should cover these.

Agreement SectionWhy It Matters
PartiesNames Shawcliffe and the client
ServicesExplains what Shawcliffe provides generally
Scope attachmentDefines the exact project
Payment termsPrevents payment confusion
Deposit/start paymentProtects build time
Final payment before launchPrevents unpaid launch
Monthly supportDefines recurring work
Client responsibilitiesMakes client homework clear
Content accuracyClient approves business facts
RevisionsLimits revision rounds
Change requestsHandles out-of-scope requests
DelaysDefines what happens if client stalls
CancellationDefines exit process
OwnershipClarifies client content vs reusable system assets
Third-party toolsExplains outside platforms/costs
Hosting/domainClarifies responsibility
Privacy/data basicsHandles customer/client info carefully
Warranty/bug-fix periodDefines post-launch bugs
Support boundariesPrevents unlimited support
Portfolio permissionAllows Shawcliffe to show work if approved
Liability limitsLimits excessive risk
Legal reviewInternal priority

20.7 Plain-English Agreement Opening

Sample Language

Agreement

This agreement is between:

Shawcliffe Digital
and
[Client Business Name]

This agreement explains the terms for Shawcliffe Digital to provide digital services, such as websites, forms, dashboards, customer systems, lead capture systems, booking request systems, quote request systems, review request systems, and related support.

The specific project details are described in the attached Scope of Work.

20.8 Scope of Work Attachment

The Scope of Work is the most important practical document.

It prevents vague promises.

Scope of Work Should Include

ItemExample
Project nameQuote Request Starter System
ClientABC Welding
Project goalBetter quote requests with photos/details
ArchetypeHome Service Trades
Included componentsBusiness Profile, Service Menu, Quote Form, Photo Upload
Excluded componentsSMS, CRM, payments, SEO campaign
Client responsibilitiesServices, prices, photos, review link
Timeline2–4 weeks after onboarding complete
Price$4,500
Payment schedule50% start, 50% before launch
Monthly supportStandard Care optional/required
Revisions1–2 rounds
Launch requirementsApproval, payment, QA, domain
Future upgradesCRM Lite, SMS, local SEO

Scope Attachment Language

The specific deliverables for this project are listed in the Scope of Work. Anything not listed as included is not included unless Shawcliffe Digital and the client agree in writing to add it.

Internal Rule

Never rely on “we talked about it” as scope.

If it matters, write it in the SOW.

20.9 Payment Terms

Payment terms must be clear before work begins.

Common Payment Structures

Project TypeSuggested Payment Structure
Small project100% upfront
Standard project50% upfront, 50% before launch
Larger projectDeposit + milestones + final before launch
Monthly supportPaid monthly in advance
SubscriptionSetup fee + recurring monthly
Add-onPaid before work starts or with milestone

Recommended Default

For Shawcliffe’s early projects:

50% due before work begins.
50% due before launch.

For smaller projects under a chosen threshold:

Full payment due before work begins.

Sample Payment Language

The project price is $[amount].

A payment of $[amount] is due before work begins.

The remaining balance of $[amount] is due before the project is launched, delivered, transferred, or made publicly available.

Shawcliffe Digital is not required to begin work before the initial payment is received and is not required to launch the project before final payment is received.

20.10 Deposits

Use the word deposit carefully.

Some businesses use “deposit” to mean non-refundable.

Some clients may not understand.

Better wording may be:

  • Initial payment
  • Start payment
  • Project start payment
  • First milestone payment

Recommended Language

The initial payment reserves project time and allows work to begin. Unless otherwise agreed in writing, the initial payment is non-refundable once work has started.

Why Non-Refundable After Work Starts

Because Shawcliffe may have already spent time on:

  • Planning
  • Onboarding
  • Design
  • Development
  • Client communication
  • Setup
  • Technical research
  • Component customization

Sample Initial Payment Clause

The initial payment is required before work begins. Once Shawcliffe Digital has started work, the initial payment is generally not refundable because it covers reserved time, planning, setup, communication, and work already performed.

20.11 Milestones

Larger projects may need milestones.

Example Milestone Structure

MilestonePayment
Agreement signed / project start40%
Initial build/demo ready30%
Final approval before launch30%

Milestone Language

Milestone payments are due when the related project stage is reached. Work on later stages may pause until the required milestone payment is received.

When to Use Milestones

Use milestones when:

  • Project is larger
  • Build is complex
  • Timeline is longer
  • Multiple components are involved
  • Client wants staged delivery
  • Cash flow risk is higher

20.12 Final Payment Before Launch

This should be a firm rule.

Internal Rule

Do not launch unpaid work.

Sample Language

Final payment must be received before launch, transfer, delivery of final files, domain connection, public release, or handoff of the completed project, unless otherwise agreed in writing.

Why This Matters

Once launched, leverage drops.

If a client delays payment after launch, Shawcliffe is stuck chasing money.

Client-Friendly Explanation

We collect final payment before launch so the project can close cleanly and support can begin without billing confusion.

20.13 Monthly Support Terms

Monthly support must be separated from the build.

The build creates the system.

Monthly support maintains, supports, and improves it.

Monthly Support Should Define

ItemNeed
Plan nameBasic, Standard, Growth, Premium
Monthly feeAmount
Billing dateWhen charged
Start dateUsually launch date
Included supportWhat is covered
Not includedNew features, major redesigns, etc.
Response expectationsNormal support timing
Cancellation termsHow either party ends monthly support
Late paymentWhat happens if unpaid
Third-party costsSMS, hosting, software, etc.
Support channelEmail/form/portal

Sample Monthly Support Language

Monthly support begins on [date] or at launch, whichever is agreed in the Scope of Work.

The selected support plan is [plan name] at $[amount] per month.

Monthly support may include the items listed in the Scope of Work or support plan description. New features, new pages, new workflows, major redesigns, integrations, automations, and work outside the selected support plan are quoted separately.

Monthly support fees are due in advance.

No Monthly Support Language

If the client does not select a monthly support plan, future updates, troubleshooting, training, support, or changes may be quoted separately and scheduled as paid work.

20.14 Late Payment

Late payment terms should be clear, but Shawcliffe should get legal review before applying interest/fees aggressively.

Late Payment May Cover

  • When payment is considered late
  • Whether work pauses
  • Whether launch is delayed
  • Whether support is paused
  • Whether late fees apply
  • Whether accounts/services may be suspended
  • What happens after repeated non-payment

Sample Late Payment Language

If an invoice is not paid by the due date, Shawcliffe Digital may pause work, delay launch, withhold delivery, or pause support until payment is received.

Monthly support may be paused or cancelled if payment is not received. Shawcliffe Digital is not responsible for issues that occur while support is paused due to non-payment.

Internal Rule

Do not keep working when payment is overdue unless there is a deliberate reason.

20.15 Client Cancellation

Clients may cancel.

Shawcliffe should define what happens.

Cancellation Should Address

ItemWhy
How client cancelsWritten notice
Fees owedWork completed/time reserved
RefundsUsually no refund for work already done
Work productWhat client receives, if anything
Third-party costsClient may still owe
Monthly supportCancellation timing
Data/accessHandoff or closure

Sample Cancellation Language

The client may cancel the project by giving written notice. If the project is cancelled after work has begun, the client remains responsible for payment for work completed, time reserved, and any non-refundable expenses or third-party costs incurred. Initial payments are generally not refundable once work has begun.

Shawcliffe Cancellation Language

Shawcliffe Digital may end the project or agreement if the client fails to pay, does not provide required materials, repeatedly delays the project, requests work outside Shawcliffe’s ability or values, behaves disrespectfully, or materially breaches the agreement.

20.16 Client Delays

Client delays are common.

Missing content, access, feedback, or approval can stall projects.

Client Delay Examples

  • No logo/photos
  • No services/prices
  • No domain access
  • No review link
  • No policy wording
  • No feedback
  • No approval
  • Changing direction
  • Missing payment
  • Another decision maker appears late

Sample Client Delay Language

The project timeline depends on the client providing required content, access, feedback, approvals, and payments on time. If the client delays providing required items, the project timeline may be extended. Shawcliffe Digital is not responsible for delays caused by missing or late client materials, feedback, access, approvals, or payments.

Project Pause Language

If the client does not provide required materials, feedback, access, or approval within [number] days, Shawcliffe Digital may pause the project. A paused project may need to be rescheduled based on Shawcliffe Digital’s availability.

Restart Fee Option

This should be lawyer-reviewed before use.

If a paused project requires significant re-onboarding, re-planning, or rework, a restart fee may apply.

20.17 Revision Limits

Revisions must be limited.

Revision Clause Should Define

  • Number of included revision rounds
  • What counts as included revision
  • What is not included
  • How feedback should be submitted
  • What happens after included revisions are used
  • New features are change requests

Sample Revision Language

This project includes [number] structured revision round(s). Revisions include corrections and adjustments within the approved scope.

Revisions do not include new pages, new features, new components, major redesigns, new workflows, change of business direction, or work outside the approved Scope of Work. Those requests are treated as change requests and may require additional cost and timeline.

Feedback Submission Language

Client feedback should be provided in one organized message or document whenever possible. Scattered feedback across multiple channels may delay revisions.

20.18 Change Requests

Change requests protect profitability.

Change Request Clause Should Define

  • What counts as change request
  • How change requests are reviewed
  • Price/timeline impact
  • Written approval required
  • Work does not begin without approval

Sample Change Request Language

A change request is any request outside the approved Scope of Work, including new features, new pages, new forms, new workflows, integrations, automations, major design changes, or additional services.

Shawcliffe Digital will review change requests and may provide a price and timeline impact. Work on change requests will not begin until approved in writing.

Add-On Approval Language

Approval by email, written message, signed change order, or paid invoice may be treated as approval to proceed, depending on the agreed process.

Get this reviewed by a lawyer before relying on it.

20.19 Client Responsibilities

The agreement should clearly state that the client has responsibilities.

Client Responsibilities Include

  • Providing accurate business information
  • Providing services/products/prices
  • Providing policies
  • Providing legal/professional/regulated wording
  • Providing photos/assets they have permission to use
  • Providing domain/hosting/access information
  • Providing payment provider access if needed
  • Reviewing and approving work
  • Responding in a timely way
  • Paying invoices
  • Using the system responsibly
  • Maintaining their own business operations

Sample Client Responsibility Language

The client is responsible for providing accurate business information, services, products, prices, policies, photos, brand assets, access credentials, approvals, and any legal, medical, financial, regulatory, or industry-specific wording required for the project.

Shawcliffe Digital may help organize or polish client-provided content, but the client remains responsible for the accuracy and legality of the information they provide and approve.

20.20 Ownership of Client Content

Client content should belong to the client.

Client Content May Include

  • Business name
  • Logo
  • Photos
  • Written content
  • Product/service descriptions
  • Policies
  • Testimonials
  • Customer lists
  • Existing brand materials
  • Videos
  • Documents
  • Pricing
  • Business data

Sample Client Content Ownership Language

The client retains ownership of content, materials, logos, photos, business information, customer data, and other materials the client provides to Shawcliffe Digital, subject to any third-party rights or licences.

Client Permission Language

The client confirms that they have the right to provide and use any materials, photos, logos, text, files, or other content supplied to Shawcliffe Digital for the project.

20.21 Ownership of Final Work

This needs careful legal review.

The agreement should distinguish between:

  • Client content
  • Final deliverable
  • Shawcliffe reusable components
  • Third-party tools
  • Open-source software
  • Licensed assets

Practical Ownership Approach

The client may own or receive a licence to use the final finished project.

Shawcliffe should retain ownership of reusable components, templates, systems, methods, internal tools, pre-existing code, and general know-how.

Sample Plain-English Ownership Language

After the client has paid all amounts owed for the project, the client may use the completed project for their business as described in the Scope of Work.

The client owns the content and materials they provided.

Shawcliffe Digital retains ownership of its pre-existing tools, reusable components, templates, code libraries, methods, systems, documentation, processes, and know-how used to create the project, unless otherwise agreed in writing.

Why This Matters

Shawcliffe must be able to reuse:

  • Forms
  • Dashboards
  • Templates
  • Field sets
  • QA checklists
  • Code patterns
  • Status trackers
  • Review systems
  • Quote workflows
  • Booking workflows
  • Design/process methods

Otherwise every client could claim ownership over reusable business assets.

20.22 Ownership of Reusable Components and Templates

This is critical for Shawcliffe’s business model.

Internal Rule

Clients pay for their project. They do not buy Shawcliffe’s entire component library.

Sample Reusable Component Language

Shawcliffe Digital may use reusable components, templates, code, processes, frameworks, systems, documentation, and prior know-how in client projects. These reusable materials remain the property of Shawcliffe Digital and may be reused, adapted, or improved for other clients.

Client-Friendly Explanation

We use reusable building blocks to keep projects efficient and practical. You are paying for your finished system and the work to configure it for your business, not for exclusive ownership of our internal tools or templates.

20.23 Third-Party Tools

Many systems depend on third-party tools.

Examples:

  • Domain registrar
  • Hosting provider
  • Email platform
  • SMS provider
  • Payment processor
  • Google Business Profile
  • Google Analytics
  • Booking tools
  • Form tools
  • CRM tools
  • Map services
  • Review platforms
  • App stores
  • APIs

Third-Party Tool Clause Should Explain

  • Client may need accounts
  • Client may pay separate fees
  • Third parties may change pricing
  • Third parties may have outages
  • Shawcliffe does not control third-party platforms
  • Client must follow third-party terms
  • Integrations may break or need support
  • Third-party work may require monthly support

Sample Third-Party Tools Language

Some parts of the project may rely on third-party services such as hosting providers, domain registrars, email services, SMS providers, payment processors, analytics tools, Google services, booking tools, or other platforms.

These third-party services may have their own fees, terms, limitations, outages, support processes, and privacy practices. Shawcliffe Digital is not responsible for third-party service failures, price changes, policy changes, or platform changes outside Shawcliffe Digital’s control.

Third-Party Cost Language

Unless specifically included in the Scope of Work, third-party fees, subscriptions, transaction fees, SMS usage fees, hosting fees, domain fees, app store fees, or payment processing fees are the client’s responsibility.

20.24 Hosting and Domain Responsibilities

Hosting/domain confusion can become a serious problem.

Agreement Should Define

IssueWhy
Who owns domainClient should usually own
Who manages DNSTechnical responsibility
Who pays hostingClient or Shawcliffe plan
Who maintains hostingMonthly support issue
What happens if support endsAccess/transfer
Whether email is affectedAvoid breaking business email
SSL responsibilityNeeded for secure site
BackupsDefine if included

Recommended Domain Rule

The client should generally own their own domain.

Shawcliffe can help connect it.

Sample Domain Language

The client is responsible for owning and maintaining their domain name unless otherwise agreed. Shawcliffe Digital may assist with connecting the domain to the project. The client is responsible for maintaining access to their domain account and paying domain renewal fees unless those services are specifically included in a support or hosting plan.

Sample Hosting Language

Hosting responsibility will be defined in the Scope of Work or support plan. If Shawcliffe Digital provides or manages hosting, hosting support is included only as described in the selected plan. If the client manages their own hosting, the client is responsible for hosting fees, renewals, access, and provider issues unless Shawcliffe Digital is separately engaged to assist.

Email Warning Language

If the client’s domain is used for business email, DNS changes must be handled carefully. Shawcliffe Digital is not responsible for email disruption caused by missing, incorrect, or incomplete access information provided by the client or third-party provider issues outside Shawcliffe Digital’s control.

Get this reviewed.

20.25 Privacy and Data Handling Basics

Shawcliffe may handle personal information such as:

  • Client contact info
  • Customer names
  • Customer phone numbers
  • Customer emails
  • Quote request details
  • Booking request details
  • Photos/files
  • Pet information
  • Property information
  • Vehicle information
  • Student information
  • Payment-related info through third-party processors
  • Professional intake details

Because Shawcliffe is in Alberta, privacy obligations may include Alberta PIPA for provincially regulated private-sector organizations, and PIPEDA may apply in broader Canadian commercial contexts. CASL may matter if Shawcliffe or its clients send commercial electronic messages such as marketing emails or texts.

Privacy Clause Should Address

TopicWhy
What data is collectedTransparency
Why data is collectedPurpose limitation
Who controls customer dataUsually client
How Shawcliffe accesses dataSupport/build purposes
Third-party toolsData may pass through platforms
Security limitsNo system is risk-free
Sensitive dataAvoid unless properly scoped
Retention/deletionWhat happens after project/support
BreachesNeed lawyer-approved policy
Client responsibilitiesClient must use data lawfully

Sample Privacy/Data Language

Shawcliffe Digital may access personal information provided by the client or submitted through the project only as needed to provide the agreed services, build, support, maintain, or troubleshoot the system.

The client is responsible for ensuring that their collection, use, storage, and communication with customers complies with applicable privacy, anti-spam, industry, and legal requirements.

Shawcliffe Digital will take reasonable steps to protect information it accesses, but no digital system or third-party service can be guaranteed completely secure.

Sensitive Data Warning

Projects involving sensitive personal information, health information, financial information, legal documents, children’s information, or regulated professional information may require additional privacy, security, legal, or compliance review before Shawcliffe Digital agrees to collect, store, or process that information.

Internal Rule

Do not casually build systems that collect sensitive information.

For sensitive fields, ask:

  • Is it truly necessary?
  • Who needs access?
  • Where is it stored?
  • How is it protected?
  • How long is it kept?
  • What law/rules may apply?
  • Is a specialist needed?

20.26 CASL / Marketing Messages Basics

If Shawcliffe builds SMS/email customer alert systems, review request flows, product alerts, rebooking messages, or marketing campaigns, Canada’s anti-spam rules may matter. The CRTC describes three general requirements for commercial electronic messages: consent, identification information, and an unsubscribe mechanism.

Agreement Should Say

  • Client is responsible for lawful customer messaging
  • Client must provide consent wording/process where required
  • Shawcliffe can help implement messaging tools but does not provide legal compliance advice
  • Marketing messages may require unsubscribe mechanisms
  • SMS/email systems may need monthly support

Sample Messaging Compliance Language

If the project includes email, SMS, or other customer messaging, the client is responsible for ensuring that messages are sent with any required consent, identification information, unsubscribe mechanism, and other legal requirements. Shawcliffe Digital may help configure messaging systems but does not provide legal advice about anti-spam or marketing compliance.

20.27 Portfolio and Case Study Permission

Shawcliffe should be able to show work, but clients may have privacy concerns.

Best approach:

  • Ask permission
  • Include default permission if acceptable
  • Allow opt-out for sensitive projects
  • Get approval before publishing detailed case studies

Sample Portfolio Language

Unless the client requests otherwise in writing, Shawcliffe Digital may identify the client as a client and display non-confidential screenshots, links, descriptions, or summaries of the completed work in Shawcliffe Digital’s portfolio, marketing materials, proposals, or case studies.

Safer Case Study Language

Detailed case studies, testimonials, client quotes, performance numbers, or sensitive business details will only be published with the client’s approval.

Client-Friendly Version

We may ask to show the finished project in our portfolio. We will not share sensitive information or detailed results without your approval.

20.28 Warranty / Bug-Fix Period

A warranty or bug-fix period gives the client confidence while preventing indefinite free support.

Warranty Period Should Define

  • How long it lasts
  • What counts as a bug
  • What does not count
  • Whether third-party failures are included
  • How bugs are reported
  • What happens after warranty ends

Suggested Starter Warranty

Example:

14 to 30 days after launch for bugs in included features.

Larger projects may have longer warranty periods.

Sample Warranty Language

Shawcliffe Digital will fix bugs in included features reported within [number] days after launch. A bug means an included feature is not working as intended based on the approved Scope of Work.

The warranty period does not include new features, new pages, new workflows, design changes, content changes, third-party platform issues, client-caused changes, or issues caused by missing/incorrect client information.

After Warranty Language

After the warranty period, support is handled according to the selected monthly support plan or as separately quoted paid support.

20.29 Liability Limitations

Liability limitations are legal and must be lawyer-reviewed.

But Shawcliffe should understand why they matter.

Risks Shawcliffe Should Limit

  • Lost profits claims
  • Lost leads claims
  • Business interruption claims
  • Third-party tool failures
  • Client misuse
  • Incorrect client-provided content
  • Security incidents beyond reasonable control
  • Google ranking/lead generation expectations
  • Payment processor issues
  • Missed messages due to client email/SMS setup
  • Data loss from third-party tools

Sample Plain-English Liability Concept

Shawcliffe Digital is responsible for providing the agreed services with reasonable care. Shawcliffe Digital is not responsible for indirect losses, lost profits, lost revenue, lost leads, business interruption, third-party platform failures, or issues caused by inaccurate client information, client misuse, or factors outside Shawcliffe Digital’s reasonable control.

Liability Cap Concept

A lawyer may recommend limiting liability to fees paid.

Example concept:

Shawcliffe Digital’s total liability related to the project is limited to the amount paid by the client for the specific services giving rise to the claim.

Do not use this without legal review.

20.30 Guarantees and Disclaimers

Shawcliffe should be explicit about what it does not guarantee.

Shawcliffe Should Not Guarantee

  • Leads
  • Sales
  • Revenue
  • Google rankings
  • Reviews
  • Customer behaviour
  • Social media growth
  • Ad performance
  • Exact launch date if client delays
  • Third-party platform uptime
  • SMS/email deliverability
  • Payment processor performance

Sample No-Guarantee Language

Shawcliffe Digital does not guarantee specific business results, leads, sales, revenue, search rankings, reviews, customer behaviour, ad performance, or third-party platform performance. Shawcliffe Digital’s role is to provide the agreed digital services and systems described in the Scope of Work.

20.31 Electronic Signatures and Approval

Shawcliffe may want clients to approve agreements by e-signature or written email.

Alberta’s Electronic Transactions Act is intended to remove barriers to electronic commerce by giving electronic records and transactions legal recognition in many contexts, but Shawcliffe should get lawyer guidance on its exact signing/approval process.

Practical Approval Methods

  • E-signature tool
  • Signed PDF
  • Email approval
  • Checkbox agreement
  • Paid invoice referencing agreement
  • Written approval in project portal

Sample Electronic Approval Language

The parties may sign or approve this agreement electronically. Electronic signatures, written email approval, or other agreed electronic acceptance methods may be used to show acceptance of this agreement, where permitted by applicable law.

Get this reviewed.

20.32 Dispute Handling

Keep this simple at first.

A lawyer should review.

Agreement Should Address

  • Good-faith discussion first
  • Written notice of issue
  • Time to resolve
  • Governing law
  • Venue/jurisdiction if needed
  • Whether mediation/arbitration is used

Sample Dispute Language

If a dispute arises, both parties agree to first try to resolve it in good faith through written communication and discussion. If the issue cannot be resolved informally, the parties may pursue any available legal remedies under the governing law.

Governing Law Concept

For Shawcliffe in Alberta:

This agreement is governed by the laws of Alberta and applicable laws of Canada.

Have a lawyer confirm wording.

20.34 Sample Plain-English Client Agreement Skeleton

This is not lawyer-approved. It is a practical draft structure.

Client Agreement

1. Parties

This agreement is between Shawcliffe Digital and [Client Business Name].

2. Services

Shawcliffe Digital provides digital services such as websites, customer systems, forms, dashboards, notifications, review request systems, booking request systems, quote request systems, live status systems, and related support.

The specific services for this project are listed in the attached Scope of Work.

3. Scope of Work

The Scope of Work describes what is included in the project, what is not included, the project price, payment schedule, timeline, revision rounds, client responsibilities, and launch requirements.

Anything not listed as included is not included unless both parties agree in writing.

4. Payment

The project price is $[amount].

Payment schedule:

  • $[amount] due before work begins
  • $[amount] due before launch

Shawcliffe Digital is not required to begin work before the initial payment is received and is not required to launch the project before final payment is received.

5. Monthly Support

If the client selects a monthly support plan, the support plan details are listed in the Scope of Work or support plan description.

If no monthly support plan is selected, future updates, troubleshooting, training, or changes may be quoted separately.

6. Client Responsibilities

The client is responsible for providing accurate business information, content, photos, services, prices, policies, access credentials, feedback, approvals, and any legal, medical, financial, regulatory, or industry-specific wording needed for the project.

7. Revisions

This project includes [number] revision round(s). Revisions are limited to changes within the approved scope.

New features, new pages, new workflows, major redesigns, and out-of-scope requests are change requests and may require additional cost and timeline.

8. Change Requests

Any request outside the approved Scope of Work may be treated as a change request. Shawcliffe Digital may provide a price and timeline impact before beginning the work.

9. Client Delays

The timeline depends on the client providing required content, access, feedback, approvals, and payments on time. Delays by the client may delay the project.

10. Cancellation

Either party may cancel according to the cancellation terms. The client remains responsible for work completed, time reserved, and non-refundable expenses incurred before cancellation.

11. Ownership

The client owns the content and materials they provide.

Shawcliffe Digital retains ownership of its reusable components, templates, code libraries, methods, systems, documentation, processes, and pre-existing tools unless otherwise agreed in writing.

After full payment, the client may use the completed project for their business as described in the Scope of Work.

12. Third-Party Tools

Some parts of the project may rely on third-party tools or platforms. Third-party fees, outages, terms, changes, and limitations are outside Shawcliffe Digital’s control unless specifically agreed otherwise.

13. Hosting and Domain

Hosting and domain responsibilities are described in the Scope of Work or support plan. The client is generally responsible for owning and maintaining their domain unless otherwise agreed.

14. Privacy and Data

Shawcliffe Digital may access personal information only as needed to provide the agreed services. The client is responsible for using customer information lawfully and providing any required privacy, consent, or compliance wording.

15. Warranty / Bug Fixes

Shawcliffe Digital will fix bugs in included features reported within [number] days after launch. New features, content changes, third-party issues, client-caused changes, or out-of-scope requests are not included in the bug-fix period.

16. No Guaranteed Results

Shawcliffe Digital does not guarantee leads, sales, revenue, rankings, reviews, or specific business outcomes.

17. Portfolio

Shawcliffe Digital may show non-confidential project work in its portfolio unless the client requests otherwise in writing. Detailed case studies or sensitive business results require client approval.

18. Limitation of Liability

Liability terms should be reviewed by a lawyer before use.

19. Governing Law

This agreement is governed by the laws of Alberta and applicable laws of Canada, unless otherwise required.

20. Acceptance

By signing or approving this agreement, both parties agree to the terms above and the attached Scope of Work.

Client: ____________________
Date: ____________________

Shawcliffe Digital: ____________________
Date: ____________________

20.36 Sample Agreement Language for First Three Offers

A. Live Status Starter System

Project Goal

  • Monthly support terms
  • No-guarantee language
  • Lawyer review as soon as practical

20.39 Common Agreement Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Starting Work Without Payment

Friendly clients can still disappear, delay, or change their minds.

Mistake 2: Launching Before Final Payment

Do not give away leverage.

Mistake 3: Not Defining What Is Excluded

Exclusions prevent conflict.

Mistake 4: Giving Away Reusable Components

Clients should not own Shawcliffe’s internal systems.

Mistake 5: Treating Monthly Support Casually

Support must have terms.

Mistake 6: Not Addressing Client Delays

Missing content can ruin timelines.

Mistake 7: Guessing Legal/Professional Wording

Clients must provide and approve regulated or industry-specific wording.

Mistake 8: Ignoring Third-Party Tools

Third-party platforms can fail, change, or charge fees.

Mistake 9: Promising Results

Do not guarantee leads, sales, rankings, reviews, or revenue.

Mistake 10: Waiting Too Long for Legal Review

A bad contract can cost more than lawyer review.

Section 21

Finance, Billing, and Project Profitability

21.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Finance Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains how Shawcliffe Digital should handle money.

That includes:

  • Invoicing
  • Deposits/start payments
  • Milestone billing
  • Final payment before launch
  • Monthly recurring billing
  • Support plan billing
  • Late payment
  • Refunds and cancellations
  • Third-party expenses
  • Software subscriptions
  • Payment methods
  • GST/tax considerations
  • Bookkeeping categories
  • Project profitability
  • Time tracking
  • Pricing review
  • Cash flow planning
  • Monthly financial review

This is not accounting, tax, or legal advice. Shawcliffe should work with a qualified accountant/bookkeeper, especially before registering for GST/HST, filing taxes, claiming business expenses, or setting up payroll/dividends.

The internal rule:

If the money is not tracked, the business is guessing.

21.2 Finance Philosophy

Shawcliffe Digital should not treat finance as something to clean up later.

Money needs to be organized from the beginning because poor finance habits create:

  • Unclear profit
  • Forgotten invoices
  • Unpaid work
  • Underpriced projects
  • Tax surprises
  • Cash flow stress
  • Confusion between personal and business money
  • Trouble knowing which services are actually worth selling

The goal is not to build a giant accounting department.

The goal is to have a simple system that answers:

  • What money came in?
  • What money is owed?
  • What money went out?
  • Which projects were profitable?
  • Which clients are underpriced?
  • What recurring revenue exists?
  • What taxes may be owed?
  • What should pricing be next time?

21.3 Core Finance Rules

Rule 1: Do Not Start Serious Work Without Payment

For most projects:

Initial payment must be received before build begins.

Rule 2: Do Not Launch Before Final Payment

For most projects:

Final payment must be received before launch, delivery, transfer, or public release.

Rule 3: Separate Build Revenue From Support Revenue

A project build is one-time revenue.

A support plan is recurring revenue.

Track them separately.

Rule 4: Track Time Even When Charging Fixed Prices

Time tracking shows whether the price was actually profitable.

Rule 5: Track Third-Party Costs Separately

Software, SMS, hosting, domains, plugins, and subscriptions can quietly eat profit.

Rule 6: Review Profit Monthly

If Shawcliffe does not review the numbers, underpricing will continue unnoticed.

21.6 Deposits / Start Payments

For clarity, Shawcliffe may prefer the term start payment instead of deposit.

A start payment means:

The client pays before work begins so Shawcliffe can reserve time, plan, and start the project.

Recommended Start Payment Rules

Project SizeSuggested Rule
Very small project100% upfront
Standard project50% upfront
Larger project30–50% upfront plus milestones
Monthly subscription setupSetup fee before start
Add-onPaid before add-on work begins

Start Payment Language

The project start payment is due before work begins. Work is not scheduled until payment is received.

Internal Rule

A verbal yes is not a paid project.

A project becomes active when:

  • Proposal/scope is accepted
  • Agreement is approved
  • Start payment is received
  • Onboarding begins

21.7 Milestone Billing

Milestones are useful for larger or longer projects.

When to Use Milestones

Use milestone billing when:

  • Project is over roughly $7,500–$10,000
  • Project will take several weeks/months
  • There are multiple major phases
  • Build includes several components
  • Client wants phased delivery
  • Shawcliffe wants lower cash flow risk

Example Milestone Structures

Option A: 50 / 50

MilestonePayment
Start payment before build50%
Final payment before launch50%

Best for most early projects.

Option B: 40 / 30 / 30

MilestonePayment
Start payment40%
Initial build/demo ready30%
Final payment before launch30%

Best for larger builds.

Option C: Phase Billing

PhasePayment
Phase 1: Foundation$X
Phase 2: Dashboard/forms$X
Phase 3: Launch/support setup$X

Best for phased systems.

Milestone Invoice Language

This invoice is due because the project has reached the agreed milestone: [milestone]. Work on the next stage may pause until payment is received.

21.8 Final Payment Before Launch

This should be one of Shawcliffe’s strongest financial rules.

Internal Rule

No final payment, no launch.

What Counts as Launch / Delivery

Final payment should usually be required before:

  • Website goes live
  • Domain is connected
  • Dashboard is handed over
  • Final files are delivered
  • Client receives final access
  • System is transferred
  • QR codes go public
  • Customer-facing system is released

Final Payment Language

Final payment is due before launch, delivery, transfer, or public release of the project.

Why This Matters

If Shawcliffe launches before final payment:

  • Client has less urgency to pay
  • Curtis has to chase money
  • Cassandra’s work is already delivered
  • Support begins with awkward billing
  • Cash flow becomes unpredictable

21.16 GST / Tax Considerations in Canada and Alberta

This section must be confirmed with an accountant.

As of current CRA guidance, many Canadian businesses must register for GST/HST after exceeding the small supplier threshold, commonly $30,000 in taxable supplies over a single calendar quarter or over four consecutive calendar quarters. CRA explains that if a business exceeds $30,000 in a single calendar quarter, it is no longer a small supplier and must start charging GST/HST on the supply that caused it to exceed the threshold.

Alberta’s current GST/HST rate table shows 5% GST and 0% provincial sales tax/HST for Alberta, meaning most taxable supplies in Alberta are charged 5% GST if the business is registered and required to collect it.

GST/HST Basics for Shawcliffe

Shawcliffe should track:

  • Total revenue
  • Taxable supplies
  • Whether it has crossed the GST/HST threshold
  • Whether registration is required
  • GST charged on invoices after registration
  • GST paid on business expenses
  • Input tax credits if registered
  • GST filing deadlines
  • GST owed to CRA

GST/HST Tracking Rule

Track revenue from day one as if GST registration will eventually matter.

Do not wait until revenue is already high and records are messy.

Before GST Registration

If Shawcliffe is still a small supplier and not registered:

  • Do not charge GST/HST unless registered
  • Track gross revenue carefully
  • Watch the $30,000 threshold
  • Ask accountant when voluntary registration makes sense
  • Keep receipts anyway

After GST Registration

If Shawcliffe registers:

  • Add GST/HST registration number to invoices where required
  • Charge GST/HST on taxable supplies as required
  • Track GST/HST collected
  • Track GST/HST paid on eligible business expenses
  • File GST/HST returns on schedule
  • Do not spend GST collected as if it is profit

GST Collected Is Not Yours

Internal rule:

GST collected belongs to the government until remitted.

A practical habit:

  • Put GST collected in a separate account or track it clearly
  • Do not treat it as spendable profit

21.17 Business Expenses and Deductions

CRA states that, generally, businesses can deduct reasonable current expenses incurred to earn business income, while personal expenses are not deductible. CRA also notes that deductible expenses include GST/HST paid on those expenses minus any input tax credit claimed.

Expense Tracking Rule

Save receipts and categorize expenses as they happen.

Do not wait until tax season.

21.19 Project Profitability Tracking

Fixed-price projects can look profitable until time is counted.

Track project profit.

Project Profit Formula

Project profit = project revenue - direct expenses - estimated labour cost/time value.

Even if Curtis and Cassandra do not pay themselves formally yet, track the time value.

Project Profit Tracker

ClientProjectPriceDirect CostsCurtis HoursCassandra HoursTotal HoursEffective Hourly RateProfit Notes

Effective Hourly Rate

Formula:

Effective hourly rate = project revenue minus direct costs divided by total hours.

Example:

Project price: $4,000
Direct costs: $200
Total hours: 40

Effective hourly rate:

($4,000 - $200) / 40 = $95/hour

Why This Matters

A $5,000 project that takes 25 hours is good.

A $5,000 project that takes 120 hours is a problem.

21.21 Pricing Review

After every project, review whether the price was right.
