Ask:

  • What did we charge?
  • How many hours did it take?
  • What was the effective hourly rate?
  • What took longer than expected?
  • What was underpriced?
  • What did the client ask for that should have been add-on?
  • What support burden did we create?
  • Would we sell this again?
  • What should the price be next time?
  • Did this create a reusable component/template?

Pricing Decision Table

SituationPricing Lesson
Project was smooth and profitableKeep or raise price slightly
Too many revisionsTighten scope/revision policy
Too much onboarding helpCharge content/strategy fee
Dashboard support heavyRequire monthly plan
Client needed lots of trainingAdd training fee/cheat sheet
Notifications complicatedCharge more for setup/support
Integration painfulHigher add-on price
Client delayed repeatedlyAdd delay/restart policy
Effective hourly rate lowRaise price or reduce scope

21.22 Cash Flow Planning

Cash flow is different from profit.

A profitable business can still run out of cash if money arrives late.

Cash Flow Basics

Track:

  • Cash in bank
  • Invoices sent
  • Invoices paid
  • Upcoming bills
  • Monthly subscriptions
  • Taxes/GST set aside
  • Contractor payments
  • Personal draws/pay
  • Emergency buffer

Cash Flow Rule

Do not count proposal money as real money until it is paid.

21.23 Tax Set-Aside

Shawcliffe should set aside money for taxes.

The exact amount depends on structure, income, deductions, GST registration, and personal/corporate tax planning.

Ask an accountant.

Simple Habit

Every time revenue comes in, set aside a percentage for:

  • Income tax
  • GST/HST collected if registered
  • CPP/payroll considerations if applicable
  • Corporate tax if incorporated
  • Accountant/bookkeeping costs

Internal Rule

Profit is not all spendable.

21.28 Support Profitability Tracking

Support can become unprofitable if not tracked.

Support Profit Tracker

ClientPlanMonthly FeeHours UsedEffective HourlyIssuesUpgrade Needed?

Support Profit Formula

Effective support rate = monthly fee / hours spent.

Example:

Monthly fee: $300
Hours spent: 3

Effective rate:

$100/hour

Monthly fee: $300
Hours spent: 10

Effective rate:

$30/hour

That client is underpriced or support-heavy.

Support Review Rule

If a support client uses more than their plan for two months in a row, review the plan.

21.29 Add-On Billing

Add-ons should not be casually absorbed into the original project.

Add-On Billing Process

  • Client requests add-on.
  • Curtis logs request.
  • Cassandra estimates complexity if needed.
  • Curtis quotes price.
  • Client approves.
  • Invoice sent.
  • Payment received or milestone agreed.
  • Work begins.
  • Add-on QA completed.
  • Support impact reviewed.

Add-On Invoice Description

Add-on: [feature/component] for [project/system], including [short scope]. This add-on is outside the original project scope.

21.30 Rush Fees

Rush work should cost more or be declined.

Rush Fee Rule

Rush work disrupts schedule and planning. It must either be priced properly or declined.

Rush Fee Options

Significant rush+25–50%
Emergency/rush outside normal scheduleCustom premium
Unsafe rushDecline

Rush Language

We may be able to rush this, but it would require moving other work and would include a rush fee. The other option is to reduce the scope and launch a smaller version first.

If a project is below the pricing floor, either simplify it, make it paid consulting, or decline.

21.36 Common Finance Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Starting Without Payment

A signed proposal is not cash.

Mistake 2: Launching Before Final Payment

Do not give away leverage.

Mistake 3: Not Tracking Time

You cannot know profit without time.

Mistake 4: Treating Revenue as Profit

Revenue must cover expenses, taxes, tools, support, and owner pay.

Mistake 5: Forgetting GST/HST Thresholds

Track revenue from day one.

Mistake 6: Letting Third-Party Costs Eat Profit

Bill them clearly or include them in pricing intentionally.

Mistake 7: Underpricing Monthly Support

Support can quietly become a second job.

Mistake 8: Not Reviewing Subscriptions

Small monthly tools add up.

Mistake 9: Mixing Personal and Business Spending

This creates tax and bookkeeping headaches.

Mistake 10: Not Asking an Accountant

Good accounting advice can save more than it costs.

21.38 Key Takeaways

  • Shawcliffe should not start serious work without payment.
  • Final payment should usually be required before launch.
  • Monthly support should be billed and tracked separately from project builds.
  • GST/HST should be tracked from day one, especially because the small supplier threshold can require registration once exceeded.
  • Alberta currently has 5% GST and no provincial sales tax/HST in CRA’s rate table.
  • Revenue is not profit.
  • GST collected is not spendable profit.
  • Track time even on fixed-price projects.
  • Track support hours so MRR stays profitable.
  • Third-party expenses must be billed or priced intentionally.
  • Review finances monthly.
  • Ask an accountant before tax season, not after things are messy.

Section 22

Internal Admin, Tools, and Operations Setup

22.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Operations Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains how Shawcliffe Digital should organize the business internally.

This includes:

  • Tools
  • Files
  • Folders
  • Client records
  • Project boards
  • Sales tracking
  • Finance tracking
  • Password/access management
  • Email/calendar setup
  • Business phone setup
  • Document templates
  • SOP storage
  • Naming conventions
  • Weekly admin routine
  • Monthly operations review
  • Data/security basics
  • Backups
  • Avoiding overbuilt admin systems

The internal rule:

The admin system should make the business easier to run, not become another business to manage.

22.2 Operations Philosophy

Shawcliffe Digital is a lean husband-and-wife agency.

The operations system should be:

  • Simple
  • Searchable
  • Repeatable
  • Easy to maintain
  • Good enough to start
  • Not dependent on memory
  • Not scattered across random messages
  • Not overcomplicated with too many tools

The goal is to know where everything lives.

At any time, Curtis and Cassandra should be able to answer:

  • Who are our active leads?
  • Who are our active clients?
  • What stage is each project in?
  • What does the client owe us?
  • What do we owe the client?
  • What are we waiting on?
  • Where are the files?
  • Where are the passwords/access notes?
  • What invoices are unpaid?
  • What support requests are open?

At the beginning, Shawcliffe does not need a complex stack.

Shawcliffe needs one simple system for each major area.

Use boring names.

General File Naming Formula

YYYY-MM-DD_Client_Project_DocumentType

Example:

2026-07-06_ABC-Welding_Quote-Request-Proposal

Simpler Formula

Client_Project_DocumentType

Example:

ABC-Welding_Quote-Request-Scope

DocumentFile Name

Or dates.

Naming Rule

Avoid:

  • finalfinal

22.21 Data and Security Basics

Shawcliffe is handling business and possibly customer information.

Security does not need to be enterprise-level at first, but it must be responsible.

Basic Security Rules

  • Use strong passwords.
  • Use unique passwords for every account.
  • Use a password manager.
  • Use two-factor authentication where possible.
  • Do not share passwords in plain text.
  • Limit client access to what is needed.
  • Do not collect sensitive data unless necessary.
  • Do not store sensitive client/customer data casually.
  • Keep devices locked.
  • Be careful with public Wi-Fi.
  • Remove access when projects end.
  • Back up important files.
  • Keep software/dev tools updated.
  • Do not click suspicious links.
  • Separate personal and business accounts where possible.

Sensitive Data Caution

Be extra careful with:

  • Health information
  • Financial information
  • Legal documents
  • Children’s information
  • Identity documents
  • Payment details
  • Sensitive customer notes
  • Private photos/files
  • Passwords
  • Home access/property codes

Internal Rule

Do not collect or store information unless the system actually needs it.

22.26 Avoiding Overbuilt Admin Systems

This is important.

Small agencies often waste time building perfect internal systems instead of selling and delivering.

Signs the Admin System Is Overbuilt

  • More time organizing than selling
  • Too many tools
  • Same data entered in five places
  • Curtis avoids updating it
  • Cassandra cannot find what she needs
  • Trackers are beautiful but empty
  • SOPs are too long to use
  • Project board has too many columns
  • Admin work becomes procrastination
  • Tools are chosen before problems exist

Right-Size Rule

Build the admin system one pain point at a time.

Examples:

  • If leads get forgotten, improve sales tracker.
  • If projects drift, improve project board.
  • If files are lost, improve folder structure.
  • If payments are missed, improve invoice tracker.
  • If support gets messy, improve support log.
  • If builds repeat, improve templates.

Internal Question

Before adding a tool, ask:

What real problem does this solve right now?

If the answer is vague, wait.

22.42 Keeping Admin Simple

Visual clarity and simple systems matter.

The admin system should be simple and low-friction.

Simple Admin Rules

  • Use fewer tools.
  • Use visual boards.
  • Use checklists.
  • Use recurring review times.
  • Use clear next actions.
  • Keep names boring and searchable.
  • Keep templates copy/paste ready.
  • Avoid giant open-ended notes.
  • Use statuses, not vague memory.
  • Make the system easy to restart after missing a few days.

Good Status Labels

  • New
  • Waiting on Client
  • Waiting on Shawcliffe
  • Ready for Build
  • In Progress
  • Needs Review
  • Blocked
  • Done
  • Follow Up
  • Nurture
  • Archived

Bad Statuses

  • Misc
  • Later
  • Stuff
  • Need to deal with
  • Maybe
  • Ongoing
  • Important

These are too vague.

22.45 Common Admin Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Too Many Tools

More tools do not automatically create more organization.

Mistake 2: No Single Source of Truth

If a project exists in three places with different statuses, nobody knows what is true.

Mistake 3: Saving Files Randomly

Client files must go in client folders.

Mistake 4: Passwords in Text Messages

Use a password manager.

Mistake 5: No Weekly Review

Even a good system decays without review.

Mistake 6: Not Tracking Leads

Conversations become forgotten opportunities.

Mistake 7: Not Tracking Support

Support becomes invisible unpaid work.

Mistake 8: Not Recording Decisions

Unrecorded decisions become future disputes.

Mistake 9: Overbuilding Admin Instead of Selling

Admin should support sales and delivery, not replace them.

Mistake 10: Not Updating SOPs

If the process changes, the SOP should change.

22.46 Minimum Viable Operations System

If Shawcliffe only does ten things, do these:

  • Use business email.
  • Use one shared calendar.
  • Use one cloud folder system.
  • Create a client folder for every client.
  • Use one sales tracker.
  • Use one project board.
  • Use one finance tracker/accounting system.
  • Use one password manager.
  • Use one support email/log.
  • Do one weekly admin review.

That is enough to start running professionally.

22.49 Key Takeaways

  • Shawcliffe’s admin system should be simple, searchable, and repeatable.
  • Use one place for leads, one place for projects, one place for client files, one place for finance, and one place for passwords.
  • Do not let admin become procrastination.
  • Every active project needs a next action.
  • Every client needs a folder and record.
  • Every lead needs to be tracked.
  • Every invoice needs to be tracked.
  • Every support request needs to be logged.
  • Passwords should be handled through a password manager, not texts.
  • Client decisions affecting money, scope, access, launch, or support should be recorded.
  • A short weekly admin review prevents chaos.
  • Upgrade tools only when the current system is causing real friction.

Section 23

Client Experience and Communication Standards

23.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Client Relationship Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section defines how Shawcliffe Digital should communicate with clients and make the client experience feel professional, clear, calm, and trustworthy.

Client experience is not just being “nice.”

Client experience includes:

  • How quickly clients understand the process
  • How clearly Shawcliffe explains next steps
  • How often clients receive updates
  • How delays are handled
  • How mistakes are handled
  • How feedback is collected
  • How launch feels
  • How training feels
  • How support is explained
  • How boundaries are maintained
  • How clients are asked for reviews and referrals

The internal rule:

Clients should never have to wonder what is happening, what is needed from them, what happens next, or whether Shawcliffe forgot about them.

23.2 Client Experience Philosophy

Shawcliffe Digital should feel like a small, caring, competent, local agency.

Not corporate.

Not chaotic.

Not fake.

Not pushy.

Not casual to the point of being sloppy.

The desired client feeling:

“These people understand my business, they are honest with me, they are organized, and they are building something useful.”

Shawcliffe’s Client Experience Promise

Shawcliffe should aim to give clients:

  • Clear communication
  • Honest recommendations
  • Practical systems
  • Defined scope
  • Organized process
  • Respectful follow-up
  • No fake guarantees
  • No surprise fees
  • No mystery timelines
  • No disappearing after launch
  • Support options that make sense

23.3 Communication Tone

Curtis should sound like a trusted local advisor.

The tone should be:

ToneMeaning
Plain-EnglishNo unnecessary jargon
RespectfulTreat owner-operators seriously
CalmDo not create panic
HonestDo not overpromise
PracticalFocus on what helps the business
WarmHuman and personable
ClearNext steps are obvious
Firm when neededBoundaries are part of professionalism

What Shawcliffe Should Sound Like

“Here is what we recommend, here is why, here is what is included, here is what is not included, and here is the next step.”

What Shawcliffe Should Avoid

AvoidBetter Instead
“No worries, we can do anything.”“We can look at that, but it may be an add-on.”
“This will definitely get you leads.”“This makes it easier for interested customers to take action.”
“That is easy.”“That may be straightforward, but we should scope it properly.”
“I’ll just squeeze it in.”“I’ll add it to the revision list and confirm whether it is included.”
“Sorry, we’re super busy.”“Thanks for your patience. Here is the current status and next step.”
“That’s not my problem.”“That part is outside the current scope, but here are your options.”

23.4 Client Expectations

Client experience improves when expectations are set early.

Clients should know:

  • What Shawcliffe does
  • What Shawcliffe does not do
  • What the process looks like
  • What the client must provide
  • How communication works
  • How revisions work
  • How support works
  • What costs extra
  • What can delay the project
  • What happens after launch

Client Expectation Script

We try to keep projects very clear. Before we build, we define what is included, what is not included, what we need from you, how many revision rounds are included, and what support looks like after launch. That way there are fewer surprises.

23.5 What Clients Should Never Have to Wonder

A good client experience means clients should not wonder:

Client QuestionShawcliffe Should Answer
Did they receive my message?Acknowledge important messages
What stage is the project in?Send status updates
What do they need from me?Use onboarding/checklists
When will I see something?Explain next stage
Is this included?Refer to scope
What happens after launch?Explain support
Who do I contact?Provide support channel
What do I owe?Clear invoices/payment terms
Why is this delayed?Explain blocker
How do I use this?Provide training/handoff

23.6 Update Cadence

Clients do not need constant updates.

They need predictable updates.

Recommended Update Cadence

Project StageUpdate Frequency
Proposal sentFollow up after 3–5 business days
OnboardingUpdate when missing items are needed
BuildWeekly update for active builds
Client reviewClear review instructions
RevisionsUpdate when revision list is confirmed
Final QAUpdate before launch
Launch prepUpdate when final approval/payment needed
After launchLaunch message + training/support handoff
Support planMonthly or as plan defines

Simple Weekly Project Update

Hi [Client Name],

Quick update on your [system name]:

  • Current stage: [stage]
  • Completed this week: [item]
  • We are working on: [item]
  • Still needed from you: [item, if any]
  • Next step: [item]

Thanks,
Curtis

No-Update Problem

If there is no visible update, still communicate.

Example:

Hi [Client Name],

Quick update: we are still in the [stage] stage. There is no major action needed from you today, but the next step is [next step]. I’ll let you know when we are ready for [review/content/approval/launch].

Thanks,
Curtis

23.7 Response Expectations

Shawcliffe should not accidentally create a 24/7 expectation.

General Response Expectation

We respond during normal working hours as soon as reasonably possible. True system issues are prioritized over general updates or new feature ideas.

Suggested Client-Facing Language

We do our best to reply promptly during normal working hours. If something is urgent because the live system is down, a form is broken, or customers cannot use an important feature, please mark it clearly as urgent.

Internal Rule

Do not train clients to expect instant replies to non-urgent messages.

Being kind does not mean being constantly available.

23.8 Meeting Etiquette

Meetings should be useful, not endless.

Meeting Rules

  • Have a purpose.
  • Have a rough agenda.
  • Start on time.
  • End with next steps.
  • Confirm who owns each task.
  • Write down decisions.
  • Avoid solving large new scope live without pricing.
  • Follow up with a summary.

Discovery Meeting Opening

Thanks for meeting with me. The goal today is to understand your business, how customers currently contact you, what is getting messy, and what kind of simple system might actually help.

Client Review Meeting Opening

Today we are reviewing the draft against the approved scope. We’ll focus on accuracy, customer flow, content, forms, and any corrections needed before launch.

Support Meeting Opening

Today we’ll focus on the support issue or improvement request you sent in. If we discover that it is outside the current support plan, I’ll explain the options before any extra work is done.

Meeting Follow-Up Template

Hi [Client Name],

Thanks for meeting today.

Here is the summary:

  • We discussed: [summary]
  • Decisions made: [decisions]
  • Shawcliffe will: [tasks]
  • You will: [client tasks]
  • Next step: [next step]

Thanks,
Curtis

23.9 Communication Channels

Use channels intentionally.

Channel Rules

ChannelUse For
EmailApprovals, proposals, summaries, support
Phone/video callDiscovery, review, training, complex issues
TextQuick scheduling or simple updates only
Project formOnboarding/support intake
Shared folderAssets/content
Support emailPost-launch support

Avoid

  • Scattered feedback across texts, calls, DMs, and random emails
  • Verbal approvals with no written record
  • Important passwords in text messages
  • Client sending assets one at a time in multiple channels
  • Major scope changes by casual message

Client Communication Boundary

To keep the project organized, important feedback, approvals, support requests, and change requests need to be written down in the agreed channel.

23.10 Welcome Experience

The welcome message sets the tone.

After the client accepts, they should feel guided.

Welcome Message

Hi [Client Name],

Thanks for moving forward with Shawcliffe Digital. We are excited to help build your [system name].

Here is what happens next:

  • We confirm payment/start terms.
  • We collect your business information, services/products, photos, policies, and access.
  • We confirm the project is ready for build.
  • We build the system.
  • We review internally.
  • You review and send organized feedback.
  • We complete agreed revisions.
  • We test and launch.
  • We train you and move into support if selected.

I’ll send the onboarding checklist next so we can collect everything in one place.

Thanks,
Curtis

23.11 Onboarding Communication

Onboarding should feel structured, not overwhelming.

Onboarding Message

Hi [Client Name],

The next step is onboarding.

This is where we collect the information needed to build properly:

  • Business details
  • Services/products and prices
  • Photos/logo
  • Policies
  • Google review link
  • Domain/hosting access if needed
  • Notification contacts
  • Dashboard user details if included

Please use the checklist/form/folder provided so everything stays organized.

If you do not have everything ready, send what you have and we’ll identify what is missing.

Thanks,
Curtis

Missing Content Message

Hi [Client Name],

We have enough to move forward with some parts of the project, but we are still missing:

  • [Item]
  • [Item]
  • [Item]

These affect [specific part of project].

We can either pause that part, use placeholder/simple wording where appropriate, or move it to a later phase.

Thanks,
Curtis

23.12 Explaining Delays

Delays should be explained early and calmly.

Do not disappear.

Common Delay Causes

Delay CauseExplanation
Missing contentClient has not sent needed info
Missing accessDomain/hosting/tool access not ready
Scope changeNew request needs review/pricing
Third-party issueOutside tool/provider problem
Technical issueBuild needs extra testing/fix
Client review delayWaiting for feedback/approval
Payment delayWork/launch paused
Availability issueUse professionally and sparingly

Delay Message: Missing Client Materials

Hi [Client Name],

Quick update: the project is currently waiting on [missing item].

This affects [specific part of project], so we cannot complete that section accurately without it.

Once we receive it, we can continue with the next step.

Thanks,
Curtis

Delay Message: Technical Issue

Hi [Client Name],

Quick update: we found a technical issue with [feature/workflow] during testing.

We are looking into it before sending it for review/launch because we do not want you or your customers to find the issue first.

I’ll update you once it is resolved or if it affects the scope/timeline.

Thanks,
Curtis

Delay Message: Scope Change

Hi [Client Name],

The new request you mentioned would change the original scope.

It may be a useful addition, but we need to review it separately so we can confirm cost and timeline before building it.

For now, we can either keep the current launch scope as planned or quote this as an add-on.

Thanks,
Curtis

23.13 Handling Mistakes

Mistakes will happen.

The client experience depends on how Shawcliffe handles them.

Mistake Handling Philosophy

Do not hide.

Do not blame.

Do not over-apologize in a way that creates panic.

Do:

  • Acknowledge
  • Explain briefly
  • Take responsibility where appropriate
  • State the fix
  • State the next step
  • Record the lesson internally

Mistake Response Template

Hi [Client Name],

Thanks for catching that.

You’re right — [brief description of issue].

We’re going to [fix/action]. I’ll let you know once it is corrected.

Thanks for your patience,
Curtis

Bigger Mistake Template

Hi [Client Name],

I want to be upfront. We found an issue with [feature/workflow].

The issue is [brief explanation]. It affects [impact].

We are working on [solution]. Before launch, we will retest [specific items] to make sure it is working properly.

I’ll keep you updated.

Thanks,
Curtis

Internal Mistake Review

After a mistake, ask:

  • Was this a communication issue?
  • Was this a QA issue?
  • Was this an onboarding issue?
  • Was this a scope issue?
  • Was this a technical issue?
  • What checklist should be updated?
  • What template should be improved?

23.14 Client Review Process

Client review must be structured.

Do not ask:

“What do you think?”

That invites vague feedback.

Ask for specific review.

Client Review Message

Hi [Client Name],

The first draft of your [system name] is ready for review.

Please review it with these questions in mind:

  • Is the business information correct?
  • Are services/products and prices correct?
  • Are hours, location, and contact details correct?
  • Does the main customer action make sense?
  • Are the form questions correct?
  • Are photos/logo/details correct?
  • Is anything spelled wrong?
  • If a dashboard is included, do the editable fields make sense?

Please send feedback in one organized message if possible.

This review round is for corrections and adjustments within the approved scope. New features or larger changes can be discussed, but may be treated as add-ons or saved for Phase 2.

Thanks,
Curtis

Client Review Rules

  • Ask for organized feedback.
  • Remind client of revision scope.
  • Sort feedback before sending to Cassandra.
  • Separate corrections from add-ons.
  • Confirm unclear feedback.
  • Track revision round.
  • Do not let review become a new discovery phase.

23.15 Revision Communication

Revisions should feel controlled and fair.

Revision Confirmation Message

Hi [Client Name],

Thanks for the feedback.

I’ve organized the revision list as follows:

Included in this revision round:

  • [Item]
  • [Item]

Needs clarification:

  • [Item]

Outside current scope / possible add-on:

  • [Item]

Future improvement idea:

  • [Item]

We’ll handle the included items first and confirm anything else before building.

Thanks,
Curtis

Revision Completed Message

Hi [Client Name],

The agreed revisions have been completed.

Please review the updated version and let me know if the included changes look correct.

At this stage, we are checking that the agreed revisions were completed properly before moving into final QA/launch prep.

Thanks,
Curtis

23.16 Training Experience

Training should make the client feel capable.

Do not overwhelm them.

Training Philosophy

The client does not need to understand the technical system.

They need to know:

  • What link to use
  • How to log in if needed
  • What they can update
  • What they should not touch
  • How leads/bookings/requests arrive
  • How to respond
  • How to ask for support
  • What is included in support

Training Message

Hi [Client Name],

Now that your [system name] is live/ready, the next step is training.

The goal is to show you only what you need for day-to-day use:

  • How customers use the system
  • Where requests go
  • How notifications work
  • How to update the dashboard if included
  • How to use review links/QR codes if included
  • How to ask for support

We’ll keep it practical.

Thanks,
Curtis

Training Checklist

ItemCovered?
Live link
Customer flow
Form/request process
Owner notifications
Dashboard login if included
Dashboard updates if included
Review link/QR if included
Payment/deposit process if included
What not to touch
Support channel
What is included in support
What costs extra

Training Tone

Use phrases like:

  • “You do not need to know the technical side.”
  • “Here are the only things you need to use.”
  • “This is what customers will see.”
  • “This is what you will receive.”
  • “This is where you go if you need help.”
  • “If you want to add features later, we can treat that as Phase 2.”

23.17 Launch Experience

Launch should feel like a meaningful handoff, not just a link tossed over.

Launch Message

Hi [Client Name],

Your [system name] is now live.

We tested the main customer flow, including:

  • [Form/status/booking/quote workflow]
  • Notifications
  • Mobile view
  • Review link/QR if included
  • Dashboard if included

Here is the live link:

[Link]

The next step is training/handoff so you know how to use the system and how support works.

Thanks,
Curtis

Launch Follow-Up

Hi [Client Name],

Just checking in after launch.

A few quick questions:

  • Have you had a chance to use the system?
  • Did any customer requests come through?
  • Did notifications arrive properly?
  • Is anything confusing?
  • Is there anything small that needs correcting?

Thanks,
Curtis

Launch Experience Rule

Launch is not complete until the client knows how to use the system and how support works.

23.18 Support Experience

Support should make clients feel cared for without creating unlimited access.

Support Experience Principles

PrincipleMeaning
One clear channelSupport requests do not get lost
Categorize requestsBug, update, training, add-on
Set expectationsNot everything is urgent
Protect developmentCurtis triages before Cassandra
Explain boundariesNew features cost extra
Track everythingSupport log
Identify upsellsRepeated needs become offers

Support Welcome Message

Hi [Client Name],

Now that your [system name] is live, support will go through [support channel].

Your current support plan is:

[Plan Name / No monthly plan selected]

Included:

  • [Item]
  • [Item]

Not included unless separately quoted:

  • New features
  • New pages
  • Major design changes
  • New workflows
  • Add-ons outside the original scope

If something is broken, please describe what happened and include a screenshot if possible. If you have a new idea, we can add it to the future improvements list or quote it as an add-on.

Thanks,
Curtis

Support Request Acknowledgement

Hi [Client Name],

Thanks for sending this. I’ve logged the request and will review whether it is a bug, small update, training issue, or new feature/change request.

If we need more information, I’ll follow up.

Thanks,
Curtis

23.19 Making Clients Feel Cared For Without Unlimited Support

This is the balance Shawcliffe needs.

Clients should feel:

  • Remembered
  • Respected
  • Guided
  • Supported
  • Not abandoned

But not entitled to unlimited unpaid labour.

Ways to Make Clients Feel Cared For

Care ActionBoundary
Send clear updatesDo not update constantly
Provide checklistClient still must complete homework
Give trainingNot unlimited retraining forever
Offer post-launch check-inNot free monthly consulting unless plan
Keep future improvements listDo not build for free
Explain optionsDo not absorb cost
Respond warmlyDo not promise instant availability
Give small helpful adviceDo not provide full strategy unpaid

Caring Boundary Script

I want to help with that, and I also want to keep the project organized. That request is outside the current scope, so I can either add it to the future improvements list or price it as an add-on.

Another Caring Boundary Script

That is a good idea. I do not want to casually add it and delay launch, so let’s keep the first version focused and revisit that after launch.

23.20 Asking for Reviews and Testimonials

Reviews and testimonials should be requested after the client has experienced value.

Good times to ask:

  • After successful launch
  • After training
  • After first useful lead/booking/request
  • After the client says something positive
  • After solving a support issue well
  • After 30-day check-in

Review Ask Message

Hi [Client Name],

I’m really glad we were able to get your [system name] launched.

If you were happy with the process, a short review for Shawcliffe Digital would mean a lot. It helps other local business owners feel more comfortable reaching out.

Here is the review link:

[Link]

Thanks again,
Curtis

Testimonial Ask

Hi [Client Name],

Would you be comfortable giving us a short testimonial about your experience working with Shawcliffe Digital?

It does not need to be long. Even 1–2 sentences about what was helpful would be useful.

Thanks,
Curtis

Testimonial Prompt for Client

If helpful, you could answer one of these:

  • What was frustrating before?
  • What did Shawcliffe build for you?
  • What feels easier now?
  • What was the process like?
  • Would you recommend us to another local business owner?

Client Said Something Positive

If client says:

“This is exactly what we needed.”

Curtis can reply:

That means a lot. Would you be comfortable if we used that as a short testimonial, or would you prefer to write something slightly different?

23.21 Asking for Referrals

Referrals should be part of the client experience.

Do not ask too early.

Ask after trust is built.

Referral Ask After Launch

Hi [Client Name],

I’m glad we could get this launched for you.

We’re trying to help more local owner-operated businesses with practical systems like quote requests, booking requests, live status pages, review links, and simple dashboards.

If you know another business owner who is dealing with scattered messages, missed inquiries, repeated questions, or messy booking/quote requests, an introduction would mean a lot.

Thanks,
Curtis

Referral Ask After Good Result

Hi [Client Name],

I’m really glad the system is helping.

If anyone comes to mind who could use something similar — a better quote request process, booking system, review flow, or live availability page — I’d be grateful for an introduction.

Referral Thank You

Hi [Client Name],

Thank you for introducing us to [Name]. I really appreciate it.

Introductions like that help us build Shawcliffe through real relationships, which is exactly how we want to grow.

Thanks,
Curtis

23.22 Asking for Case Study Permission

Case studies help Shawcliffe grow, but clients should approve what is shared.

Case Study Ask

Hi [Client Name],

Would you be open to us creating a short case study about your project?

It would explain:

  • What changed after launch
  • Any results or feedback you are comfortable sharing

We would only share details you approve.

Thanks,
Curtis

Case Study Permission Options

Client can approve:

  • Business name shown
  • Business name hidden
  • Screenshots allowed
  • Screenshots not allowed
  • Results shared
  • Results anonymized
  • Testimonial included
  • Testimonial not included

23.23 Client Appreciation

Small gestures matter.

Simple Appreciation Ideas

  • Thank-you email after launch
  • Handwritten card for good clients
  • Small printed QR cards if relevant
  • Free one-page cheat sheet
  • 30-day check-in
  • “Future improvements” note
  • Congratulate client on business milestone
  • Share their business if appropriate and permission-based

Appreciation Message

Hi [Client Name],

Thanks again for trusting us with this project.

We really appreciate the opportunity to help build something useful for your business. It means a lot to us as a small husband-and-wife agency.

Thanks,
Curtis and Cassandra

23.24 Handling Difficult Communication

Some clients will be unclear, emotional, demanding, or scattered.

Curtis should stay calm and bring the conversation back to process.

If Client Sends Scattered Feedback

Hi [Client Name],

Thanks for the notes. To make sure nothing gets missed, could you please send the feedback in one organized list?

I’ll separate what is included in the revision round, what needs clarification, and what would be an add-on or future improvement.

Thanks,
Curtis

If Client Is Upset

Hi [Client Name],

I hear your concern.

Let me review what happened and compare it against the approved scope and current project stage. I’ll come back with a clear explanation and next step.

Thanks,
Curtis

If Client Is Demanding Instant Response

Hi [Client Name],

I understand this feels important.

We handle support and project communication during normal working hours unless a priority support arrangement is in place. I’ve logged the request and will review it according to urgency and support scope.

Thanks,
Curtis

If Client Keeps Expanding Scope

Hi [Client Name],

These are good ideas, but they go beyond the first version we agreed to build.

To keep the project moving, I recommend we launch the agreed version first and place these ideas on the future improvements list. If you want any of them included now, I can quote them as add-ons.

Thanks,
Curtis

23.26 Client Experience Standards by Phase

Sales Phase

Client should feel:

  • Heard
  • Not pressured
  • Clear on what Shawcliffe does
  • Clear on next step

Standard:

Ask good questions before recommending.

Proposal Phase

Client should feel:

  • The proposal matches their business
  • Scope is clear
  • Price is clear
  • Monthly support is explained
  • There are no hidden surprises

Standard:

Every proposal includes included and excluded items.

Onboarding Phase

Client should feel:

  • Guided
  • Clear on homework
  • Not overwhelmed
  • Aware of missing items

Standard:

Use checklist/form/folder.

Build Phase

Client should feel:

  • Shawcliffe is working
  • They are not forgotten
  • Next step is known

Standard:

Send periodic updates.

Review Phase

Client should feel:

  • Invited to review carefully
  • Clear on what feedback is needed
  • Clear on revision boundaries

Standard:

Ask specific review questions.

Launch Phase

Client should feel:

  • Excited
  • Confident
  • Supported
  • Clear on what happens next

Standard:

Launch includes link, testing note, and training/support handoff.

Support Phase

Client should feel:

  • Help is available
  • Support boundaries are clear
  • Requests are tracked
  • New features can be added properly

Standard:

Use support channel and support log.

23.27 How to Make the Experience Feel Premium Without Overdelivering

A premium experience does not always mean more work.

It often means more clarity.

Low-Effort, High-Trust Actions

ActionWhy It Works
Clear welcome emailClient feels guided
Organized checklistClient knows what to send
Weekly updateClient feels remembered
Review instructionsClient gives better feedback
Launch checklistClient trusts quality
Training sheetClient feels capable
Support handoffClient knows boundaries
30-day check-inClient feels cared for
Future improvements listClient sees long-term path
Thank-you noteHuman relationship

Premium Feeling Rule

Professionalism is often just clarity delivered consistently.

23.28 Avoiding Over-Apologizing

Sometimes Shawcliffe will be delayed or make mistakes.

Apologize when appropriate, but do not make every message sound guilty.

Weak

So sorry, we’re super behind and everything is crazy.

Stronger

Thanks for your patience. The project is currently waiting on [item]. The next step is [next step]. I’ll update you when [condition].

Weak

Sorry, sorry, sorry, this is taking longer than expected.

Stronger

This is taking longer than expected because [reason]. We are handling [specific action] before moving to launch so the system is not released with that issue.

23.29 Client Trust Builders

Trust comes from repeated small behaviours.

Trust Builders

  • Send summaries after calls
  • Put decisions in writing
  • Explain what is not included
  • Admit when something is not a good idea
  • Say “I do not know” when needed
  • Do not guarantee results
  • Keep invoices clear
  • Keep project stages clear
  • Test before launch
  • Follow up after launch
  • Protect client from overbuilding
  • Protect Shawcliffe from underpricing

Trust-Damagers

  • Vague promises
  • Missed follow-ups
  • Surprise costs
  • Unclear scope
  • Disappearing during build
  • Ignoring client concerns
  • Launching with obvious bugs
  • Blaming client harshly
  • Saying yes and resenting it later
  • Pretending everything is included

Use this internally after projects.

Score 1–5.

QuestionScore
Did client understand process?

Did client seem cared for?

ScoreMeaning
45–50Excellent experience

Under 25Serious client experience problem

23.31 First Three Offer Client Experience Notes

A. Live Status Starter System

Client experience priorities:

  • Teach owner to update from phone
  • Make status labels clear
  • Explain that accuracy depends on updating
  • Test QR code with client
  • Recommend seasonal support
  • Provide dashboard cheat sheet

Training Must Cover

  • Open/closed status
  • Sold-out status
  • Product availability
  • Prices if editable
  • Location updates
  • QR code use
  • Support process

Client Care Note

Seasonal sellers may be very busy during their active season. Keep communication short and practical.

B. Quote Request Starter System

Client experience priorities:

  • Make quote fields feel useful, not overwhelming
  • Explain that better requests do not replace owner judgment
  • Test photo upload with client
  • Confirm notification email
  • Explain CRM/SMS as future upgrades
  • Review service area carefully

Training Must Cover

  • How quote requests arrive
  • What information is included
  • How to access photos
  • How to respond
  • How review requests work
  • What to do if notification seems missing

Client Care Note

Tradespeople may be busy on job sites. Keep messages direct and action-focused.

C. Booking & Review Starter System

Client experience priorities:

  • Make clear whether booking is requested or confirmed
  • Review service/pricing accuracy carefully
  • Confirm cancellation/no-show wording
  • Test booking request flow
  • Explain review link/QR
  • Explain deposits/reminders as upgrades

Training Must Cover

  • How booking requests arrive
  • How client confirms appointment
  • What customer confirmation says
  • How review link works
  • How to update services/prices if support plan includes it
  • What is not live calendar booking unless scoped

Client Care Note

Personal care businesses often care about presentation and tone. Make the system feel polished and customer-friendly.

23.32 Common Client Experience Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Assuming Silence Feels Fine

Silence often feels like neglect.

Send short updates.

Mistake 2: Asking for Vague Feedback

“What do you think?” creates vague answers.

Ask specific review questions.

Mistake 3: Not Explaining Boundaries Until Conflict

Boundaries should be explained before they are tested.

Mistake 4: Treating Training as Optional

If the client does not know how to use the system, the project feels unfinished.

Mistake 5: Launching Without Support Handoff

Post-launch confusion becomes support conflict.

Mistake 6: Overhelping Without Logging It

Kindness becomes unpaid support if it is not tracked.

Mistake 7: Hiding Delays

Clients can usually handle delays better than uncertainty.

Mistake 8: Overpromising to Be Nice

Overpromising creates future disappointment.

Mistake 9: Not Asking for Reviews

Happy clients may not think to leave one unless asked.

Mistake 10: Not Asking for Referrals

Good clients often know other good clients.

23.33 Minimum Viable Client Experience System

At the beginning, Shawcliffe needs:

  • Welcome email
  • Onboarding checklist
  • Weekly update template
  • Client review instructions
  • Revision summary template
  • Launch message
  • Training checklist
  • Support handoff message
  • Review/testimonial ask
  • Referral ask

That is enough to feel professional.

23.34 Must-Have Now vs Nice-to-Have Later

Must-Have Now

Create immediately:

  • Communication tone guide
  • Client welcome email
  • Onboarding communication template
  • Missing content template
  • Weekly project update template
  • Client review template
  • Revision summary template
  • Launch message
  • Training checklist
  • Support handoff message
  • Review ask template
  • Referral ask template

Nice-to-Have Later

Do not delay sales while waiting for:

  • Full client portal
  • Automated status updates
  • Video training library
  • Fancy onboarding dashboard
  • Formal customer satisfaction surveys
  • Automated review request system for Shawcliffe

Section 24

Risk Management, Quality Control, and Red Flags

24.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Risk Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains how Shawcliffe Digital should identify, prevent, manage, and learn from risk.

Risk does not mean panic.

Risk means:

“What could go wrong, how likely is it, how bad would it be, and what should we do before it becomes expensive, embarrassing, or damaging?”

Shawcliffe’s goal is not to avoid all risk. That is impossible.

The goal is to avoid careless risk.

This section covers:

  • Client risk
  • Project risk
  • Technical risk
  • Financial risk
  • Legal/privacy risk
  • Scope creep risk
  • Support risk
  • Reputation risk
  • Third-party tool risk
  • Launch risk
  • Data/security risk
  • Promises to avoid
  • When to decline projects
  • Red-flag clients
  • Red-flag requests
  • Emergency escalation
  • Incident logging
  • Learning from mistakes
  • Risk notes for the first three offers

The internal rule:

A good project is not only one we can build. A good project is one we can scope, price, launch, support, and stand behind responsibly.

24.2 Risk Management Philosophy

Shawcliffe Digital is a lean husband-and-wife agency.

That means risk matters more, not less.

A large agency can absorb messy clients, unpaid work, failed tools, unclear scope, and support chaos more easily.

Shawcliffe cannot.

The business needs to protect:

  • Time
  • Cash flow
  • Personal schedule
  • Reputation
  • Client trust
  • Cassandra’s development capacity
  • Curtis’s sales credibility
  • Reusable components
  • Future support obligations

Risk management is not about being afraid.

It is about being honest before problems grow.

24.3 The Shawcliffe Risk Filter

Before accepting any project, ask:

  • Do we understand the client’s actual problem?
  • Does this fit one of our archetypes or reusable templates?
  • Can we define the scope clearly?
  • Can we price it properly?
  • Can the client provide the needed content/access?
  • Can Cassandra build it responsibly?
  • Can Curtis manage the client relationship?
  • Can we support it after launch?
  • Does it involve sensitive data or regulated claims?
  • Would we be comfortable showing this project publicly?

If several answers are “no,” slow down.

A clear, respectful client with a simple project is usually manageable.

A chaotic, unrealistic client can make even a simple project miserable.

Client Risk Response

If client risk is moderate:

I think there may be a fit, but we need to keep the first version very clearly scoped. I would recommend starting smaller and defining exactly what is included before anything is built.

If client risk is high:

I do not think this is the right fit for Shawcliffe as currently described. We work best with clear, practical projects where the first version solves a specific business problem.

Project risk happens when the work itself is unclear.

Project Risk Signs

RiskExample

Project Risk Prevention

Use:

  • Discovery

  • Included/excluded components
  • Client onboarding checklist

  • QA checklist
  • Launch checklist
  • Support handoff

Project Risk Rule

If the project cannot be described in one sentence, it is not ready to build.

Example:

Good:

Build a quote request system for a welder so customers can submit job details, location, urgency, and photos.

Bad:

Build a custom app/website/portal thing to modernize the business.

24.8 Technical Risk

Technical risk happens when the build may become fragile, overcomplicated, hard to test, or hard to support.

Technical Risk Signs

RiskExample
Too many integrationsSMS + CRM + payments + calendar + AI
Third-party API dependenceTool changes could break system
Unclear data storageNobody knows where customer info goes
Sensitive file uploadsHealth/legal/financial documents
Complex permissionsMultiple staff roles
Real-time inventoryHard to keep accurate
Payment logicRefunds, deposits, taxes, disputes
Automation chainsSilent failures possible
No testing pathHard to confirm working
No support planTechnical risk unpaid after launch

Technical Risk Prevention

  • Start with simpler version
  • Use known components
  • Avoid unnecessary integrations
  • Test end-to-end
  • Document dependencies
  • Require support for high-risk components
  • Avoid sensitive data unless necessary
  • Price complexity properly
  • Use staging/test mode where possible
  • Document known limitations

Cassandra Technical Risk Review

Before approving a complex project, Cassandra should ask:

  • Have we built something like this before?
  • What components can be reused?
  • What is truly custom?
  • What third-party tools are required?
  • What data is collected/stored?
  • What can fail silently?
  • What needs monitoring?
  • What is the support burden?
  • What must be tested before launch?
  • What should be excluded from starter scope?

Financial risk is a major threat for small agencies.

Financial Boundary Script

We can absolutely move forward once the start payment is received. That is what reserves the build time and moves the project into active work.

Final Payment Script

We are ready for launch once final payment is received and final QA is complete.

24.10 Legal and Privacy Risk

This section is not legal advice.

Shawcliffe should get legal review for contracts, privacy/data handling, subscriptions, liability, and regulated industries.

Legal/privacy risk is higher when Shawcliffe handles:

  • Personal information
  • Customer lists
  • SMS/email marketing
  • Payment flows
  • Health or wellness information
  • Legal/financial/professional intake
  • Children’s information
  • File uploads
  • Sensitive photos
  • Home access/property details
  • Pet medical notes
  • Student records

In Alberta, PIPA is Alberta’s private-sector privacy law for provincially regulated private-sector organizations. PIPEDA applies to many private-sector organizations across Canada that collect, use, or disclose personal information in the course of commercial activity. CASL requirements may apply to commercial electronic messages such as marketing emails and texts.

Legal/Privacy Risk Questions

Ask before collecting data:

  • What personal information is being collected?
  • Is it necessary?
  • Who sees it?
  • Where is it stored?
  • How long is it kept?
  • Is it sensitive?
  • Does the client understand their responsibility?
  • Is consent needed?
  • Does the customer need privacy notice language?
  • Should a lawyer/privacy specialist review this?

Higher-Risk Data

Data TypeRisk
Health informationHigh
Legal documentsHigh
Financial informationHigh
Government IDHigh
Children’s informationHigh
Home access codesHigh
Sensitive photosHigh
Payment detailsHigh
Customer lists for marketingMedium/high
Pet medical/behaviour notesMedium
Property access notesMedium
Vehicle details/VINMedium
Basic name/email/phoneLower but still personal information

Legal/Privacy Risk Prevention

  • Collect minimum necessary information
  • Avoid sensitive data unless clearly needed
  • Use secure tools
  • Use privacy/consent language
  • Make client responsible for regulated content
  • Avoid giving legal compliance advice
  • Require legal review for high-risk projects
  • Document data flow
  • Limit access
  • Use password manager
  • Do not store customer data casually

Privacy Boundary Script

We can help structure the form and workflow, but because this involves personal or sensitive information, we need to be careful about what is collected, where it is stored, and what wording the customer sees. We may need legal/privacy review before building that part.

24.11 CASL / SMS / Email Risk

SMS and email campaigns are powerful but risky.

Commercial electronic messages in Canada generally require consent, sender identification, and an unsubscribe mechanism under CASL guidance from the CRTC.

SMS/Email Risk Signs

RiskExample
No consent processClient uploads random phone numbers
No unsubscribeCustomers cannot opt out
No identificationMessage does not identify business
Too many messagesCustomers get annoyed
Wrong timingReview request before service complete
Poor list qualitySpam complaints
Client wants mass textingCompliance/support risk
No monthly supportFailures go unnoticed

SMS/Email Prevention

  • Use proper consent process
  • Include identification
  • Include unsubscribe where required
  • Keep message purpose clear
  • Avoid importing questionable lists
  • Document client responsibility
  • Require monthly support for SMS/email systems
  • Get legal review for larger campaigns

SMS Boundary Script

SMS can be very effective, but it needs to be handled carefully. We need clear consent, appropriate message wording, and a support plan because SMS has compliance, cost, and deliverability risks.

24.12 Scope Creep Risk

Scope creep is one of the most common agency risks.

It often sounds friendly.

Scope Creep Phrases

  • “Can we just add…”
  • “While you’re in there…”
  • “This should be quick…”
  • “Can we try something different?”
  • “I forgot one thing…”
  • “My friend said we should…”
  • “Can you also do…”
  • “Can we change the whole layout?”
  • “Can you add SMS/payments/CRM?”
  • “Can you update this every week?”

Scope Creep Prevention

  • Clear SOW
  • Included/excluded list
  • Revision limits
  • Change request process
  • Future improvements list
  • Add-on pricing
  • Curtis triage before Cassandra builds
  • Do not verbally agree to features
  • Do not build before approval/payment

Scope Creep Script

That is a good idea, but it is outside the current scope. We can either save it for Phase 2 or price it as an add-on before building it.

Scope Risk Rule

A request is not approved just because the client mentioned it.

Because this system includes active features like [dashboard/forms/notifications/SMS], I recommend a monthly support plan. Without support, future troubleshooting and updates would be quoted separately.

24.18 Promises to Avoid

Some promises create legal, financial, and reputation risk.

Never Promise

PromiseSafer Language
“This will get you more customers.”“This makes it easier for interested customers to take action.”
“You’ll rank on Google.”“We can improve local visibility basics.”
“You’ll get more reviews.”“We can make asking for reviews easier.”
“This will pay for itself.”“A good lead may be worth more than the system, but results vary.”
“This is easy.”“This may be straightforward, but we should scope it.”
“Unlimited support.”“Support is defined by your plan.”
“We can do anything.”“We’ll confirm what is practical and supportable.”
“No downtime.”“We plan launch carefully, but third-party issues can happen.”
“Completely secure.”“We take reasonable precautions.”
“Fully compliant.”“Compliance should be reviewed by a qualified professional.”
“AI will handle everything.”“AI may help with specific workflows, with monitoring.”

Safe Sales Language

  • “The goal is…”
  • “This can help…”
  • “This is designed to…”
  • “A practical first step would be…”
  • “We do not guarantee…”
  • “This depends on…”
  • “We should test that…”
  • “That should be reviewed legally/professionally.”

I do not think we can responsibly do that as requested. There may be legal, privacy, reputation, or support risks. We can look at a safer version, but I do not want to build something that creates problems for you or Shawcliffe.

24.20 When to Decline Projects

Declining a project can be good business.

Decline When

  • Client is disrespectful
  • Scope cannot be defined
  • Budget is far below need
  • Client wants guaranteed results
  • Client requests dishonest/misleading work
  • Client requires expertise Shawcliffe does not have
  • Sensitive data risk is too high
  • Legal/regulatory risk is unclear
  • Technical complexity is beyond support capacity
  • Client refuses payment terms
  • Client expects unlimited support
  • Timeline is unsafe
  • Project distracts from core strategy
  • Cassandra cannot support the build
  • Curtis cannot manage the relationship

Decline Script

Thanks for explaining the project.

After thinking it through, I do not think Shawcliffe Digital is the right fit for this as currently described.

We work best on practical websites, quote request systems, booking request systems, live status systems, review request systems, dashboards, and simple customer systems for local businesses.

I would rather be honest now than take on work we cannot scope, support, or deliver responsibly.

Narrow-Scope Alternative

If you want to simplify this into a smaller first version focused on [specific customer action], there may be a fit. But I would not recommend starting with the full version as described.

Hi [Client Name],

Thanks for flagging this.

This appears to affect [system/function], so we are treating it as urgent.

We are checking:

  • What is affected
  • Whether customers are impacted
  • What immediate fix or workaround is available
  • What needs to be tested after the fix

I’ll update you as soon as we know more.

Thanks,
Curtis

24.24 Learning From Mistakes

  • Which component needs improvement?

Risk management and quality control are connected.

Quality control means Shawcliffe has standards it does not skip.

Universal Quality Standards

Every launched project should have:

  • Notification testing if included
  • Dashboard testing if included
  • Review link testing if included

Speed is good. Skipping QA is not.

24.26 Risk Notes: Live Status Starter System

Main Risks

RiskWhy It Matters
Status inaccurateCustomers may drive out unnecessarily
Owner forgets to updateSystem becomes untrustworthy
Product availability wrongCustomer disappointment
Location wrongCustomers go to wrong place
QR code brokenPhysical marketing fails
Dashboard confusingOwner stops using it
No seasonal supportSystem goes stale
Customer alerts without consentSMS/email risk
Weather/closures not updatedCustomer frustration
Client expects Shawcliffe to update dailySupport creep

Risk Prevention

  • Train owner carefully
  • Dashboard must work on phone
  • Use simple status labels
  • Add “last updated” if useful
  • Test QR code before printing
  • Explain owner responsibility
  • Recommend seasonal support
  • Do not include SMS/email alerts without proper setup
  • Add clear limitations to proposal

Proposal Risk Language

Accuracy of live status, product availability, prices, and location depends on the client updating the system after launch unless Shawcliffe Digital is separately engaged to provide ongoing update support.

Launch Blockers

Do not launch if:

  • Dashboard cannot update status
  • Public page does not reflect updates
  • Location is wrong
  • QR code points to wrong URL
  • Product/pricing info unapproved
  • Owner cannot access dashboard
  • Mobile experience fails

24.27 Risk Notes: Quote Request Starter System

Main Risks

RiskWhy It Matters
Form brokenLeads lost
Notification missingOwner misses job
Photo upload failsQuote details incomplete
Service area wrongPoor-fit leads
Form too longCustomers abandon
Form too vagueOwner still chases details
Client expects automated quoteScope mismatch
Customer expects guaranteed priceConflict
CRM not included but expectedScope creep
Sensitive job/location dataPrivacy/security concern

Risk Prevention

  • Test form end-to-end
  • Verify owner notification
  • Test photo upload on phone
  • Keep form focused
  • Make customer confirmation clear
  • Avoid automated price promises
  • Include “request, not guaranteed quote” wording if needed
  • Clarify CRM/SMS/payments are add-ons
  • Review privacy/data storage if collecting detailed property info

Proposal Risk Language

This system collects quote requests and sends the details to the business owner. It does not automatically generate quotes, guarantee job value, guarantee leads, or replace the owner’s judgment and follow-up.

Launch Blockers

Do not launch if:

  • Quote form does not submit
  • Owner notification fails
  • Photo upload fails if included
  • Customer confirmation missing
  • Service area wrong
  • Contact info wrong
  • Client has not approved quote questions
  • Form implies automatic pricing when not intended

24.28 Risk Notes: Booking & Review Starter System

Main Risks

RiskWhy It Matters
Customer thinks appointment is confirmedScheduling conflict
Booking notification failsMissed appointment request
Services/prices wrongClient/customer conflict
Policy wording missingCancellation/deposit confusion
Review link wrongReputation issue
Client expects calendar syncScope mismatch
Client expects SMS remindersScope creep
No-show/deposit rules unclearMoney conflict

Client does not respond to requestsSystem blamed unfairly

Risk Prevention

  • Use clear “booking request” language
  • Test notification
  • Confirm services/prices
  • Confirm policies before launch
  • Test review link
  • Exclude live calendar unless scoped
  • Exclude SMS/deposits unless scoped
  • Client approves all service/policy wording
  • Avoid writing regulated health claims

Proposal Risk Language

This system collects booking requests. Unless specifically included, it does not automatically confirm appointments, sync with calendars, take deposits, send SMS reminders, or manage cancellations/rescheduling.

Launch Blockers

Do not launch if:

  • Booking form does not submit
  • Owner notification fails
  • Customer confirmation unclear
  • Services/prices unapproved
  • Review link wrong
  • Policy/deposit wording missing when needed
  • Page implies appointment is confirmed when it is only requested

24.33 Risk Communication With Clients

Do not dump internal worry on clients.

Explain risks calmly and practically.

Good Risk Communication

This is possible, but it adds complexity because it depends on [tool/workflow/data]. I recommend we keep it out of the starter version and consider it as Phase 2 once the core system is working.

Privacy Risk Communication

Because this involves more sensitive information, we should be careful about what we collect and where it is stored. We may need proper privacy/legal wording before building that part.

Timeline Risk Communication

That timeline may be tight unless we reduce scope. I would rather launch a smaller version properly than rush a larger version and risk mistakes.

Support Risk Communication

This feature will likely need ongoing support. If we include it, I recommend adding it to a monthly plan rather than treating it as a one-time setup.

24.34 Internal Stoplight System

Use stoplight colours for quick decisions.

Green

Proceed.

  • Clear scope
  • Clear client
  • Clear payment
  • Clear build
  • Low privacy risk
  • Support understood

Yellow

Proceed carefully.

  • Some uncertainty
  • Needs tighter scope
  • Needs legal/privacy review
  • Needs support plan
  • Needs technical review
  • Needs payment clarity

Red

Stop or decline.

  • Dishonest request
  • No budget
  • Abusive client
  • Major privacy/legal risk
  • Unclear scope
  • Unsafe launch
  • Unsupported technical complexity
  • Refuses agreement/payment
  • Wants guarantees

24.35 Red / Yellow / Green Examples

Green Project

A welder wants a quote request form with photos, service area, owner email notification, and review link.

  • Clear problem
  • Clear template
  • Manageable support
  • Low data sensitivity
  • Good starter project

Yellow Project

A wellness provider wants intake forms, file uploads, automated follow-ups, and SMS reminders.

  • Possible
  • Higher privacy/claims risk
  • Needs legal/privacy caution
  • Needs scope reduction
  • Needs support plan

Red Project

A client wants Shawcliffe to scrape phone numbers and mass text promotions without consent.

  • Decline
  • CASL/privacy/reputation risk
  • Not aligned with Shawcliffe values

24.36 Common Risk Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake 1: Ignoring Gut Feelings

If a client feels chaotic before payment, they may be worse after payment.

Mistake 2: Saying Yes Before Cassandra Reviews Technical Risk

Curtis should not sell technical complexity blindly.

Mistake 3: Treating Privacy as “Later”

Privacy should be considered before forms and data collection are built.

Mistake 4: Selling SMS Casually

SMS is not just a feature. It has costs, compliance, consent, and support concerns.

Mistake 5: Launching Without Written Approval

Written approval protects both sides.

Mistake 6: Not Testing Live Systems

Staging success does not equal live success.

Mistake 7: Letting Scope Creep Feel Like Kindness

Unpaid extras become resentment.

Mistake 8: Not Tracking Incidents

If you do not log it, you cannot learn from it.

Mistake 9: Not Declining Bad Fits

A bad-fit client can consume time needed for good clients.

Mistake 10: Guaranteeing Outcomes

Shawcliffe can build better systems. It cannot guarantee customer behaviour.

That is enough to start managing risk professionally.

24.40 Key Takeaways

  • Risk management is not fear. It is responsible business.
  • The biggest risks are usually unclear clients, unclear scope, underpriced support, privacy/data issues, and untested launches.
  • Do not sell vague projects.
  • Do not start serious work without payment and scope.
  • Do not launch with Severity 1 bugs.
  • Do not guarantee leads, rankings, reviews, revenue, or compliance.
  • Do not collect sensitive data casually.
  • SMS/email systems need consent, wording, unsubscribe handling, and support consideration.
  • Third-party tools must be documented and bounded.
  • Bad-fit clients should be declined politely.
  • Every serious incident should improve a checklist, SOP, component, or template.
  • A few clear boundaries now prevent major conflict later.

Section 25

Growth, Hiring, Delegation, and Scaling

25.1 Overview

Shawcliffe Digital Internal Growth Manual

1. Purpose of This Section

This section explains how Shawcliffe Digital can grow from a husband-and-wife agency into a small, organized, profitable agency without becoming chaotic.

Growth does not simply mean:

  • More clients
  • More projects
  • More tools
  • More employees
  • More services
  • More complexity

Good growth means:

Shawcliffe earns more money, serves clients better, protects Curtis and Cassandra’s time, improves systems, and stays true to its practical local-business focus.

The internal rule:

Do not scale chaos. Systematize first, then delegate.

25.2 Growth Philosophy

Shawcliffe Digital should grow carefully.

A small agency can fail by growing too slowly, but it can also fail by growing too quickly.

Bad growth creates:

  • Too many clients
  • Too much support
  • Too many custom promises
  • Cassandra overloaded with development
  • Curtis buried in admin instead of sales
  • Poor QA
  • Messy communication
  • Undertrained contractors
  • Inconsistent client experience
  • Low-profit projects
  • Personal stress

Good growth creates:

  • More recurring revenue
  • More reusable components
  • Better templates
  • Clearer sales offers
  • Better project margins
  • Better client experience
  • Less repeated work
  • More protected development time
  • More time for Curtis to sell
  • More stability for the business

25.3 What Shawcliffe Is Scaling

Shawcliffe should not simply scale “custom work.”

Shawcliffe should scale a repeatable model.

The Model

Shawcliffe sells:

  • Practical business systems
  • Built from reusable components
  • Packaged into archetype templates
  • Sold through clear starter offers
  • Supported with monthly plans
  • Improved through real client feedback

What Should Scale

Scale ThisWhy
Reusable componentsFaster builds
Archetype templatesEasier sales and delivery
Discovery processBetter qualification
Proposal processFaster closing
QA processFewer mistakes
Support plansRecurring revenue
Client experienceReferrals and trust
DocumentationEasier delegation
Sales pipelinePredictable growth
Case studiesBetter proof

What Should Not Scale

Do Not ScaleWhy
Vague custom projectsHard to price/support
Free supportDestroys profitability
Scattered communicationCreates chaos
Unclear scopeCauses disputes
Underpriced buildsBurns out team
One-off unsupported featuresCreates maintenance problems

Hiring before processCreates more management work

25.4 Growth Stages

Shawcliffe should think in stages.

Do not try to become a full agency immediately.

Stage 1: Husband-and-Wife Foundation

Main Goal

Get real clients, prove offers, document process.

Team

  • Curtis: sales, discovery, PM, client communication, support intake
  • Cassandra: development, technical build, deployment, technical QA

Focus

  • First 3 offers
  • First few clients
  • Basic support plans
  • Component documentation
  • Case studies
  • Pricing validation

Danger

Trying to do too much too soon.

Stage 2: Repeatable Delivery

Main Goal

Deliver similar projects faster and more profitably.

Team

Still mostly Curtis and Cassandra.

May use occasional contractor for small tasks.

Focus

  • Better templates
  • Better onboarding
  • Better QA
  • Better project board
  • Better pricing
  • More MRR
  • Reduce custom chaos

Danger

Taking on too many one-off projects before systems are mature.

Stage 3: Contractor Support

Main Goal

Delegate repeatable tasks that do not require Curtis or Cassandra personally.

Possible Contractors

  • Designer
  • Copywriter
  • Virtual assistant
  • QA tester
  • No-code/helper developer
  • SEO/local listings assistant
  • Bookkeeper
  • Video/demo editor

Focus

  • Protect Cassandra’s development time
  • Free Curtis for sales
  • Improve speed
  • Maintain quality
  • Avoid overhiring

Danger

Hiring people before SOPs exist.

Stage 4: Small Agency Team

Main Goal

Create a small team around sales, delivery, support, and operations.

Possible Roles

  • Project coordinator
  • Support assistant
  • Junior developer
  • Designer
  • Copywriter/content specialist
  • Local SEO/review specialist
  • Part-time bookkeeper/admin

Focus

  • Client experience consistency
  • Quality control
  • Recurring revenue
  • More standardized offers
  • Better internal training

Danger

Losing the Shawcliffe personal touch.

Stage 5: Productized Agency / Systems Studio

Main Goal

Sell and support repeatable systems at higher volume.

Focus

  • Productized templates
  • Strong component library
  • Subscription-style systems
  • Local-business verticals
  • Strong support tiers
  • Case studies
  • Better automation
  • Selective custom work

Danger

Becoming too generic or too complex.

25.9 Contractor vs Employee

Early on, contractors usually make more sense than employees.

Contractor

Best for:

  • Specific projects
  • Part-time help
  • Specialized skills
  • Low commitment
  • Testing a role
  • Overflow work

Examples:

  • Designer
  • Copywriter
  • QA tester
  • Bookkeeper
  • VA
  • Video editor
  • SEO specialist
  • Junior dev for defined tasks

Employee

Best when:

  • Work is consistent
  • Role is core
  • Processes are clear
  • Revenue is stable
  • Management capacity exists
  • Quality standards are documented
  • You need long-term commitment

Internal Rule

Use contractors to test roles before hiring employees.

25.10 When to Hire Contractors

Hire a contractor when:

  • The task repeats.
  • The task has clear instructions.
  • The task does not require founder judgment.
  • The task is slowing revenue or delivery.
  • The task can be checked for quality.
  • The contractor cost is less than the opportunity cost.
  • Shawcliffe has enough cash or MRR to pay comfortably.
  • There is a clear outcome.
  • The contractor will not create more work than they remove.
  • There is an SOP or checklist.

Contractor Readiness Checklist

QuestionPass?
Is the task clearly defined?
Is there an SOP/checklist?
Is there an example of good work?
Is there an example of bad work?
Can Curtis/Cassandra review it quickly?
Is access limited to what they need?
Is budget approved?
Is deadline clear?
Is ownership/confidentiality clear?
Is payment structure clear?

25.13 Delegation Process

Delegation should be structured.

Delegation Steps

  • Identify repeated task.
  • Document current process.
  • Create checklist.
  • Create example output.
  • Decide quality standard.
  • Assign small test task.
  • Review work.
  • Give feedback.
  • Improve SOP.
  • Delegate larger version only after quality is proven.

Delegation Script

Here is the task, here is why it matters, here is the checklist, here is an example of good work, here is what to avoid, and here is when to ask before continuing.

Delegation Rule

Start with small tasks and review carefully.

Do not hand over a whole client relationship or major build process immediately.

25.14 Quality Control for Delegated Work

Delegation does not remove responsibility.

Shawcliffe remains responsible for quality.

QC Checklist for Delegated Work

QuestionPass?
Was the task completed according to SOP?
Are files named correctly?
Is client information accurate?
Is scope respected?
Are links working?
Is the tone correct?
Are there privacy/access concerns?
Does Curtis need to review before client sees?
Does Cassandra need technical review?
Should SOP be updated?

QC Rule

No contractor work goes directly to client without Shawcliffe review until trust and standards are proven.

25.15 Preserving Shawcliffe’s Client Experience

As Shawcliffe grows, the danger is losing the warm, clear, honest client experience.

Client Experience Standards That Must Stay

StandardWhy
Plain-English communicationOwner-operators understand

Clear scopePrevents conflict
Warm toneFits husband-wife brand
Practical systemsCore positioning
No fake guaranteesEthical foundation

Founder-level careReferral strength

What Should Not Change With Growth

Shawcliffe should still feel:

  • Local
  • Practical
  • Human
  • Honest
  • Clear
  • Family-run in spirit
  • Systems-focused

Even if contractors help behind the scenes.

Client Experience Rule

Delegation should make the client experience more consistent, not more distant.

25.16 Protecting Cassandra’s Development Time

Cassandra’s development time is one of Shawcliffe’s most valuable resources.

It must be protected.

What Steals Cassandra’s Time

  • Raw client requests
  • Unclear scope
  • Missing content
  • Vague feedback
  • Constant interruptions
  • Underpriced custom features
  • Rebuilding similar components
  • Support requests not triaged
  • Client changes sent directly to her
  • Urgent work caused by poor planning

Protection Rules

  • Curtis triages client requests.
  • Build handoff must be clear.
  • Cassandra should not chase client content.
  • Scope changes go through Curtis.
  • Support requests go through support intake.
  • QA checklists reduce repeated debugging.
  • Components should be documented.
  • Deep work time should be blocked.
  • Rush work must be priced or declined.
  • Cassandra reviews technical risk before promises.

Cassandra Time Protection Script

Internal:

This request is not ready for Cassandra yet. Curtis needs to clarify scope, content, budget, or client approval first.

Curtis’s highest-value role is bringing in and shaping good opportunities.

Admin can swallow this if not controlled.

What Steals Curtis’s Sales Time

  • File organization
  • Rewriting emails from scratch
  • Chasing missing content
  • Invoice follow-up
  • Lead research
  • Proposal formatting
  • Support requests
  • Scheduling
  • Updating trackers
  • Re-explaining process
  • Searching for old decisions

ProblemSolution

Proposals slowUse proposal template

Curtis should spend protected time every week on lead generation, follow-up, discovery, and referrals.

25.18 Recurring Revenue and Hiring

Recurring revenue makes hiring safer.

Do not hire based only on one-time project spikes.

Why MRR Matters for Hiring

MRR helps cover:

  • Contractors
  • Support staff
  • Tools
  • Bookkeeping
  • Admin help
  • Marketing help
  • Slow sales months
  • Software subscriptions
  • Buffer for mistakes

Hiring From MRR

A simple rule:

Do not commit to recurring labour unless recurring revenue can support it.

Conservative Hiring Guide

MRR LevelPossible Move
$0–$1,000Avoid recurring hires; use occasional contractors
$1,000–$2,500Consider bookkeeper/one-off admin help
$2,500–$5,000Part-time VA or QA help may be possible
$5,000–$10,000More regular contractor support possible
$10,000+Consider part-time roles around support/delivery
$20,000+Small team structure becomes more realistic

Contractor Budget Rule

Contractor cost should either free founder time for higher-value work or directly help deliver profitable client work.

25.19 Avoiding Overhiring

Overhiring creates stress.

Hiring someone does not automatically remove work.

It adds:

  • Recruiting
  • Training
  • Management
  • Quality review
  • Payroll/payment
  • Communication
  • Process documentation
  • Access/security concerns

Signs You Are Not Ready to Hire

  • No clear SOP
  • No consistent work volume
  • No cash buffer
  • No clear role
  • No quality standard
  • No time to train
  • No way to measure success
  • Curtis/Cassandra still changing process weekly
  • You want to hire because you feel overwhelmed but cannot define the task

Overhiring Prevention

  • Use contractors first.
  • Start with small test tasks.
  • Hire for a specific bottleneck.
  • Avoid vague “help with everything” roles.
  • Keep access limited.
  • Review cost monthly.
  • Stop work if contractor does not save time or improve output.

25.20 Avoiding Tool and Process Bloat

Growth often tempts businesses into unnecessary software.

Tool Bloat Signs

  • Paying for tools not used
  • Same information in multiple places
  • More admin than delivery
  • Team confused where work lives
  • Tool chosen before process exists
  • Automation added before workflow is stable
  • Reports nobody reads
  • Fancy dashboards with stale data

Tool Decision Filter

Before adding a tool, ask:

  • What problem does this solve?
  • Do we already have a tool for this?
  • Who will update it?
  • How often will we use it?
  • Does it save more time than it costs?
  • Will it confuse Curtis or Cassandra?
  • Does it improve sales, delivery, support, or finance?
  • Can we start with a simpler version?

Tool Rule

Add tools to support a working process. Do not use tools to avoid defining the process.

Phase 1: Prove the First Offers

Focus

Do Not Focus On Yet

  • Too many services
  • Complex automation
  • Enterprise systems
  • Perfect internal tools

Success Looks Like

  • 1–3 paid clients
  • 1 successful launch
  • 1 testimonial
  • First support plan
  • Lessons documented

Phase 2: Document and Repeat

Goal

Make delivery repeatable.

Focus

  • SOPs
  • Component documentation
  • QA checklists
  • Offer pages
  • Sales scripts
  • Proposal templates
  • Support process
  • Pricing refinement

Do Not Focus On Yet

  • Full-time hires
  • Complex custom builds
  • Too many archetypes
  • Full product subscriptions unless ready

Success Looks Like

  • 3–5 launched projects
  • 3 documented templates
  • 12 priority components documented
  • Basic MRR tracker
  • Improved proposals

Phase 3: Add Contractor Help

Goal

Remove bottlenecks.

First Contractor Options

  • Bookkeeper
  • VA/admin assistant
  • Designer
  • QA tester
  • Copywriter

Success Looks Like

  • Curtis has more sales time
  • Cassandra has more development time

  • Contractor output is reviewed and useful
  • SOPs improve

Phase 4: Build Recurring Revenue Base

Goal

Stabilize income with support plans.

Focus

  • Standard Care
  • Growth Support
  • Seasonal Support
  • Review support
  • GBP/local SEO support
  • Dashboard support
  • CRM Lite support

Success Looks Like
